June's figure will be welcomed by new Prime Minister Andy Burnham and his government, but analysts warn the fall is temporary, as higher energy prices in July are expected to push inflation back up.

Lower fuel costs - particularly lower diesel prices - also pushed inflation down, with prices at the pump falling for the first time since the start of the war in the Middle East.

Clothing costs fell as well due to the summer sales, with many retailers offering larger discounts than last year.

News.title: More young women in their 20s are getting type 2 diabetes
News.content:
England is seeing a "worrying increase" in young women in their 20s developing type 2 diabetes, experts at Imperial College London have warned.

The rise has largely occurred since the Covid pandemic and is closely linked to increasing obesity levels, according to an analysis of NHS data from 2011 to 2024, external.

Type 2 diabetes is serious, and can lead to severe complications, such as heart attacks and strokes.

When it develops at a younger age, the disease tends to be more aggressive, raising the risk of devastating complications and cutting lives short, according to Diabetes UK.

News.title: No helicopters to fight wildfires as 'crisis management' plans activated in Wales
News.content:
The Welsh government has activated "crisis management arrangements" due to the number of wildfires across the nation.

It comes amid criticism from residents over a lack of resources like helicopters to tackle the fires, some of which have been burning for days across north and south Wales.

The Welsh government said North Wales Fire and Rescue had received extra resources but aerial support was not available anywhere in the UK.

However, it said "urgent discussions are now underway both within Wales and at a UK level to identify how this can be resolved".

Meanwhile, firefighters are tackling a big blaze in south Wales for a third day, with the smoke travelling 30 miles (48km) away.

A 4,000-name petition calling for aerial help was prompted by one fire spreading into Coed y Brenin in Conwy county.

The Welsh government said the most effective means of fighting wildfires "was at ground level, and that is exactly what our firefighters are doing with great skill and dedication".

North Wales Fire and Rescue Service said crews were continuing to deal with a wildfire at Capelulo near Sychnant Pass, in the wake of a large grass fire on Conwy Mountain.

There is also a multi-agency response following a blaze on Rhinogydd mountains in Gwynedd, where householders have been advised to keep windows and doors closed.

Elsewhere, firefighters are dealing with grass fires at Hope Mountain and Brymbo in Wrexham county, Pentrefelin, Holyhead, and Pentre Halkyn, overlooking the A55 in Flintshire.

News.title: Over £100,000 raised for boy, 3, in croc attack
News.content:
More than Â£100,000 has been raised for a three-year-old boy who was attacked in a crocodile enclosure.

The boy was visiting Johnsons of Old Hurst near Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, on 18 June when he was attacked by at least one of the animals.

A fundraising page has raised Â£105,000 for the boy and his family after the three-year-old was taken to Addenbrooke's Hospital, where he has undergone seven surgeries.

Cambridgeshire Police arrested and bailed a 30-year-old man from Norfolk on suspicion of attempted murder after the incident.

News.title: Liverpool issue bans as £1.2m seized from ticket touts
News.content:
Liverpool have issued over 400 lifetime bans after more than Â£1.2m of assets relating to the illegal selling of tickets was seized by police.

The club worked with Merseyside Police to seize the assets from organised ticket touts.

The police operation focused on the laundering of criminal proceeds from illicit ticket sales and took place alongside the club's crackdown on ticket touting, both online and in the ground.

The club has since issued 432 lifetime bans to the guilty parties, as well as 115 indefinite suspensions.

Detective Chief Inspector Nick Suffield said: "This is a fantastic example of partnership working between ourselves and Liverpool Football Club for the good of the fans and the general public.

"We will always take action to protect genuine fans who fall victim to touts when all they are trying to do is simply purchase tickets to support their team."

From the assets seized, the money was split between Merseyside Police and the Home Office.

Last year, BBC Sport revealed Liverpool had shut down 145,000 ticket accounts over the previous two years as part of a crackdown on touting.

And last season alone, Liverpool analysed almost 700,000 ticket registrations, with 67,663 suspected fake accounts blocked or cancelled, and a further 121,379 accounts currently under investigation.

A further 3,847 tickets were cancelled for suspicious purchase activity in the 2025-26 season. They were put back on sale as general admission tickets, increasing the number available for genuine fans.

There was also a significant increase in targeted stops carried out on matchdays by the club, who prevented access to the turnstiles for accounts with suspicious activity.

These stops were carried out at Anfield â an average of 300 per home game â and at away games both in the Premier League and in Europe.

News.title: Mid-air 10-person brawl halts easyJet   flight
News.content:
A mid-air brawl involving around 10 passengers forced a Liverpool-bound easyJet plane to fly back to Tenerife, according to air traffic control.

The captain decided to return to the Spanish island about 30 minutes after departure "due to the danger" the fight "posed to the safety of the flight", the air traffic controller said.

Police met flight EZY3352 when it touched down at Tenerife South airport on Tuesday evening, per the crew's request.

The 186-passenger aircraft then continued to Liverpool.

The air traffic controller said in its statement, originally written in Spanish: "Our full support goes out to the crews and passengers who are increasingly having to endure these situations."

EasyJet said the plane "returned to the airport and was met by police due to a group of passengers behaving disruptively.

News.title: Former Lloyd's of London boss's relationship breached rules, firm says
News.content:
Lloyd's of London's former boss's close relationship with another director breached compliance rules, the insurance market has said after an internal investigation.

Former chief executive John Neal and former corporate affairs director Rebekah Clement's relationship was "sufficiently close... that it could be viewed as creating a perceived conflict of interest", the firm said.

Lloyd's said the pair breached compliance rules by not disclosing their relationship but found no conclusive evidence they had a romantic relationship while at Lloyd's.

Neal told the Financial Times all parties can now move on. Clement's lawyer said she is considering legal action.

"Rebekah is hugely disappointed with Lloyd's conduct over the course of this investigation, the nature and length of which have caused her unnecessary stress and significant reputational damage relative to its 'findings'," Clement's lawyer added.

"She is not surprised that Lloyd's found no evidence of an inappropriate relationship with John Neal, nor any evidence of any failings in her promotion. She also co-operated with the investigation throughout.

"Yet, Lloyd's has still chosen to find against Rebekah, on the pretext of 'perception', the source of which was rumour, gossip and innuendo."

The BBC has contacted Neal for comment. He told the Financial Times:, external "I am pleased, but not at all surprised, that the investigation found there was no inappropriate relationship.

"I would have hoped less time and resource had been spent in reaching a conclusion on the central question that was, in truth, never in doubt.

"I am disappointed with the other findings and do not accept them."

Lloyd's said on Wednesday that it first received "certain whistleblowing reports" in November 2023 but that it didn't act on them.

It said its chairman Sir Charles Roxburgh judged this to be a governance failure and informed the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) about it in October 2025.

Lloyd's said it could not share the nature of these allegations or the identities of the people involved.

In November 2025, Lloyd's said Sir Charles became aware of "new information related to an alleged personal relationship" between Neal and Clement and "immediately launched an expanded investigation into the matter".

Lloyd's said its investigation was hampered by the fact that Neal and Clement had both left the company and refused to answer questions, but Lloyd's said it interviewed nearly 40 witnesses in its probe.

It added that it has kept the FCA informed throughout the process.

Sir Charles said on Wednesday: "Based on the findings of this investigation, we have concluded that the conduct of the former chief executive fell significantly below the standards expected of him."

He added the investigation "established serious failings in the governance standards and in following processes, most worryingly in the handling of whistleblowing reports. These were serious failures that should never have been allowed to happen."

Lloyd's history as a City institution stretches back well over 300 years, with its first recorded mention appearing in 1688.

News.title: Glasgow School of Art cannot afford to restore fire-hit Mackintosh building
News.content:
Glasgow School of Art says it cannot fully restore the city's iconic Mackintosh Building to its former state without additional financial support.

The art school previously insisted it was committed to a faithful reinstatement of the building, which was designed by Charles Rennie Mackintosh but wrecked by two fires in 2014 and 2018.

However it now says "financial clarity", provided by an insurance settlement regarding the 2018 blaze, has shown it "cannot take forward the faithful reinstatement on its own."

Instead it suggests the building has potential to be an anchor for a "creative and cultural production innovation district".

But this claim that has attracted scorn from figures in the art world.

News.title: EA Sports FC 27 launches this week – here’s everything to know
News.content:
EA Sports’s Fifa franchise has been dominating the world of football games for decades, thanks in large part to its vast portfolio of official licences. Now the developer is finally ready to lift the curtain on the next entry in the series.

With the World Cup behind us now, EA is ramping up its promotion of FC 27. The rumour mill is churning, but a few things have been confirmed, such as the game’s cover stars and when the gameplay trailer will release

While some fans think the series is in its best shape yet, with competitive and authentic gameplay modes, the addition of live challenges in Manager Career mode and slight changes to Ultimate Team in FC 26, others want something more drastic. With the launch of FC 27 expected imminently, here's everything we know so far.

‘EA Sports FC 27’ release date: When could the game come out?

open image in gallery EA recently released it's 'The World's Game' update for FC 26 to tie in with the FIFA World Cup ( EA Sports )

This one is actually quite straightforward to predict because, since the mid-2000s with the launch of Fifa 06, EA has released its annual football title on the final Friday of September.

With that in mind, EA Sports FC 27 is likely to launch on Friday 25 September 2026. There’s also usually a week of early access for those who pre-order and purchase an Ultimate Edition of the game. Early access could open on 17 September.

There’s nothing to indicate so far EA will deviate from this.

When could ‘EA Sports FC 27’ be announced?

EA Sports FC 27 has been officially confirmed and was revealed through Kylian Mbappe starring as the Ultimate Edition star. He’s the cover star for the Standard Edition, too.

EA confirmed a gameplay trailer will release this Thursday (23 July).

‘EA Sports FC 27’ cover star

Despite widespread speculation pointing to Jude Bellingham featuring as the standard edition cover star, with Cristiano Ronaldo on the cover of the Ultimate Edition, it’s actually France and Real Madrid forward Kylian Mbappe who is on the cover of both the standard and Ultimate editions.

Although France finished fourth at the 2026 World Cup, the forward had a great tournament from an individual perspective, scoring 10 goals to collect the tournament's Golden Boot award and becoming the tournament's top scorer of all time, sitting on 22 and one above Lionel Messi. He's only 27-years-old.

Mbappe said: "To be featured on the cover of an EA Sports FC title for the first time is a very special moment for me. It's an honour to continue my long-term relationship with the franchise in its latest chapter, alongside the players who have shaped its history. I can't wait for everyone to experience FC 27."

Mbappe has appeared on the cover of EA’s football franchise before but his last appearance was on Fifa 23, the last year EA had the FIFA license. The French forward will also be the cover star for EA Sports FC Mobile.

open image in gallery Kylian Mbappe is the cover star for EA Sports FC 27 ( EA Sports )

‘EA Sports FC 27’ features

While nothing has been officially confirmed at the time of writing on this front, the big, heavily speculated new feature understood to be coming to EA Sports FC 27 is the inclusion of a new open-world mode. If it happens, it’s expected to be called ‘The Grounds’.

It’s rumoured this mode will operate in a similar way to the one found in the NBA 2K series, where players can jump in and out of minigames, explore an open world and build up their player. It’s understood EA has previously playtested this feature, but nothing has yet been confirmed.

Other rumoured features are the inclusion of a better replay system, so players can more easily analyse their performances. There could also be dynamic weather during matches. That means a game could start out dry, but then rain in the second half, affecting how the ball behaves on the pitch.

Aside from that, expect the usual graphical upgrades, updated teams and squads, gameplay tweaks and slight changes to modes such as Ultimate Team, Career Mode and Clubs, plus further quality of life updates.

‘EA Sports FC 27’ platforms

According to a new report from reliable insider publication Dealabs, EA Sports FC 27 will be available on PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Nintendo Switch 2, PC, PS4, Xbox One and the original Nintendo Switch console. If true, it means you won’t have to upgrade to the latest console generation to play the game.

‘EA Sports FC 26’, PS5: Was £44.99, now £21.99, Amazon.co.uk

open image in gallery ( Amazon )

If you’ve not yet picked up a copy of FC 26, now is a great time to do so with the business end of the Fifa World Cup approaching and EA Sports having launched ‘The World’s Game’ update, it’s take on unofficial World Cup content. The PS5 disc version has been slashed by half price at Amazon.

For more on all things gaming, check out our review of Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced

News.content:

Three Sudanese students are challenging the Home Office’s ban on certain visas for foreign nationals from four countries in the courts.

Home secretary Shabana Mahmood halted study visas for people from Afghanistan, Cameroon, Myanmar and Sudan in March, accusing some of exploiting the system by using it as a gateway to enter the UK before later claiming asylum.

The drastic measure drew criticism from the university sector, with the vice chancellor of the University of Sussex, Sasha Roseneil, saying the move had profound consequences “for the UK’s global reputation and soft power”.

Now, three Sudanese women in their twenties, supported by law firm Duncan Lewis, are seeking to bring a legal challenge at the High Court to overturn the ban. They will argue that the way the Home Office selected the nationalities to ban is flawed, and that officials failed to properly investigate whether widespread visa abuse was occurring before they imposed a blanket ban.

Two of the women are doctors and one is a pharmacist. They had offers to study masters at Oxford University and University College London (UCL) in Digital Health, International Health and Tropical Medicine, and Public Health.

One of the women, who wanted to remain anonymous, said that the legal challenge was about ensuring “fairness”. She explained: “When I received my offer from Oxford, I saw it as an opportunity to gain the knowledge and skills needed to help rebuild health systems in a country long devastated by war.

“As a Sudanese doctor with an established international career, I have spent years working on reproductive health and supporting communities affected by displacement. The idea that I am now being treated as a potential abuser of the immigration system, simply because of my nationality, is deeply painful.”

She added: “Sudan has already lost universities, hospitals, and countless opportunities to this war. Many of us have lost friends, family members, and any sense of normality. Education is one of the few remaining pathways available to young Sudanese who want to contribute, lead, and help rebuild our country. This policy does not just affect visa applications; it risks taking away the future of a generation that has already lost so much.”

Shabana Mahmood has halted student visas for nationals from Afghanistan, Cameroon, Myanmar and Sudan for at least 18 months ( Getty/iStock )

Announcing the ban in March, the Home Office said they needed to “protect UK border security from these unsustainable levels of visa-linked asylum claims”, saying that students who arrive in the UK were going on to claim asylum.

The Home Office estimated that the 18-month ban would impact 4,300 students from the four countries. In the year ending September 2025, there were 120 asylum claims from Sudanese nationals on study visas in the UK – compared to a total of 5,869 Sudanese asylum claimants in 2025.

The four countries affected by the ban made up just 0.7 per cent of study visas issued in 2025. Together, visas granted to foreign nationals from Myanmar, Cameroon, Afghanistan and Sudan made up 3,142 visas out of the 429,254 study visas issued in 2025.

Manini Menon, solicitor at law firm Duncan Lewis, told The Independent: “Our clients are talented, high-achieving women who have secured admission to some of the top universities in the world.

“It is disappointing that the home secretary has decided that they should be deprived of the opportunity to take up their offers of study, solely on account of their nationality, without any assessment of the individual facts of their cases.

“This is particularly so in circumstances where our clients are all medical professionals working on issues of public health and sexual and reproductive rights (including eradication of the practice of FGM), all of which the government has recognised in its foreign policy as being key UK priorities in Sudan.”

Earlier this year, leading universities urged Ms Mahmood to exempt outstanding students from the ban. Some 34 institutions, represented by higher-education associations the Russell Group and ResearchPlus, called for an exception for Chevening scholars, who are part of a government-funded programme that enables outstanding emerging leaders from around the world to do a one-year master’s degree in the UK.

In June, the Home Office announced in a further crackdown, saying universities would be stripped of the right to recruit international students if too many drop out over fears they are being exploited for visa abuse.

The claim brought by the three Sudanese women is due to be heard at the High Court at the beginning of next week.

The Home Office has been contacted for comment.

News.content:

A New York City woman is suing McDonald’s after allegedly sustaining “serious and severe personal injuries and burns to [her] mouth and tongue, as a result of being served extremely hot fries,” according to a civil complaint obtained by The Independent.

In it, Catherine Luongo blames the March 5 incident, which occurred at a McDonald’s restaurant across the street from Manhattan’s Bryant Park, on the employees who “fail[ed] to provide [her] with a safe order of fries.”

Her purported physical trauma was “due solely… [to] the carelessness, recklessness and negligence” of the unnamed workers who prepared the fries in question, which the complaint describes as “overheated and not safe for human consumption.”

Luongo should never have been “permitt[ed] and allow[ed]” to “be served and consume extremely hot and overheated fries,” the complaint states. It contends that Luongo was not given ample warning of “the dangers to be encountered” when tucking into the fries, and that “the aforesaid occurrence was due solely by reason of the negligence of the Defendants,” and “through no fault or lack of care” on Luongo’s part.

On top of Luongo’s alleged mouth and tongue injuries, she also endured “a severe shock to the nervous system,” “suffered great physical pain and mental anguish,” and “was confined to bed and home and caused to abstain from usual duties and activities,” according to the complaint, which was filed July 21 in New York State Supreme Court.

open image in gallery A New York woman is suing McDonald's over injuries she claims she suffered while digging into an order of allegedly superheated fries ( Getty Images )

It says Luongo was “forced to seek medical aid and attention,” which she had to pay for herself, and claims her fry-related health issues “may be permanent and lasting.” The complaint does not provide further details of Luongo’s alleged injuries.

McDonald’s did not respond to a request for comment.

In 2013, the chain was hauled into court by a Massachusetts mom who sued after her 3-year-old daughter suffered first- and second-degree burns on her thighs from an order of “unreasonably and dangerously hot” fries.

“As a direct and proximate cause of the unreasonably and dangerously hot French Fries, M.C. is now disfigured and scarred,” the lawsuit claimed. “M.C. is undergoing surgery due to the disfigurement and scarring.”

That same year, a Florida woman was awarded $800,000 after her 4-year-old daughter received second-degree burns from a “dangerously hot” Chicken McNugget that fell from its packaging and became wedged between the child’s leg and her seat belt. Philana Holmes used her iPhone to record the girl’s screams, which were played in court.

Lawyers for McDonald’s unsuccessfully argued that the McNugget had to be heated to a certain temperature to stave off the possibility of salmonella poisoning, and, as PBS reported at the time, that the nuggets “were not meant to be pressed between a seat belt and human flesh for more than two minutes.”

A similar suit, this one filed in 2009, involved an order of “dangerously hot” Dunkin’ Donuts hash browns and a Boston-area toddler, who they said received “serious and permanent burn injuries” when the hot potatoes fell from his mouth onto his neck. Before Robin MacLeod gave her son the hash brown, she checked it and found it “lukewarm,” the family’s complaint said.

open image in gallery Catherine Luongo claims she was injured by an order of scaldingly hot fries she purchased at a McDonald's on East 42 Street in Manhattan ( Google Maps )

However, the hash brown had been heated “unevenly,” according to the filing, which claimed the inside of the item was so hot, it was “unsafe for public consumption.”

Beyond the fast-food realm, a Philadelphia man sued Frontier Airlines in 2024 after sustaining third-degree burns and being “left with disfiguring scars on his genitals and thighs” after a flight attendant allegedly spilled hot tea on his lap.

As The Independent first reported, Sean Miller’s complaint detailed the “highly unsightly and embarrassing discoloration,” along with “significantly decreased sensation,” “post-traumatic stress disorder,” and “lack of self-esteem,” plus at least one herniated disc he suffered while writhing in distress.

Upon landing, the 56-year-old was rushed to an area burn center for specialized treatment “due to the severity” of his injuries.

Such lawsuits, including Luongo’s, bring to mind the well-known and widely misunderstood case of 79-year-old Stella Liebeck, who was maligned for bringing a “frivolous” lawsuit over a blisteringly hot cup of McDonald’s coffee, but which turned out to be anything but trivial.

Liebeck suffered horrific third-degree burns across six percent of her body and led to permanent tissue damage after the cup’s superheated contents spilled on her, causing what her physician called one of the worst scalding cases he had ever seen. The New Mexico resident spent a week in the hospital, three weeks recovering at home, and was then hospitalized again to undergo painful debridement and skin grafts.

Liebeck offered to settle for the costs of her medical treatment, about $20,000, and only sued when McDonald’s refused to cooperate.

A jury awarded Liebeck $2.7 million in punitive damages for her injuries, which a judge later reduced to $480,000, for what he deemed “willful, wanton, reckless” and “callous” conduct on the part of McDonald's.

Food service establishments have argued that a reasonable adult is aware that certain foods and beverages are hot, and that a potential burn is an “open and obvious” risk they knowingly assume. At the same time, if a product is so hot that normal use could land someone in the hospital, the seller is required to provide an explicit warning to all.

Luongo’s suit says she “has been damaged in a sum which exceeds the jurisdictional limits of all lower Courts,” and is seeking money damages to be determined at trial

Police have released a photo of a man they want to talk to after a serious assault in London after England’s World Cup game with Norway.

An assault happened just after 1am on Saturday, 12 July on Gascoyne Road, close to the junction with Bradstock Road in Hackney.

It is believed that the 24-year-old victim was involved in an altercation with a group of men after the match. One member of the group then assaulted the victim, who sustained serious head injuries as a result.

The victim was taken to hospital by the London Ambulance Service. He remains in hospital with serious injuries.

open image in gallery Police would like to talk to this man about the incident ( Metropolitan Police )

Detective Sergeant Steve Rafferty, who is leading the investigation, said: "This was a violent assault which has left a young man with serious injuries.

"Since launching our investigation, officers have carried out extensive enquiries, including analysing CCTV footage and speaking to witnesses. The assault took placed after the England vs Norway World Cup match, and we know that the area was extremely busy at the time. As a result, there may be additional witnesses who can provide crucial information.

"We are releasing an image of a man, who we believe may have important information which could assist our investigation, and I would urge anyone who recognises him to get in touch with police. He’s described as a White man, believed to be in his 20s or 30s, with light brown hair. He was wearing a blue and white England shirt with a navy collar.

"If you were in the Gascoyne Road area during the early hours of 12 July, witnessed the incident, or have any information which could assist our enquiries, please come forward."

No arrests have been made, and enquiries are progressing at pace.

Anyone who witnessed the incident or has information is urged to contact police on 101, quoting reference CAD 600/12JUL.

Information can also be provided anonymously to independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

After days of protests, Volodymyr Zelensky acquiesced to demands to sack his military’s commander-in-chief, General Oleksandr Syrskyi, and replaced him with the much younger Major General Mykhailo Drapatyi, who enjoys a formidable battlefield reputation.

Sirskyi, 60, appointed in 2023, was credited with forcing Russian forces to retreat from their attempt to capture the capital, Kyiv, at the start of Moscow’s February 2022 full scale invasion. Later that year, he masterminded a surprise offensive that routed Russians occupying large swathes of territory in Ukraine’s north eastern Kharkiv region.

But many Ukrainians disliked Sirskyi, saying he retained the rigid traits and strict hierarchical attitude from his Soviet-era military training and service. They also accused him of not caring enough about how many of his men lost their lives.

In contrast, 43-year-old Drapatyi’s appointment has met wide approval.

Among those welcoming him was a major with the nom de guerre “Hrizny”, who leads an anti-missile air defence unit protecting Kyiv.

The 26-year-old, who studied law before the war, said Sirskyi alienated many younger officers who had been brought up in Ukraine’s post-independence democracy and had received training from Nato militaries.

open image in gallery Volodymyr Zelensky, newly appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Ukrainian Armed Forces Major General Mykhailo Drapatyi, his predecessor General Oleksandr Syrskyi, and Acting Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara ( Reuters )

Hrizny said Drapatyi is regarded as untainted by Soviet military culture: “He has a reputation as a person who is receptive to new ideas and ready to listen to others, including his subordinates. So I, and other soldiers I’ve spoken to, feel very positive.”

One of the biggest causes of tension within the Ukrainian military is the lack of time off.

Hrizny said: “One reason, of course, is manpower shortages. But old-school officers are often reluctant to allow people leave and prefer to keep them close by, even performing unnecessary tasks.

“I think that Drapatiy understands the importance of regular leave so service people can spend time with their families and maintain personal relationships. That would lift morale enormously.”

Colonel Andriy F, who asked not to use his surname, was formerly a member of the Ukrainian military’s general staff and is now involved in acquiring weapons from around the world.

Unlike Hrizny, the colonel regarded General Sirsky as an able military leader but was quick to praise Drapatiy.

He said the younger man first came to attention in 2014 when Moscow first invaded Ukraine, annexing Crimea and occupying parts of eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region including, for a time, the city of Mariupol.

open image in gallery Activists hold a portrait of Ukraine's Armed Forces Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi demanding his resignation during a rally to denounce President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's decision to dismiss Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov after six months in the post, in Kyiv, on July 18, 2026 ( AP )

Drapatyi was the commander of one of two battalions surrounded by Russian forces in Mariupol. One Ukrainian commander agreed to Russian demands to lay down weapons in return for safe passage home, humiliatingly via Russia.

Drapatyi refused to follow suit and instead launched a breakout, spearheaded by armoured vehicles, enabling the battalion to reach Ukrainian-held territory without any losses.

“He is a thoughtful, intelligent person who doesn’t waste his words on bravado or bluster. He is also a considerate person who talked about the importance of listening to others.”

The protests that led to the changes at the top were triggered after Zelensky sacked defence minister, Mykhailo Fedorov after tension between the defence minister and Syrskyi.

Fedorov, 35, a computer expert and formerly IT minister, had been hailed for his innovative drone warfare development which enabled Ukraine to halt, and even reverse, Moscow’s previous advances to take territory.

The colonel said: “I admire Fedorov because he was the first to outline and communicate to the military and public what he regarded as strategic objectives - to kill more Russians soldiers each month than Moscow could replace, to use drones to compensate for artillery and missile ammunition that Ukraine lacks, to diminish Moscow’s war economy by attacks on oil and gas facilities and weapons manufacturing or logistics facilities, and to broaden cooperation with foreign defence industry partners.

“To a great extent he was achieving these objectives. He was also a person our allies and foreign partners respected and found easy to deal with.”

Fedorov was also seen as rooting out corruption in the defence ministry.

open image in gallery Activists shout slogans during a rally to denounce President Volodymyr Zelensky's decision to dismiss Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov after six months in the post, Friday, July 17 ( AP )

However, said the colonel, Fedorov seemed to neglect his promise to devise ways to address the Ukrainian military’s manpower shortages which have become more critical by the month. “And that was, probably, an important reason the president fell out with Fedorov.”

Fedorov, a friend of Drapatyi’s, applauded the change of commander-in-chief.

Zelensky replaced Fedorov with Yevhenii Khmara, who was formerly a senior member of Ukraine's SBU Security Service.

The president has said he wants to offer Fedorov another important position after the reshuffle but so far Fedorov has not accepted a new job. Zelensky said the two men will have further discussions about a new role.

The colonel said Zelensky had consulted many senior figures in the Ukrainian military before promoting Drapatyi. “I think Zelensky’s decision will win the approval of most senior officers and Drapatyi’s appointment will be a morale-booster for the military as a whole.”

The decision to designate a stretch of Tennessee highway after Charlie Kirk has been reversed, with state officials now moving to relocate signs after Vietnam veterans objected to sharing the name, according to a county official.

State Route 386 —an east–west corridor cutting through Sumner and Davidson counties — has long been known as Vietnam Veterans Boulevard. However, following Kirk’s assassination last September, the roadway was also designated the Charlie Kirk Memorial Highway.

On Monday, Sumner County Commissioner Jeremy Mansfield announced that the additional name had been rescinded and the signage moved, citing what he described as irritation among veterans who felt caught off guard by the decision.

“Many of our Vietnam veterans were angry and frustrated to see this designation placed on ground set aside to honor their brothers in arms,” Mansfield wrote on Facebook, noting that 25 service members from Sumner County died in Vietnam.

“To every Vietnam veteran who spoke up, thank you,” Mansfield added. “Thank you for your service and for your sacrifice. Your opinion on this mattered, and I was surprised to learn they were never consulted before the first sign went up.”

open image in gallery A decision to designate a Tennessee highway after Charlie Kirk has been reversed and signs are slated to be moved after a group of Vietnam veterans expressed frustration ( Getty Images )

Mansfield said that the Charlie Kirk Memorial Highway designation has been moved to Long Hollow Pike, located in Goodlettsville, Tennessee.

“I am excited to see it find a home there, a place that honors Charlie Kirk without taking anything away from those we already promised to remember,” he wrote.

State Representative Johnny Garrett, a Republican, is “responsible for the state bill getting the designation / signs as well as the location,” Mansfield told The Independent in an email.

“I am not involved other than reporting to my constituents in Goodlettsville, TN, what the state is doing,” Mansfield said. “It is not a county matter.”

The Independent has contacted Garrett, who describes himself as a “Trump conservative” and is running for Congress in the state’s 6th District.

open image in gallery 'The signs that went up on State Route 386 are being relocated,' the Sumner County commissioner wrote on Monday. 'State Route 386 has always been Vietnam Veterans Boulevard' ( Jeremy Mansfield )

“The Tennessee General Assembly approves memorial designation of roadways, while the Tennessee Department of Transportation (TDOT) is responsible for fabricating and installing the signage,” a spokesperson for the DOT told Fox8. “Regarding the placement or removal of the signage, TDOT will follow the direction provided by the General Assembly, which we have not yet received.”

Kirk, an influential conservative activist and founder of Turning Point USA, was fatally shot in Utah on September 10.

After his death, GOP lawmakers across the country proposed various ways to memorialize him. In Minnesota, a bill was put forward to fund a statue at the University of Minnesota’s Twin Cities campus. In the House, an Arizona Republican proposed legislation to create commemorative coins with Kirk’s likeness.

A New York City sculptor also said this week that he spent $100,000 to build a lifelike statue of Kirk — but so far, no one has expressed interest in buying it.

We need to be a cost-of-living government – getting that cost of living down, looking at all possible ways of doing that...” As a clear statement of intent, Andy Burnham’s message to colleagues at the first meeting of the new cabinet cannot be faulted. Each will be tasked with finding innovative ways that their own department can contribute to helping people to manage.

The prime minister is doing his job. He is responding to the public’s overriding concern, and visibly trying to assist. It is a healthy instinct – but it cannot overshadow the imperative of rebuilding the public finances, a job far from complete.

Mr Burnham is obviously in the very early days of his administration, and most of the announcements he has made so far to give people a “breathing space” have been relatively easy to accommodate within existing spending plans. These small but eye-catching initiatives are what might be called “Tesco government” – every little helps.

As such, they should not be derided. The latest, reducing the cap on bus fares in most of England, from £3 to £2, is a case in point. While many people, especially outside London, hardly use a bus, and a pound either way in the fare is negligible, for someone on the minimum wage who has to use public transport to get to work, it is a more significant matter – representing a possible saving of as much as £40 per month.

The money for the cap is to come from cutting – “reprioritising”, in Burnham-speak – funds once destined for net zero projects abroad. Similarly, the £45-a-year from ending VAT on electricity bills will help the most vulnerable, although the “savings” from scrapping the Digital ID scheme are, strictly speaking, unfunded.

But Mr Burnham’s ambitions are far higher than that. On the steps of Downing Street, before entering No 10 for the first time as prime minister, he instructed his civil servants to “end rough sleeping in our country” – an objective far more expensive and difficult to achieve than the more modest reforms he set out elsewhere.

During his leadership campaign and since, he has also repeatedly put social care reform at the top of his agenda. Indeed, he did so almost two decades ago when he served as health secretary under Gordon Brown. Then, he advocated the creation of a “National Care Service”, on the same principle of free access at the point of use as applies to the NHS; and he reiterates that approach now.

He knows from his own experience of his father’s dementia how much of an unfair lottery the system is today, and he is right to want to reform it – and to succeed where so many others have failed. Yet there is, as yet, not even the vaguest funding plan for a National Care Service.

Mr Burnham’s problem is that he has no more resources available to him, at least in the short term, than did his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer. This is becoming apparent by the day.

Somewhat embarrassingly, his spokespeople have already had to execute their first U-turn on his behalf. Mr Burnham has an unfortunate habit of thinking aloud about problems, and giving the wrong impression. So when he described the voters’ frustration about the frozen personal tax-free income allowance that he had heard during the Makerfield by-election, the logical conclusion was that he might do something about it. Now, it seems, he won’t – and not least because raising the tax threshold by as little as £500 would cost the Treasury around £5bn a year – and leave a basic-rate taxpayer only £100 better off annually.

It is a similar story for the PM, his new defence secretary and chancellor over defence spending. Despite John Healey resigning over the previous prime minister’s reluctance to boost defence spending, none of the three has thus far committed to devoting 3 per cent of the national income on the armed forces by 2030, as Mr Healey previously demanded.

Unlike when he was a city mayor with a grant from central government, Mr Burnham now has to find the money to fulfil his honourable aspirations. Free from parliamentary commitments, he and his team now have some months to reconcile these with resources, and make hard choices on spending and taxation.

In the meantime, alongside its welcome sense of urgency and compassion, the government must also convey an impression of fiscal discipline.

News.title: Inflation fall a ‘false dawn’, Burnham warned
News.content:
Falling inflation is a “false dawn” for Andy Burnham, economists warned after the pace of price rises slowed in June.

The consumer prices index (CPI) fell from 2.8pc in May to 2.6pc last month, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), beating economists’ expectations of a drop to 2.7pc to mark the lowest rate in 15 months.

Lower petrol and diesel prices drove the slowdown amid a short-lived peace deal between the US and Iran, while price pressures from chocolate, oils and fats, dairy and meat also weakened.

However, economists warned a rise in household energy bills in July may already have pushed inflation back up above 3pc.

Suren Thiru, chief economist at the Institute of Chartered Accountants, said: “June’s slowdown is a false dawn as it may have already been reversed this month with higher energy bills, following Ofgem’s energy price cap rise, likely to have lifted inflation above 3pc.”

July’s 13pc increase in the energy price cap has pushed typical annual bills to around £1,862, while renewed fighting between the US and Iran has reignited concerns over oil and gas supplies.

Mr Thiru said elevated inflation would create a fresh headache for John Healey, the newly appointed Chancellor, by squeezing household budgets, raising government borrowing costs and limiting his room for tax cuts or spending increases.

Charlotte O’Leary, at the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, said: “June’s peace deal and the subsequent reduction in oil and gas prices helped cool consumer price inflation. This will be a welcome figure to start the new Prime Minister’s premiership, but the honeymoon period will be short-lived.”

The Bank of England will also be watching closely as it weighs further interest rate cuts, though economists warned renewed instability in the Middle East and higher energy bills could keep inflation close to 3pc for the rest of the year.

Mr Healey said: “Falling inflation is news families want to hear, but there is much more to do to give people the breathing space they need.”

News.title: Russia destroys Ukraine HIV warehouse
News.content:
A Russian missile strike has destroyed $2.6m (£1.9m) worth of HIV prevention supplies in Ukraine, according to an international aid group.

The Alliance for Public Health said the attack on Sunday night near Kyiv hit a warehouse holding 62 million prevention items earmarked for Ukraine’s harm reduction programmes next year. It includes syringes, needles, alcohol wipes, and condoms intended to support more than 300,000 people.

“This is not just another strike. It is an attack on 300,000 Ukrainians who depend on HIV prevention services and on their fundamental right to health,” said Andriy Klepikov, executive director of the Alliance for Public Health.

Efforts to prevent the spread of HIV rely heavily on harm reduction programmes that supply sterile syringes and needles to people who inject drugs, alongside condoms and other supplies that help curb sexual transmission.

Mr Klepikov said the destruction of the warehouse would not immediately disrupt services, because his organisation had moved its supplies for the rest of the year out of central storage and into regional distribution centres several weeks ago as part of contingency planning.

“Russia failed,” he said, adding that the Alliance had notified international partners and appealed for urgent support to rebuild next year’s inventory.

News.title: Private sector pay suffers worst growth since Covid
News.content:
Private sector wages are growing at their slowest pace since the pandemic, piling pressure on Andy Burnham as he enters Downing Street facing a fragile economy and strained public finances.

Salaries rose by 2.9pc in the three months to May, the first time growth has dipped below 3pc since October 2020 and only narrowly ahead of inflation at 2.8pc.

The slowdown was most acute in key industries, with wages in finance and business services up just 2.3pc, manufacturing at 2.5pc and construction earnings falling by 0.2pc over the year.

In contrast, public sector pay accelerated to 5.5pc after striking workers secured higher settlements, widening the gap between state and private sectors.

The cooling labour market came as borrowing overshot official forecasts, leaving John Healey, the new Chancellor, with a £2.7bn gap against expectations.

The Government borrowed £57.6bn between April and June – less than a year earlier but still ahead of projections – pushing public debt to nearly £3tn, or 94.9pc of GDP.

Mr Healey said: “The Prime Minister and I have talked about how we will work in lockstep to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty and how we’ll make life more affordable for working people right across the UK.”

However, Sir Mel Stride, the shadow business secretary, said: “If Andy Burnham and John Healey are really serious about the future of our economy then they must get borrowing under control.”

News.title: Scammers stole $114 billion as Southeast Asia’s crime gangs go corporate
News.content:
Scam gangs stole up to $114 billion from people in Asia-Pacific alone in 2025, the UN has warned, as crime syndicates rapidly professionalise their tactics to evade law enforcement in Southeast Asia.

By way of comparison, the sum dwarfs the $85 billion the UK spends each year on defence.

The Asia-Pacific region has emerged as an epicentre for massive cyber fraud operations since the Covid pandemic. Scammers – some willingly, others under duress – are now stealing billions from internet users across the world via fake romance and cryptocurrency investment schemes.

In 2025, these fraud operations stole between $88.3 and $114.1bn from just people across East Asia, Southeast Asia, Australia and New Zealand, according to a report on Tuesday from the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC).

Those figures are triple the estimated losses in 2023, between $18 and $37bn, and don’t account for victims in Europe or the US.

The scam centres – which began in fortified compounds but are now increasingly housed in innocuous office blocks and villas – are found across the region, but have especially exploited power vacuums caused by war, corruption and weak governance in Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos.

Although the scammers initially targeted people in China, they have dramatically expanded their ambitions. The UNODC said people from at least 80 countries and territories had been identified in compounds, with recruiters seeking people from outside Asia as they look to expand new markets.

News.title: UK borrowing costs rise at fastest pace in G7
News.content:
Britain’s borrowing costs rose at the fastest pace in the G7 after Andy Burnham said he would take a “flexible” approach to the UK’s fiscal rules.

In his maiden speech as prime minister, Mr Burnham on Monday signalled he could bend the rules underpinning Britain’s finances, spooking financial markets fearful of higher government spending.

UK gilts – a benchmark for how much the Government pays on its debt – saw yields rise 0.08 percentage points to an eight-week high of 5.03pc for the 10-year bond. Thirty-year gilts also pushed higher.

The rise was the fastest in the G7, excluding Japan, whose markets are closed for a national holiday.

After markets closed on Monday, Mr Burnham surprised the City by picking John Healey as his next Chancellor.

Mr Healey, who quit over defence funding rising too slowly, will now be tasked with finding billions of pounds in Britain’s stretched public finances.

Shabana Mahmood, the Home Secretary, had widely been expected for the role. Ed Miliband, the former Energy Secretary, was also in contention.

Mr Healey will replace Rachel Reeves, who resigned on Monday.

The appointment of Mr Healey, a veteran of the Blair-Brown government, may calm fears in the City after Mr Burnham pledged to stretch the fiscal rules by using “flexibility” within them.

Speaking in Downing Street, Mr Burnham said: “I’ve said we’ll stick to the fiscal rules, and by that I mean the existing fiscal rules, and use obviously any flexibility within them.”

James Athey, a fund manager at Marlborough, said: “It’s not a good start because bandying around the words fiscal rules seems to be believed within government circles to be a sufficient condition to get financial markets on side, and that just misunderstands an element of the problem.”

He added that investors were watching closely for any signs that the Government will increase borrowing.

Matt Amis, investment director at Aberdeen, said Mr Burnham’s comments had “got the markets’ attention.”

He said “It just shows this week in particular the language from the Burnham administration, the new chancellor, is going to be key here. The gilt market is on edge.”

Mr Burnham, who has become the UK’s seventh prime minister in just a decade, has inherited a troubled economy as businesses grapple with low confidence and strained public finances.

Monday’s comment suggests the new prime minister will use measures to raise borrowing while keeping the additional sums off the Government’s book.

The Resolution Foundation, a think tank, said he could do this by expanding the remit of institutions like the National Wealth Fund, an arms-length government investment vehicle.

His plan to use “flexibility” in the fiscal rules comes after Ms Reeves altered the main indicator of government debt in 2024.

She tweaked the primary measure of the UK’s debt to Public Sector Net Financial Liabilities, meaning that when public financial institutions borrow to invest in a private business it does not count towards the government’s fiscal rules.

However, the think tank warned that boosting the financial capacity of public financial institutions like the National Wealth Fund by £16bn would cost around £400 million a year in debt interest.

Helen Miller, director at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, warned that challenging public finances will mean Mr Burnham will be forced to make tough choices on spending.

She said: “While chancellors come and go, the underlying fiscal constraints remain the same. Public debt, borrowing and debt-interest costs are all high. One in every £12 the government spends currently goes on debt interest.”

Higher borrowing costs threaten to increase the Government’s debt interest bill, which is already forecast to hit £111.2bn for the financial year - equivalent to 8.3pc of public spending.

Mr Burnham said he would announce a set of measures on Tuesday to give households “breathing space” to help with the cost of living.

“I will set out some of those measures starting tomorrow, including how we pay for them,” he said.

“We will help more young people into education... and we will build more council homes. That is the fair and sustainable way to bring the welfare bill down, to meet our fiscal rules and to honour our commitments on defence to our international partners.”

Mr Amis said: “Tomorrow we’re getting some cost of living news. [Burnham] said he was going to state where that funding’s come from. I think that’s key, any unfunded spending from here would get the market’s attention.”

News.title: India approves first dengue vaccine as cases surge in South Asia
News.content:
India has approved its first dengue vaccine as cases of the mosquito-borne disease surge in South Asia.

Japan’s Takeda Pharmaceutical’s dengue vaccine QDENGA has been approved by India’s drug regulator, the Centre Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO).

The global threat posed by dengue has been rising for years, as climate change, urbanisation and international travel aid the spread of the mosquitoes that transmit it.

The approval comes as hospitals across South Asia grapple with a surge in dengue infections.

In Sri Lanka, health authorities reported 2,652 new cases on Sunday alone, taking the total to 76,044 dengue cases so far this year. At least 53 people have died.

Bangladesh is also suffering a major outbreak with over 9,000 cases and 30 deaths that has piled pressure on its health system even as it battles a measles epidemic.

Dengue is transmitted to humans through the bites of infected Aedes mosquitoes.

Its symptoms include fever, severe muscle pain, and in severe cases, shock and internal bleeding that can be fatal.

Although mortality is relatively low, outbreaks place a substantial burden on health systems.

Takeda’s QDENGA jab is a live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes. It can be given regardless of previous dengue infections.

“The approval comes at a critical time for public health, as reported dengue cases in India have increased 11-fold in the past two decades,” the company said in a statement.

News.title: Burnham’s plan to restore UK aid spending
News.content:
Andy Burnham is planning to reverse the cuts to Britain’s aid budget made by his predecessors Sir Keir Starmer and Rishi Sunak, according to reports.

A roadmap for returning the UK to spending 0.7 per cent of Gross National Income (GNI) on international aid will be drawn up as part of a major shake-up of the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), The Independent reported.

Ed Miliband is set to be named Foreign Secretary and put in charge of overhauling Britain’s international development aims, as well as prioritising climate goals, senior Labour sources said.

The aid spending plan was absent from Mr Burnham’s brief first speech as Prime Minister, in which he pledged to end rough sleeping and bring down the welfare bill in order to fund defence and council housing.

But it follows anger within the Labour Party over what was seen as a broken manifesto promise, when Sir Keir and Rachel Reeves, the Chancellor, slashed aid spending to 0.3 per cent of GNI.

Senior Labour MPs have been lobbying for a return to the 0.7 per cent commitment, a target first established by the United Nations in the 1970s.

It has since become a key yardstick for international efforts to reduce poverty and tackle major health issues like the HIV/AIDS epidemic, vaccine access, and maternal mortality in poor countries.

Sports.title: Aston Villa are inviting a nightmare to their door with ludicrous Alejandro Garnacho transfer
Sports.content:
Aston Villa are inviting a nightmare to their door with ludicrous Alejandro Garnacho transfer

Aston Villa have sold Morgan Rogers to Chelsea in a record-breaking £117million transfer and as they look to bring in players of their own have turned to Alejandro Garnacho

View 2 Images Unai Emery led Aston Villa into the Champions League but has lost key players this summer (Image: 2026 Getty Images)

Aston Villa are about to swing violently from the sublime to the ridiculous. With a decision so bizarre, it feels akin to parking a Robin Reliant where a Ferrari has just been.

‌



Perhaps Unai Emery thinks he can be the manager to release the handbreak belonging to Alejandro Garnacho. What other reason could there be for the Villa manager to think there is some logic to replacing Morgan Rogers with Garnacho?

‌



But the real mistake Emery has made is convincing himself Garnacho is a good footballer in the first place.

‌



There were several reasons Garnacho failed to make the Argentina squad for this summer's World Cup. These included his attitude in training, approach to the game in general and an unhealthy obsession with social media. But the one which stuck out like a sore thumb, was also the one which saw Lionel Messi raise concerns about how disruptive Garnacho is capable of being in a squad and its dressing room.

In short, Emery has invited a nightmare to his own doorstep.

‌



Emery has earned a reputation for reviving lost causes in the past. The likes of Marcus Rashford and Marco Asensio spring to mind.

But the Spaniard has bitten off more than he can chew, this time.

When Chelsea agreed to hand over £40m to Manchester United for Garnacho last summer, Sir Jim Ratcliffe was said to be doing a dance of delight around the swimming pool of his mansion on the outskirts of Monaco. The United co-owner must have felt like popping an expensive bottle of the finest French champagne.

‌



He had rid his club of a footballer who had helped inject poison into the Old Trafford dressing room. Someone who personified United's previous indulgences with spoiled brats. A footballer with the ego of Eric Cantona, but the footballing talent of Eric Morecambe.

Villa supporters won't be laughing though. In fact, no-one associated with the club should be.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌



View 2 Images Alejandro Garnacho has no future at Chelsea under Xabi Alonso (Image: John Walton/PA Wire)

Garnacho is someone who tries to write cheques his abilities cannot cash. The bright lights of London came calling, but Garnacho remained glued to the dimmer switch.

In a combined 117 league appearances for both United and Chelsea, Garnacho has scored the sum total of 17 goals.

‌



When Chelsea made the mind-boggling decision to sign Garnacho, United's gain was their loss. It summed up the London club's obsession with disfunction and arrogance.

And now, it seems, Emery is about to fall into the same trap.

He cannot seem to see what the rest of football can. The game is about the company you keep, and Emery is about to invite a troublemaker into his ranks. Because the only thing Garnacho is good at is getting managers the sack.

Article continues below

And if this trend continues in Birmingham, then Emery will only have himself to blame.

Sports.title: Man Utd given green light to complete transfer as forward 'says yes' to move
Sports.content:
Man Utd given green light to complete transfer as forward 'says yes' to move

Manchester United are looking to bolster their squad ahead of a return to the Champions League with the Red Devils considering signing a new striker

View 2 Images Michael Carrick's Manchester United side are gearing up for a return to the Champions League. (Image: (Photo by Ash Donelon/Manchester United via Getty Images))

Manchester United forward Joshua Zirkzee is willing to join Juventus, which could see Michael Carrick's side head into the market for an attacking addition of their own. The 25-year-old started in United's pre-season curtain raiser against Wrexham last weekend but looks set to leave the club.

‌



The Dutch international has managed just 127 minutes of competitive football under Carrick since his return to Old Trafford. Despite struggling since his move to Manchester, there's been plenty of interest from Italian clubs having impressed at Bologna prior to his Old Trafford move.

‌



Several Serie A clubs are keen on signing Zirkzee this summer, with Juventus leading the race to sign him. The Old Lady appeared focused on signing Randal Kolo Muani, but talks with PSG have hit a stumbling point, forcing Juve into a rethink.

‌



Man Utd and Arsenal locked in £40million transfer battle as duo hold talks over deal READ MORE :

FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

La Gazzetta Dello Sport now reports that Zirkzee has given an initial 'yes' to the prospect of joining Juventus and is attracted by the idea of returning to Italy. The Italian publication states that Luciano Spalletti's side would prefer an initial loan arrangement, while continuing to pursue Kolo Muani separately.

United would almost certainly favour a permanent sale of Zirkzee in order to reinvest the proceeds back into the squad, potentially funding a replacement, with the option of a deal incorporating an obligation to buy. Zirkzee had been eager to depart in January but was refused permission by United.

‌



View 2 Images Joshua Zirkzee could leave Man Utd this summer. (Image: Ash Donelon, Manchester United via Getty Images)

Had that been approved, Benjamin Sesko would have been the sole recognised fit centre-forward, though he is currently recovering from a shin injury. While attention appears to remain firmly on midfield, United are also casting their eye over the striker market and weighing up their choices.

The most probable outcome points towards an experienced forward arriving - perhaps not the most headline-grabbing acquisition, but one well-versed in the demands of the Premier League. Karl Darlow, Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos have already officially put pen to paper at the club, with a third midfield signing anticipated.

‌



AS Roma's Manu Kone and Bournemouth's Alex Scott appear to sit at the top of United's shortlist, though both players are attracting considerable interest from rival clubs. Chelsea even had a £64million bid for Scott rejected.

A new left-wing addition is also under consideration, with Crysencio Summerville and Iliman Ndiaye both linked, although the former appears destined for Saudi Pro League outfit Al-Hilal, who have had an offer accepted by West Ham. Marcus Rashford's future will have a bearing on any potential frontline reinforcement, though offloading Zirkzee could free up funds towards securing a forward capable of helping lead the line.

Sports.content:
Liverpool confident of beating Arsenal to £100m star as they move on second winger

Liverpool have been eyeing a new winger all summer and are confident they will beat Arsenal to the signing of Bradley Barcola as they make enquires for Monaco's Maghnes Akliouche

View 2 Images Bradley Barcola is tipped to leave PSG (Image: Maxime Delacroix/Anadolu)

Liverpool have made an approach for Monaco star Maghnes Akliouche as they continue to scour the market for a new winger - but remain 'confident' they will land PSG superstar Bradley Barcola.

‌



The Reds have seen Mohamed Salah depart Anfield and need to replace the iconic Egyptian this summer. A number of players have been identified but, as of yet, they've been unable to get a deal over the line.

‌



Their approach for Akliouche comes after they checked on the Frenchman's availability, reports Sky Sports. PSG too are keen on the 24-year-old and have seen several offers declined by Monaco, the most recent of which was around the £34million mark.

‌



Akliouche made one appearance for France at the World Cup following a season that saw him score seven times in 43 outings for the Ligue 1 side. He came through the ranks in Monaco and those from the Principality haven't hidden the fact he could be available for the right price.

Liverpool's search for attacking reinforcements involves a number of moving parts. They've been eyeing Barcola for much of the summer and the winger could well leave Paris with Arsenal also keen. He is valued around the £100m mark but the Reds are leading the race for his signature.

Bayern Munich too are eyeing him, but The Sun claims those from Anfield are at the front of the queue. Liverpool have already missed out on Yan Diomande, who is set to join PSG from RB Leipzig once the German side seal a replacement.

Sports.title: 'Anthony Taylor quitting is a huge pity - but grassroots referees will quit unless action is taken'
Sports.content:
'Anthony Taylor quitting is a huge pity - but grassroots referees will quit unless action is taken'

Anthony Taylor has decided to call full time on his refereeing career at 47 after serving on the Premier League for 16 years — and he had previously indicated he had been considering quitting

View 3 Images Our man, Bradley Jolly, is a football referee having taken the whistle as a young adult

Anthony Taylor's full-time whistle is such a pity — but sadly it is unexpected.

‌



Referees across the UK will have spotted subtle signs Taylor, 47, had been weighing up retirement in recent months. He hinted in interviews at the pressures of refereeing, alluding to experiences with which many grassroots officials will have found far too familiar.

‌



Is it any wonder then that Taylor — often described as the country's best referee — has hung up his whistle? I am a referee with nearly 10 years of experience and the issues Taylor has pointed out happen on park pitches and the semi-pro level. I've experienced myself, and seen my colleagues plagued by the ugly side.

‌



Players surround the public enemy, managers use him or her as their scapegoat and refs are abused. Little is done to help us. Taylor's retirement — after 16 years at the top — will resonate with the approximate 28,000 of us in the UK. A staggering 7,000 of us leave the game each year and, with Taylor often regarded as an idol, I fear many more — from exciting prospects to veteran whistleblowers — will follow in his footsteps.

Thomas Tuchel has no regrets as Argentina boss rubs salt in the wounds after beating England READ MORE :

Premier League referee Anthony Taylor retires from football and teases what's next READ MORE :

Announcing his retirement, Taylor said: "Officiating at the elite level has been an immense privilege, but the pressure is intense and the scrutiny is constant."

And, in October last year, Taylor, who is a former prison officer, said: "There's certainly been moments — and I won't be alone in this — there's certainly been moments where you are thinking, 'Is it worth it?... And certainly, moments where you're thinking, 'What's being said is completely unfair'."

‌



View 3 Images Anthony Taylor is pictured during the 2026 World Cup match between Portugal and Spain, which would turn out to be his final professional match (Image: EYE4images/NurPhoto/Shutterstock)

I, for one, was not surprised the Wythenshawe-born referee, who had been on Fifa's list of officials for 14 years, quit after overseeing Spain's 1-0 win over Portugal in the World Cup last 16 on 6 July.

I actually admired Taylor's strength for continuing after a chair and drinks were thrown in the direction of the English referee and his group as they made their way through a gathering of Roma fans at Budapest Airport. He had refereed Roma in the 2023 Europa League final, which Roma lost. The dad was ushered to a safe area by airport security, and since revealed his family had not attended big games following this incident.

‌



Don't get me wrong — I have of course not encountered anything of such nature during my tenure, way below Taylor's level. I have been attacked after a game, though, and know multiple others who have been.

View 3 Images Anthony Taylor shows a red card to Arsenal's Mikel Merino their clash against Liverpool last year (Image: Arsenal FC via Getty Images)

In his interview last year, Taylor also said: "We have this archaic psychological tactic of 'let's bombard the ref or bombard the fourth official with the hope of getting a decision out of it'."

Article continues below

And he's right. It must stop. We will continue to lose amazing top-flight referees, we will continue to lose the dedicated grassroots officials who turn up week in, week in, in the gales, rain and snow. I know I am considering giving football the red card — and who can blame me?

Thank you, Anthony Taylor. Your service to the game has been fantastic. You've refereed more than 800 matches across two decades. You've officiated every major domestic cup final. Yet, you've been treated disgracefully time and time again.

Sports.title: 5 attackers Arsenal could still sign after Morgan Rogers transfer setback
Sports.content:
5 attackers Arsenal could still sign after Morgan Rogers transfer setback

Arsenal are looking to level up their attack this summer but now know a blockbuster deal for Morgan Rogers will not be happening following his £117m switch to rivals Chelsea

View 5 Images Arsenal could move for Bradley Barcola after missing out on Morgan Rogers (Image: Getty)

After weeks of speculation that Arsenal were in pole position to land Morgan Rogers, the sight of the England star in the blue of Chelsea will sting for Mikel Arteta.

‌



After all, the Spaniard is seeking quality additions to a squad that won the Premier League for the first time since 2004 last term. And Rogers would most certainly have been that after establishing himself as one of the most exciting young attackers in England over the last couple of years at Aston Villa.

‌



With Rogers' £117million transfer to Chelsea now wrapped up, Arsenal will have to take their search for a new left attacker elsewhere.

‌



The good news is there are still plenty of quality players Arsenal could sign to level up their attack, particularly given they were ready to drop some serious cash on Rogers. Here are five players they could move for now...

1. Bradley Barcola

Perhaps the most obvious candidate with Rogers now out of the picture, Arsenal's admiration for Barcola is no secret. Nor is the fact that Liverpool have also courted the Frenchman, so this wouldn't exactly be a foregone conclusion. In fact, at the time of writing, it's now emerged that they are confident of BEATING the Premier League champions to his signature, if both teams decide to make their move.

In terms of quality options for the left wing who are realistically attainable this summer, Barcola is right up there. He would represent an upgrade on the departed Leandro Trossard and Gabriel Martinelli, whose future is uncertain. He has hit double figures for goals in Ligue 1 in each of the last two seasons so can clearly handle the weight of expectation that comes with starring for a team chasing major honours. As impressive as Barcola is, PSG's embarrassment of riches in attack and their interest in Yan Diomande makes him disposable — much to Arsenal's benefit.

‌



2. Yan Diomande

View 5 Images Yan Diomande is on the radar of plenty of clubs this summer (Image: Joe Prior/Visionhaus via Getty Images)

Yes, Diomande is seemingly leaning towards a move to PSG if he is sold by RB Leipzig this summer despite strong interest from Liverpool. But maybe Arsenal could pull a hijack of their own if there is an appetite to acquire a marquee name for their attack.

Young, dynamic and capable of excelling on either wing, Diomande would be a real statement signing for Arsenal if things were to fall into place. One obstacle to a deal could be Leipzig's asking price; Liverpool indicated that they were prepared to pay €100m (£86.8m) to sign the 19-year-old. Leipzig are understood to be holding out for €130m (£110.9m)

‌



3. Kenan Yildiz

View 5 Images Kenan Yildiz is a player Arsenal are known to admire (Image: (Photo by Image Photo Agency/Getty Images))

Yildiz is another player Arsenal are no stranger to given previous links to him. It emerged earlier this month that an enquiry for the 21-year-old Turkish sensation had been knocked back by Juventus, forcing Arsenal to take their search elsewhere.

But with Rogers now off the table, maybe it's time for Arsenal to really test Juventus' resolve by laying down some serious money for Yildiz. Unlike his current club, Arsenal would be unable to offer Yildiz Champions League football. That, plus the chance to be one of the main men in Arsenal's new-look attack, could prove to be persuasive.

‌



4. Marcus Rashford

View 5 Images Marcus Rashford could still leave Manchester United this summer (Image: Tullio Puglia - FIFA, FIFA via Getty Images)

This would raise eyebrows, no doubt. But Rashford is a proven, Premier League-ready player. Would it really be that big a punt to pursue the England star after a fine season on loan at Barcelona?

We all know Rashford has had his challenges in recent years. But on his day he is a matchwinner. The caveat is that it isn't his day enough. A fresh start with a strong XI around him, in the familiar surroundings of the Premier League, could make Rashford a shrewd option. Any deal would come in far cheaper than alternatives on this list, too, meaning Arsenal could also spend more elsewhere.

‌



5. Nico Williams

View 5 Images Nico Williams signed a new contract at Athletic Club last summer but has a chunky release clause (Image: Getty Images)

A player Arsenal are no stranger to following links to the Spain international in the past, could a move for Williams be resurrected?

Williams was pursued strongly last summer, only to sign an extraordinary 10-year contract to commit his future to Athletic Bilbao. But with Arsenal now showing they are the real deal after winning the Premier League and coming so close to doubling that up with the Champions League, perhaps Williams could now be lured to north London.

Article continues below

He would be an upgrade on Arsenal's current left wing options. And stranger things have definitely happened when it comes to transfers. After all, Williams' contract is said to include a £90m release clause, so maybe he won't spend the next decade in Bilbao.
