Sports.title: Anthony Taylor's biggest controversies, huge career earnings and real reason for quitting
Sports.content:
Anthony Taylor's biggest controversies, huge career earnings and real reason for quitting

Anthony Taylor has been involved in some controversy moments as well as refereeing on the biggest stage

View 4 Images Anthony Taylor went out on a high, taking charge of the World Cup clash between Portugal and Spain (Image: FIFA via Getty Images)

One of English football's most respected referees, Anthony Taylor, has announced his sudden retirement following a career spanning 20 years and more than 800 games. The Manchester official, 47, officiated 668 professional domestic games and oversaw every major English cup final.

‌



Taylor, who was promoted to the Premier League in 2010, refereed at four major tournaments, including the last two World Cups and at the 2020 and 2024 European Championships.

‌



In all, he took charge of 163 international matches and his final game was this month's World Cup last-16 tie between Portugal and Spain. Taylor said: "I want to express my deepest gratitude to my two assistants Gary [Beswick] and Adam [Nunn], my refereeing colleagues and everyone connected with the game for all their support over the years.

‌



"Most importantly, I want to thank my family and friends for their unwavering support throughout the immense sacrifices this career has demanded."

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Controversies

Like any top referee, Taylor has come under fire from managers, players and fans at times during his career. In 2023, he was confronted by Jose Mourinho in a car park following Roma's penalty shootout defeat to Sevilla in the Europa League final in Budapest.

‌



Taylor and his family were then harangued by Roma fans at Budapest Airport. He subsequently told his family to stop coming to his games, saying: "That's for sure the worst situation I've dealt with in terms of abuse.

Premier League referee Anthony Taylor retires from football and teases what's next READ MORE :

Reason why two English referees have been banned from officiating the World Cup final READ MORE :

"Not only because I was travelling with family members at the time, but it also highlights the impact of people's behaviour on others. It makes you reflect back on whether you made a mistake travelling with your family in the first place."

Mourinho, Roma's manager at the time, was charged with using insulting or abusive language and banned for four matches by UEFA.

‌



Taylor was the man in the middle during the Euro 2020 match in which Christian Eriksen collapsed from cardiac arrest. Taylor was praised for his calmness and the speed at which he stopped the match and called for medical attention.

At the following Euros in Germany, Taylor was criticised for failing to award the host nation a penalty in their quarter-final against Spain. Taylor played on after Jamal Musiala's shot was blocked by the arm of Marc Cucarella, with his decision not to award a spot-kick backed by VAR . However, a subsequent UEFA report said Taylor had erred by not awarding the penalty.

View 4 Images Jose Mourinho fumed at Taylor during and after the 2023 Europa League final (Image: PA)

‌



Taylor has had his moments of controversy in the Premier League as well. In September 2024, he dished out a record 14 yellow cards during Chelsea's match against Bournemouth and was demoted to fourth official duty the following week.

Taylor suffered another demotion in 2023, this time to the Championship, after he was deemed to have got it wrong by awarding Newcastle a penalty in a 2-2 draw with Wolves. The following week, instead of a Premier League game, he took charge of Preston vs Coventry at Deepdale, before returning to Premier League action.

Given his longevity and the scrutiny on referees, avoiding controversy was impossible. Taylor was widely regarded as one of the best and vied with Michael Oliver to take charge of English football's biggest games.

‌



View 4 Images Germany players appeal to Taylor during the Euro 2024 quarter-final against Spain (Image: James Baylis - AMA/Getty Images)

Premier League pay

Having spent 16 years refereeing in the English top flight, Taylor will have benefited from the burgeoning pay for officials. While not in the same league as the players he was taking charge of, he will have been earning around £250,000 per year at the time of his retirement.

While the average wage of a Premier League referee is around the £180,000 mark, as one of the best and most experienced officials, he will have been one of the top earners. Those figures do not include match fees, which exceed £1,000 per game.

‌



Taylor will have worked his way up the pay scale during his time in the Premier League. A conservative estimate would put his top-flight earnings at over £2.5m. He will have received one final match refereeing payday at the World Cup, where officials can earn up to £75,000.

View 4 Images Taylor issues one of his 14 yellow cards during a match between Chelsea and Bournemouth (Image: Ryan Hiscott/Getty Images)

Retirement reason

While Taylor's sudden decision has surprised many within the game, his statement referenced the pressure and scrutiny that come with being a top-tier official.

‌



He said: "Officiating at the elite level has been an immense privilege, but the pressure is intense and the scrutiny is constant. The time is now right to step aside and look forward to transitioning to the next chapter of my career."

The last part of that statement suggests he has already planned his next move. Various roles could open up to him if he follows in the footsteps of the likes of Webb and Mark Clattenburg, who have both held lucrative positions in Saudi Arabian football. Webb has also previously worked with the MLS in the US.

Sports.title: Antonelli among five drivers to miss Hungarian GP first practice
Sports.content:
Championship leader Kimi Antonelli will be among five drivers to sit out first practice for the Hungarian Grand Prix on Friday.

During the season, each Formula 1 team must run a rookie in at least two practice sessions for both of their cars and the familiarity of the Hungaroring, and it not being a Sprint weekend, means five teams have taken the opportunity to fulfil their obligation.

Antonelli, who leads Lewis Hamilton by 45 points and George Russell by 50 points in the Drivers' Championship, will be replaced by Mercedes reserve driver Frederik Vesti in Friday's first practice session.

Vesti drove Antonelli's car in first practice at the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix last month, so the Italian will not miss any further practice sessions.

But, Russell has yet to hand his car over to a rookie so will miss two practice sessions during the 11 scheduled rounds following the summer break.

"I'm really excited to get back behind the wheel of the W17 and continue building my experience with the car. It's a great opportunity and one I'm looking forward to making the most of," said Vesti, who was the 2023 Formula 2 runner-up.

Image: Frederik Vesti is Mercedes' reserve driver (Memmler/picture-alliance/dpa/AP Images)

Which rookies will be running in Hungarian first practice? Mercedes - Frederik Vesti (Kimi Antonelli)

McLaren - Leonardo Fornaroli (Oscar Piastri)

Alpine - Paul Aron (Franco Colapinto)

Haas - Ryo Hirakawa (Oliver Bearman)

Cadillac - Colton Herta (Valtteri Bottas)

F2 champion Fornaroli replaces Piastri amid Haas rumours

Reigning Formula 2 champion Leonardo Fornaroli will make his second Friday outing of the season when he takes over Oscar Piastri's car at McLaren.

Fornaroli, who won the F3 and F2 titles in consecutive seasons in 2024 and 2025, drove Lando Norris' car in Barcelona last month and has been linked to a Haas seat for next year.

Also in June, McLaren loaned the 21-year-old Italian out to Haas for a TPC (Testing of Previous Cars) test amid speculation Fornaroli could join Haas full-time in 2027 to replace Esteban Ocon.

"At the moment we are not deciding anything. We're simply keeping the options open. We are not in a hurry, but Leo did a great job [in the test]," said Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu.

Image: Leonardo Fornaroli celebrates winning the 2025 F2 title

Haas' Oliver Bearman will also miss first practice in Budapest as Ryo Hirakawa gets his second outing of the season, while Paul Aron will have his third of 2026 when he drives Franco Colapinto's Alpine.

Aron was previously loaned out to Audi earlier this year for practice sessions in Barcelona and Austria.

Former IndyCar star Colton Herta will also be in action in first practice as he gets behind the wheel of Valtteri Bottas' Cadillac.

Sports.title: 'Silly Mr Bodybuilder!' - Fury casts doubt over Joshua fight
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury says he is prepared to "fight somebody else" at the end of 2026 if his long-awaited showdown with Anthony Joshua does not go ahead.

Fury is fighting this Friday in Thailand against Poland's Mariusz Wach, although the fight will not be broadcast, before Joshua fights on Saturday against Kristian Prenga in Saudi Arabia.

Should Fury and Joshua win their warm-up fights, they have agreed to finally meet each other in November or December later this year - although a date and venue is yet to be announced.

However, speaking to Dev Sahni on Sky Sports News, Fury cast doubt on the fight with Joshua in an expletive rant about his compatriot.

"Let's not make this about silly Mr Bodybuilder. I'm not interested in him or his mates or anybody else. I don't give a **** about him. I don't care if I ever see him again in my life. If I do, I do. If I don't, I don't," he said.

"I'm not interested in him, anybody should do for him - his manager, his wife, his sister, his cousin. No interest.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Barry Jones discusses the best iterations of former World champions Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua

"We have got five months left of the year, so I want to get this fella [Wach] boxed, do well, and do what I can.

"I know I can beat this fella. I beat this fella with one hand, and that's not to say anything bad about Mariusz, but I'm in good form. I could beat all of these heavyweights with one hand. But I'm in good shape. I'm in fine fettle, injury-free and I'm ready to rock and roll.

"There's five months to get another fight in before the end of year ends. And if it is your man Anthony Joshua, good. And if it's not, then I'll be fighting somebody else."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Barry Hearn backs Anthony Joshua to beat Tyson Fury when the British rivals finally meet later this year, insisting Wembley Stadium is the ideal venue for fans

Fury has no plans to watch Joshua's fight

Fury's fight with Wach on Friday will take place at around 4pm UK time in front of 1,500 spectators in Pattaya, with Joshua fighting on Saturday night in Jeddah.

Joshua attended Fury's victory over Arslanbek Makhmudov in April earlier this year in London but Fury will not travel to Saudi Arabia.

"I'm going home. I've got about as much interest in Anthony Joshua versus 'some Pringles' as I have of spewing that all over the floor. None. I'm going home. I'm not interested in AJ and his mate boxing," he said.

Asked if facing off against Joshua in Saudi Arabia on Saturday would send a signal to everyone that the fight is happening, Fury added: "You can send out as many signals as you want.

"You've been told for 10 years it's happening. It hasn't happened, has it? So don't hold your breath. I've always had my doubts. But if it happens, good. If it doesn't, also good."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Turki Al-Sheikh provides an update on where Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua will take place. Credit: SELA.

Fury: Wach is a tough man

Wach was last a heavyweight world champion in 2012 but has continued to fight annually, although has lost eight of his last 12 fights.

The 46-year-old wants to "ruin" the plans of Fury fighting Joshua and Fury is not overlooking his opponent.

"It's going to be crazy but I'm looking forward to the challenge. It's going to be good," said 'The Gypsy King'.

"He's a tough man. He's a veteran, and he's been around the game 20 years plus. So he's a dangerous man, a big heavyweight and anything can happen. I've got to obviously be wary of him and be on my A-game and do what I do.

"I've been out here 10 weeks training, so I'm not left any stones unturned. I'm ready to go. I'm in great shape and I'm fit as a fiddle."

Sports.title: Why Hungary could ignite Hamilton's title fight against Antonelli
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton says Ferrari must "come and fight for the win" at this weekend's Hungarian Grand Prix while McLaren boss Andrea Stella expects the Scuderia to be "extremely competitive".

Ferrari and Mercedes have shared two wins each in the last four rounds although the Silver Arrows have had the upper hand on outright pace for most of the season.

Kimi Antonelli, who is now 45 points in front of Hamilton and 50 points ahead of George Russell in the Drivers' Championship, was on flying form last weekend in Belgium, even overturning the misfortune of not being able to pit under a Virtual Safety Car to beat Charles Leclerc on Sunday.

However, Ferrari were closer than anticipated at Spa-Francorchamps which bodes well for the Hungaroring as the track features lots of corners and that should play into Ferrari's hands.

"I think in Hungary, the Netherlands we will see the Ferrari being back to probably being the fastest car we see in the corners there. Extremely competitive," Stella told Sky Sports F1.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Despite being given a five-second penalty for an opening lap collision with George Russell, Lewis Hamilton was left more frustrated with his performance over the weekend as he finished fourth in Belgium

Hamilton has a record eight wins at the Hungarian Grand Prix but five-second time penalties at the last two races mean he has not challenged for victory since his triumph at the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix last month.

"I'm hoping we can be [competitive]. I need to come correct this week and make sure I deliver the way I know I can deliver in Budapest," he said.

"We have to come and fight for that win."

Why Ferrari might be the team to beat in Budapest

Ferrari have been the benchmark in the corners this year while their main weakness has been their power unit, although they have closed their deficit to Mercedes and Red Bull recently.

The last two tracks - Silverstone and Spa-Francorchamps - relied on a strong power unit due to the long flat out zones but the Hungaroring is largely about the chassis.

Energy deployment, or a lack of, will not be an issue so the cars with the best chassis will be strong, so Sky Sports F1's Karun Chandhok thinks we could see a repeat of Barcelona - where Hamilton was victorious.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton claimed his first win in red at the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix

"Ferrari have been behind Mercedes if you look at the trend across the season, apart from Barcelona where I think Lewis Hamilton genuinely had the outright pace to beat Mercedes," said Chandhok.

"I think Ferrari will be very strong [in Budapest]. We saw in Barcelona the aerodynamic package and the cornering speeds of the Ferrari is very strong."

Sky Sports F1's Bernie Collins added: "Hungary and Zandvoort (the first race after the summer break) are both tracks where the straight-line performance is not tested on these cars, or any car at all. Those are downforce circuits where you are trying to get the most out of the car through those corners and that will promote Ferrari."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lewis Hamilton watches back his first Ferrari win at the Barcelona-Catalunya GP in the cool down room alongside George Russell and Lando Norris

Vasseur, Leclerc play down Ferrari chances

There were similar expectations about Ferrari heading into the Monaco Grand Prix in June, only for Antonelli to convert pole position into victory.

Leclerc said: "I think it's very difficult to predict the level of performance of every team. I recall very well what the overall feeling was before Monaco, and we arrived in Monaco and were underperforming compared to what everybody thought we would, so I think we need to be cautious.

"We just need to do our homework, just like we do at every different track. I think what we did particularly well over these last two weekends was to really make sure that we maximised our package, and that's the mentality we should keep for Budapest, without thinking about expectations."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Charles Leclerc wins the British Grand Prix after the Safety Car was redeployed at the last moment for the final lap

But, Ferrari have brought upgrades to the car since Monaco which further improved their cornering performance. Nevertheless, Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur is also managing expectations.

"I think everybody will bring upgrades and we don't know the picture of the performance. Everybody is pushing," he said.

"You have a lot of performance in the execution on tyre management, tyre preparation, set-up, and the layout of the track. I think if we do the same qualify of job as this weekend, it will pay off, but it is not a given. It's not a given for us and not a given for the others. Each weekend we are starting from scratch.

"For sure on paper the layout like Silverstone and Spa are probably a bit more difficult than some others. But on the other hand, in Monaco, we are not shining. That means we have to continue to push, to keep the same approach and never think that it will be ease, because it is never easy."

Hilltop, Kaori and Mojito contest a trappy-looking Download The At The Races App Fillies' Handicap at Lingfield.

Top weight Hilltop is a consistent performer who ran another solid race when third over this course and distance in May and should give another bold bid off the same mark.

Jack Jones' in-form mare landed her final start for trainer Henry Daly in May and has two wins from two starts for her new connections. She stayed on strongly when outpointing Fringill Dike at Market Rasen and this looks a good opportunity to follow up despite a 2lb rise.

Harry Hope looks a danger for the Ben Pauling and Jones combination. He has an excellent strike-rate over fences and should strip fitter for his last outing at Stratford.

Axel Bleue scored over this track and trip 21 days ago and remains unexposed over fences.

Media Mogul recorded a first hurdling success when challenging late over this course and distance last month and makes appeal as he heads into handicaps off a mark 105.

Sports.title: Southampton boss Eckert charged by FA over Spygate scandal
Sports.content:
Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert has been charged by the FA with misconduct and potentially bringing the game into disrepute over the 'Spygate' scandal.

The EFL expelled Southampton from the Championship play-offs in May and handed the club a four-point deduction for the 2026/27 season after they admitted "multiple breaches" relating to the unauthorised filming of their opponents' training, including before their semi-final against Middlesbrough.

Southampton beat Middlesbrough and were due to play Hull City in the play-off final before Boro were reinstated. Southampton appealed the decision, but the punishments were upheld by a League Arbitration Panel.

During the Spygate hearing, the EFL only had the power to charge clubs, not individuals. The FA waited for the EFL process to run its course before launching its own investigation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Keith Downie explains how Spygate unfolded at Middlesbrough's training ground.

The FA has now charged Eckert with three breaches of rule E3.1, during the period between December 2025 and May 2026, by "directing and/or observing" training sessions of Oxford United, Ipswich Town and Middlesbrough ahead of fixtures against those clubs.

Rule E3.1 states: "A participant shall at all times act in the best interests of the game and not act in any manner which is improper or brings the game into disrepute or use any one, or a combination of violent conduct, serious foul play, threatening, abusive, indecent or insulting words or behaviour".

In response, Southampton say they remain "fully supportive" of Eckert and will "continue to cooperate fully and openly with The FA".

Eckert has until Tuesday July 28 to provide his responses.

Eckert 'loved' spying information

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Southampton boss Tonda Eckert 'loved' the information gathered by a junior analyst intern when spying on one of his team's opponents, according to newly released messages.

In June, Eckert said he took full responsibility "for everything that happened", apologising to players, staff and supporters.

At that time, Southampton chairman Dragan Solak admitted Eckert had made a "mistake" but said the club was "fully behind him", reaffirming their target of winning promotion to the Premier League.

In the written reasons released following the League Arbitration Panel's decision to dismiss Southampton's appeal against their punishment, Saints' conduct was described as a "contrived and determined plan from the top down".

Eckert "loved" the information a junior analyst intern gathered when spying on one of his team's opponents, according to messages used as evidence in the hearing.

The written reasons detail how analysts felt pressure to carry out jobs asked of them as a colleague had lost their job earlier in the season.

The panel added: "A reprimand is considered appropriate because of the way in which junior members of staff were put under pressure to carry out activities which they felt were, at the least, morally wrong."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking exclusively to Sky Sports' Mark McAdam, Southampton boss Tonda Eckert reveals the challenges he has faced after the Spygate scandal that resulted in their expulsion from the Championship play-offs.

Eckert told Sky Sports News last week that he had received police protection amid threats during the Spygate scandal.

"It's been an emotional summer. I can't lie, obviously, when the news broke towards the back end of last season, it's tough. It's not easy in that very moment. It's not easy to look into the eyes of the players. They're just so disappointed, and so many emotions coming out.

"You get so many threats at one point. You have police protection at one point; you can't drive a car. It's tough to deal with that for the very moment.

"When things calmed down with time, and I went back home, different challenges at home, you have a moment to reflect. I think that over the months there's also been a lot of positives that we can take into next season.

"After a couple of weeks, that excitement comes back in to go again and show what we are about. That's been the feeling since coming back into the training ground. We are in the second week of pre-season now. Players have come back in very good shape, with a smile on their face and ready to go again."

Spygate timeline: How did we get here?

May 7: Middlesbrough make formal complaint to the EFL alleging a Southampton member of staff spied on their training session three days before their Championship play-off semi-final first leg.

May 9: Boro boss Kim Hellberg accuses Southampton of cheating after the first leg ends in a 0-0 draw at the Riverside Stadium.

May 12: Southampton charged with a breach of EFL regulations in relation to the spying accusations. Southampton request additional time to conduct an internal review.

The play-off semi-final second leg is played at St Mary's. Shea Charles' extra-time winner earns Southampton a 2-1 victory and a place in the Championship play-off final.

Emotional Hellberg hits out at "disgraceful spying", before Saints boss Tonda Eckert storms out of his press conference after being asked: "Are you a cheat?"

May 13: Photos allegedly showing the Southampton analyst near Middlesbrough's training ground released publicly.

May 14: It is announced the independent hearing to determine Southampton's fate will take place on or before Tuesday May 19. In a statement, the EFL say "the outcome of the disciplinary proceedings may yet result in changes to the fixture."

May 15: Middlesbrough publicly call for Southampton's expulsion from the play-offs. In a statement, they said: "In these circumstances, the only appropriate response is a sporting sanction which would prevent Southampton FC from participating in the EFL Championship play-off final."

May 18: Middlesbrough players return to training as the outcome of the independent disciplinary hearing nears.

May 19: EFL announces Southampton expelled from play-off final after hearing.

May 20: Southampton appeal rejected.

May 21: FA confirm they will begin their own investigation into Spygate.

May 23: Middlesbrough lose 1-0 to Hull City in the Championship play-off final.

June 1: WhatsApp messages reveal Eckert "loved" spying information despite the concerns of junior members of Southampton staff.

June 2: Eckert takes full responsibility for Spygate as Southampton owner Dragan Solak backs head coach.

June 17: Eckert tells Sky Sports News he received police protection amid threats during Spygate.

July 22: FA charges Southampton head coach Eckert with three breaches of rule E3.1.

"Playing for this club is all I've ever wanted to do and it's always an honour to wear the shirt.

"It's not lost on me that I've been lucky enough to be part of a historic period with so many titles won, but we're always looking to the future and trying to win more.

"I can only thank the club, staff, team-mates and fans who continue to put their faith in me and trust that I give everything I can for City and I hope I'll be able to repay you for years to come.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports football journalist Laura Hunter says Enzo Maresca won't be afforded time to excel as Manchester City boss.

"I can't wait to work with Enzo [Maresca] again. He was brilliant during the Treble season - someone all the players respected and loved working with. To have him back here is exciting.

"Personally, I know I've improved so much from working with our coaches and world-class squad and as many of the legends who were here when I first broke through move on, I am excited for the next phase of my career at this great club."

Foden has made 369 appearances and scored 110 goals for City's first team since making his debut in a Champions League game against Feyenoord on November 21 2017.

Image: The 26-year-old has won 20 trophies with City

In 2025/26, he played 50 times, scoring 10 goals and providing seven assists.

Alongside John Stones and Bernardo Silva - who both left the Etihad this summer - the academy graduate is the most decorated player in the club's history, having won 20 major trophies, including six Premier League titles, one UEFA Champions League, three FA Cups, five League Cups, one UEFA Super Cup, one FIFA Club World Cup and three Community Shields.

Foden needs to reinvent himself - now might be the perfect time

Analysis by Sky Sports' Laura Hunter:

The curious case of Phil Foden, once a boy wonder, now somewhat of an afterthought. His omission from this summer's England group was expected but will have been no less dispiriting.

This is a player that England built their Euro 2024 bid around.

Since then, the 26-year-old has only exhibited flashes of his immense talent. Consistency has failed him. Pep Guardiola was forced to come to his aid a few times last season, insisting he's still a "top, top player", but it was clear he was no longer trusted to turn up in the big games.

Against that backdrop, a new deal seems bizarrely timed.

And yet, there is some logic to it. City have waved goodbye to Bernardo Silva this summer, leaving a big void in midfield. Guardiola himself is also gone. Foden still holds cohesive power, a player adored by fans because of his Mancunian roots and maverick style.

Now it's up to Enzo Maresca, who knows Foden well, to unlock the quality that resides within. This deal reflects the fact this next period has the potential to be Foden's peak years. A calculated risk, but one worth taking.

Sports.title: Liverpool issue 432 life bans and seize £1.2m in ticket tout investigation
Sports.content:
More than £1.2m in assets have been seized and 432 lifetime bans issued as part of a clampdown by Liverpool FC and Merseyside police on ticket touting. In the first operation of its kind between a Premier League club and their local police authority, Liverpool’s investigations team worked with the force’s economic crime team to analyse almost 700,000 ticket registrations last season and to focus on the laundering of criminal proceeds from illicit ticket sales.

The joint investigation has led to £1.2m in assets related to organised ticket touts being detained with several cases taking place under the Proceeds of Crime Act. Two people have been convicted and another is due in court next month. The assets seized will be split between Merseyside police and the Home Office.

Liverpool blocked or cancelled 67,663 suspected fake accounts last season and a further 121,379 accounts remain under investigation. As well as 432 lifetime bans, the club issued 115 indefinite suspensions where the account holder faces a three-year wait on average before they can apply for reinstatement.

Most bans were imposed for the unauthorised selling of season tickets, membership tickets or hospitality tickets. Lifetime bans and suspensions were also imposed in three cases of racist and homophobic abuse, 13 instances of inappropriate touching or language, four for assault and one for tragedy chanting.

Investigations by the club and police outside Anfield on match days last season resulted in a 33% increase in the number of burner phones either identified or seized.

Detective chief inspector Nick Suffield, from Merseyside police’s economic crime team, said: “We will always take action to protect genuine fans who fall victim to touts when all they are trying to do is simply purchase tickets to support their team.

“Our activities to target touts operating both online and on match days will continue and we work closely with supporters and clubs to keep identifying ticket touts and doing all we can to prevent them taking advantage of supporters and spoiling people’s experience of football and the city.

Sports.title: World Cup 2026 awards: the Guardian team give their final tournament verdicts
Sports.content:
Match of the tournament

Paraguay 1-1 Germany. There were plenty more games with more goals but none could match the drama of the penalty shootout in this last-32 tie. Germany aren’t supposed to lose in them but they did this time in spectacular fashion. Ed Aarons

Algeria 3-3 Austria was a completely strange fever dream, seeming to exist on a separate plane of reality. I know that sounds grandiose but remember, going into this one the expectation was that it would be a biscotto – a meaningless, pre-arranged kickabout where a draw would see both sides through. For a while in the second half, it looked like that would happen. And finally, in stoppage time, chaos. There were certainly better matches in terms of quality, and maybe a couple that had this beat for drama, but no game was weirder. Alexander Abnos

From the 14 I attended, it has to be Mexico 2-3 England at the awesome Azteca. The buildup seemed to start as soon as the draw was made – fortunately the stars aligned and a grippingly tense game ensued in a venue like no other. It was a high point for England that should cut through despite later disappointments, too. Nick Ames

France 4-6 England was borderline hilarious. Egypt 1-1 Iran in Seattle had plenty of late drama, Iran’s disallowed stoppage-time winner bookended by them twice hitting the woodwork in the final minutes. The draw ultimately proved insufficient for unbeaten Iran, faced with endless hurdles, to progress. Ben Fisher

Argentina 3-2 Egypt. The defending champions looked down and out, thinking about their flights home, before a late Lionel Messi-inspired comeback enabled them to claw back a two-goal deficit and win this last-16 match in normal time. Barry Glendenning

The game no one wanted to play. Sid Lowe

Mexico 2-3 England. I have decided that all my answers should relate to things that happened while I was at the tournament and this was one. I mean, I wasn’t there ticking off the “bucket list” of a visit to the Azteca (I think I saw at least half a dozen British hacks claim that), but I did watch it on TV. Besides being like drinking cortisol neat, this was so dramatic, the images so evocative, that even if you are an ardent England fan (as I am) this was pure cinema. Paul MacInnes

View image in fullscreen England’s players sing Wonderwall in front of their fans after their last-16 victory over Mexico. Photograph: José Méndez/EPA

I am biased here in the sense I attended it but Cape Verde 2-2 Uruguay in Miami was superb. Cape Verde’s attitude and discipline were a joy. Such fun to watch. Ewan Murray

Argentina 3-2 Egypt. Incredible drama, despite the questionable behaviour of the referee. Osasu Obayiuwana

Tough to pick from over 100 options, but Mexico 2-3 England with Thomas Tuchel’s men surviving the vaunted Azteca and the best first half Mexico could have mustered narrowly takes this category. Jeff Rueter

Bias says Mexico v England, but Argentina 3-2 Cape Verde was incredible, Sidny Lopes Cabral bending it top right. Max Rushden

For improbable wonder there was Argentina v Cape Verde, for sheer unpredictability there was Mexico v England. Often, though, one is drawn to something more predictable, more familiar: England 1-2 Argentina. Jack Snape

Argentina 3-2 Cape Verde. It’s not a debate. Jacob Steinberg

Argentina 3-2 Egypt. The possibility of a shock, a great Messi-inspired turnaround, a couple of great goals, refereeing controversy … what else do you want? Jonathan Wilson

View image in fullscreen Lionel Messi (second left) fires a shot past Egypt’s keeper Mostafa Shobeir for Argentina’s equaliser in their 3-2 win. Photograph: Elsa/Getty Images

Player of the tournament

Rodri was the standout player for the best team in a tournament where the big stars came to the party but all ultimately fell short. EA

Kylian Mbappé. Yes, his Golden Boot was padded a bit by that insane third-place game, but the France striker was the best player on what looked to be the best team in the tournament ... at least until that loss to Spain in the semi-final. AA

It’s impossible to look further than Rodri, who looks back to his best and absolutely in his element as the fulcrum of this Spain setup. Otherwise it was good to see a World Cup where the stars largely shone. Jude Bellingham, Erling Haaland, Messi and Mbappé were all one more decisive knockout display away from rising above the rest. NA

Rodri. Michael Olise was majestic, though should have scored a hat-trick against England. Bellingham was equally instrumental for Tuchel’s side – it is crazy to think there were people questioning his inclusion in the squad. BF

Rodri – capitán, líder, leyenda. BG

Lionel Messi. SL

Vozinha. What a man. I think it’s largely because his story is so relatable in these parts – middle-aged man finally receives the plaudits he has always deserved! – but the saves were also top drawer. Add in the pedigree of the teams he either shut out or frustrated, and this was an actual fairytale that didn’t need to be spun by any marketing department. And did you know that he’s 40? PM

Pau Cubarsí. EM

Vozinha, the Cape Verde goalkeeper. At 40, and without a club, he was brilliant for the World Cup debutants. OO

While Rodri is an incredibly worthy Golden Ball winner and others made their marks, Erling Haaland leaves this World Cup with the greatest possible souvenirs: a credible if short Golden Boot campaign, a famous first Norwegian foray into the quarter-final stage, and perhaps the biggest boost in star appeal in the lucrative North American market. JR

View image in fullscreen Even the World Cup mascots stand in awe of Erling Haaland. Photograph: Maddie Meyer/Fifa/Getty Images

Hard not to say Rodri although I thought Dani Olmo was great too, and a shout for Pico Lopes. MR

Haaland, Mbappé and Messi have lived up to expectations. But in those moments where a contest teeters – evading pressure with the ball, in transition to defence or staring down a 50-50 – no player has shown his quality more consistently than Rodri. JSn

Rodri. If only England had a player like the Spain captain. JSt

Rodri. As Spain have reverted to a more possession-driven model, their metronome in midfield has been the outstanding figure, setting the tempo and providing control. JW

Goal of the tournament

For sheer drama, it has to be Sidny Lopes Cabral’s brilliant equaliser for Cape Verde against Argentina. His reaction was almost as good as the goal itself, clasping his hands to his head before picking out his girlfriend in the crowd to celebrate with. EA

I mean, it’s Sidny Lopes Cabral v Argentina. But I feel that the goal from Uzbekistan’s Eldor Shomurodov against the Democratic Republic of the Congo deserves mention too: an instinctive, oddly satisfying lob from a tight angle. No other goal in the tournament was quite like it. AA

Julián Alvarez had a largely quiet World Cup but his vicious, swerving long-range goal in extra time against Switzerland was a jaw-dropping moment and lit up the cauldron-like stadium in Kansas City. NA

Those seen in the flesh always seem to score more points. A buzz surrounded Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Kerim Alajbegovic coming into the tournament and the 18-year-old eliminating a clutch of defenders and blasting in, off balance, from the outside of the box against Qatar only enhanced his reputation. Johan Manzambi’s run and pass in the buildup to Breel Embolo’s opener against Algeria was also a joy. BF

View image in fullscreen Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Kerim Alajbegovic is embraced after opening the scoring against Qatar. Photograph: Carlos Barría/Reuters

While Morocco’s superior quality would ultimately see them through their group-stage win against Haiti, Wilson Isidor’s breathtaking long-range strike to put the Caribbean nation 2-1 up was as good a goal as any scored in the World Cup. Ever. BG

Sidny Lopes Cabral, of course. SL

I had the privilege of reading the paper by the Seoul Women’s University on the aerodynamic effect known as “drag crisis” which is particularly common when people smack an Adidas Trionda, so as such I thought a lot of the big hits were overrated. I do, however, exempt Sidny Lopes Cabral from that critique. Absolute long-range worldie from the Cape Verde full-back-cum-winger. That it pegged Argentina to parity in extra time of a knockout round only made it more memorable. PM

Harry Kane’s second for England against DRC. EM

Sidny Lopes Cabral of Cape Verde, against Argentina. Magical goal. OO

I will never, in all my years, be able to recreate the sound that left my body as Sidny Lopes Cabral’s audacious effort against Argentina completed its curl between a diving Emi Martínez and his far post. Masterful execution in an unprecedented moment. One of many proud moments for Cape Verde at this tournament. JR

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Cape Verde’s Sidny Lopes Cabral unleashes his audacious effort … Photograph: Newscom/Alamy

View image in fullscreen … which flies past Argentina’s keeper Emi Martínez to level the scores in extra time. Photograph: Paul Childs/Reuters

Beyond Sidny Lopes Cabral – the disallowed Uzbekistan one (was it Uzbekistan?) – someone walloped one into the top left-hand corner and it didn’t count. MR

Erling Haaland’s second against Brazil, placed into the bottom-right corner from outside the box to seal the upset, was a microcosm of his effectiveness at the tournament: precise and powerful with a hint of whimsy. JSn

Sidny Lopes Cabral’s equaliser for Cape Verde against Argentina was a proper jaw-dropping moment. One of the great World Cup goals. JSt

Wilson Isidor v Morocco. There were more consequential goals, but none struck quite as sweetly or quite as accurately. If Haiti have nothing else, they’ll always have that. JW

Personal highlight

It was a joy to watch Eloy Room’s performance in goal for Curaçao against Ecuador as he broke the World Cup record for the most saves made in a 90-minute match. While Cape Verde’s veteran Vozinha stole most of the headlines for his heroics, the 37-year-old Room clearly enjoyed his moment in the spotlight. “I think I need a statue in Curaçao now,” he joked. EA

Fifa and the stadium authorities typically guard the natural grass pitches heavily, and with good reason. But after the last games in each venue I went to, I loved watching those pitches get taken over by the people whose names you’ll never know but who actually made this tournament run: stadium workers and low-level Fifa staffers, volunteers, security guards, longtime local club representatives and others. Some used the opportunity to have a little kickabout, take selfies, or just run around. An awesome perk for what were almost certainly very hard, stressful jobs over these last several weeks. AA

My first visit to the Azteca was Mexico’s win over Ecuador and I’ve never heard a noise like it. The place really is as magical and monumental as they say. The celebrations afterwards weren’t conducive to a good night’s sleep but were incredible in scale too. Football-wise I’ll also add Messi’s record-breaking goals against Austria in Dallas, which seem an awfully long time ago now but were such a thrill to witness. Those early Argentina games were essentially mass Messi pilgrimages. One more? The view from Monterrey Stadium. Just go, if you can. NA

View image in fullscreen A view of Mexico’s last-32 game against Ecuador from high up inside the Azteca stands. Photograph: Hannah Peters/Fifa/Getty Images

Watching Senegalese journalists pass around a pack of malted milks during their anthem before their collapse against Belgium. And playing eight-a-side with Danny Cipriani, who once spent six weeks training at Tottenham, Harry Kane among his teammates, will stick in the memory. BF

Watching my Irish compatriot Roberto “Pico” Lopes excel while repeatedly putting his body on the line for Cape Verde, his father’s homeland. It would be nice to think Pico’s performances will earn him a life-changing move to a more lucrative league in the twilight of his career but his age could stand against him and he may well be content with being a Shamrock Rovers and Cape Verde legend. BG

Explaining to a mariachi in a gigantic sombrero how it could possibly be that a team in third could get through the group and how it might still be Spain turning up at the Azteca. Alas, it wasn’t. Sharing a birthday with Martin Ainstein and Luis de la Fuente and my family. And watching a motorcade with the Spain bus pass from the sixth-floor window where Lee Harvey Oswald shot JFK was pretty surreal. SL

I loved watching both France eviscerate Sweden and the Instagram reels of Americans acting like they thought the Tartan Army had permanently changed their lives. PM

View image in fullscreen Members of the Tartan Army have a kickabout in a Boston street. Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Reuters

Players running out to warm-up to the tune of Scotland the Brave, via bagpipes, before the game against Haiti in Foxborough. Scotland’s 28-year World Cup wait was over. The less said about all that happened next, the better. EM

Seeing Vozinha’s mum, against all expectations, travelling from Cape Verde to the World Cup to see her son play. OO

Having covered the nation’s third-to-fifth most popular sport for more than a decade and lived through ICE’s heinous occupation of Minnesota this winter, the sheer scale of interest in soccer was overwhelming and so invigorating – a welcome reprieve in the isolationist second Trump era. Impossible to go through a couple of hours in a World Cup host city without some stranger striking up a conversation about the sport. Long may this remain a part of American society. JR

Shouting Paraguay. Number 10. Cover his mouth. Decision is RED CARD. Jonathan Wilson thinking Robbie Williams was Kevin Pietersen. Mark Langdon’s chow mein bridge. The pancakes at Mile End Deli. Doing a live show in Manhattan and legitimately getting to say “HELLO NEW YORK!” MR

Covering Australia, the tournament petered out from an extraordinary high. Twenty-six minutes into the Socceroos’ opening victory against Turkey, goalscorer Nestory Irankunda revived Tim Cahill’s goal celebration in a ceremonial handover to mark a new generation. JSn

View image in fullscreen Australia’s Nestory Irankunda throws punches while shadowboxing the corner flag, à la Tim Cahill. Photograph: Kaleb Tatum/AP

Being at the Azteca for Mexico 2-3 England. It did not have the most quality but it was hard to beat as an occasion. An epic night at an iconic stadium. A thunderstorm pushing kick-off back, a brilliant display from Bellingham, everyone exhausted when it was over. Things didn’t end well for England but this was easily their greatest away win. JSt

Standing knee-deep in raging floods in Monterrey waiting for a bus having only gone to the stadium to collect a mislaid iPad that I then lost in Houston a week later anyway. That or the weirdly beautiful flyovers outside Dallas. JW

What did you make of the hosts?

The level of interest from the American public surprised me and it was fascinating to meet so many who were interested in what was happening in the tournament. Many people in the US definitely caught World Cup fever. Logistically it was a real test of endurance with so much travelling required between venues and that wasn’t helped by so many being miles from the city centre. And it would have been much better to have played the final in Mexico City or Atlanta’s impressive downtown stadium. EA

I felt unfortunate not to make it to any games in Mexico and only one in Canada. But overall I’m happy that the everyday people who populate the US seemed to show visitors their good side throughout the month. This country has plenty of infrastructure issues I’d like to have seen fixed, but the personal impact is arguably more important, and it seems like the US mostly got that right. AA

If first impressions are everything then I refer you to the often troubling weirdness of the Texas Republican party convention in Houston. But more seriously I was very happy, in the US, to find the hoped-for warmth and openness pretty much everywhere – and in bundles. In their different ways, people really did engage with the World Cup. Less welcome was the US administration’s attempt, duly pandered to by Fifa, to bend the course of the tournament with Folarin Balogun’s reprieve. In Mexico I found a fervent, febrile, fascinating football culture that deserved not to be dwarfed by other co-hosts. NA

Americans love a big-ticket event but it was clear they were hooked by Mauricio Pochettino’s side as they progressed. It was a privilege to witness Canada’s first World Cup game on home soil in Toronto, where there was a match-day buzz and an afterglow despite being held to a draw by Bosnia and Herzegovina. BF

View image in fullscreen Canada fans react to Cyle Larin’s goal during their opening group game against Bosnia and Herzegovina. Photograph: Joosep Martinson/Fifa/Getty Images

While I didn’t meet Donald Trump, the handful of Americans whose acquaintance I did make – hotel staff, a few bartenders and one LA-based reality TV show star – could not have been friendlier. BG

So many people came up to us to say they really hoped we were enjoying this and that we understood that that wasn’t them. We did and they were so nice. SL

I spent two days in Toronto, around Canada Day, and I think they were both welcoming and very keen to hear that they qualified as an actual football nation. People in the US were pleasant, although for travelling fans most experiences will have been complicated by the ubiquitous request for a tip. I did think, though, that sometimes there was an expectation that we should all be delighted to be there. Which we were, but perhaps not for the reasons some wanted. PM

Canada and Mexico? Excellent. US stadiums were first class, as was the extent to which the nation embraced the World Cup. It is just impossible to ignore the stench of the Balogun situation. EM

On an on-field football level? Far from spectacular. The US needs a new player-development architecture to ensure there is a pipeline of high-quality players. They also need a new head coach, with the right vision for the future. Tournament organisation? The fact that Fifa took direct control of it should be a cautionary tale. A local organising committee is always needed. OO

View image in fullscreen Mauricio Pochettino speaks to his USA players after their defeat by Belgium which eliminated the co-hosts. Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/Reuters

All three co-hosts fared about as well as I had projected, but each may have exceeded my expectations in terms of how they went about it. Canada were thrilling at times – I covered their 6-0 win over Qatar at BC Place – and had plenty of pluck with Jesse Marsch as their coach-cum-hype man. The USA played some of the prettiest soccer ever seen by a US national team of any gender, and will for ever rue a missed opportunity to do something greater against Belgium. Mexico were one of the biggest bandwagon teams as they barnstormed Group A, then outclassed an Ecuador team on the rise and pushed England to the brink until they ran out of ideas in the final half-hour. Jobs well done across the board. JR

I had six weeks in America. All the Americans were lovely. MR

This tournament put the whirled in the World Cup, its scale ensuring it evaded generalisation. Cities such as Vancouver and Seattle – with downtown stadiums and soccer traditions – were fitting hosts, while metropolises such as Dallas and San Francisco accommodated the month-long novelty without embracing it. JSn

The people in Mexico could not have been more welcoming, even when England beat their side. It was the same in Kansas City, England’s base and where I spent most of my time. On the other hand it would have been better if getting around some US cities was easier. Public transport infrastructure isn’t really a thing in some places. Florida especially. The Boston traffic was ridiculous, too. JSt

A wide range depending on venue but broadly friendly, welcoming and enthusiastic. Would benefit from improved public transport and generally lower volume. Wifi hopeless, coffee weak. JW

Sports.title: New faces, gulfs in class and flawed drama: how 48 teams changed the World Cup
Sports.content:
It was less than 12 months after Gianni Infantino succeeded Sepp Blatter as president that Fifa announced the expansion of the men’s World Cup from 32 to 48 teams. The reaction was mixed. Diego Maradona said he was “delighted by Gianni’s initiative” because it allowed each country to dream of reaching the tournament, renewing their passion for football. Joachim Löw, then in charge of world champions Germany, said: “I don’t think it’s a good idea to dilute the sporting value … In the long term, the quality suffers.”

On the evidence of the first 48-team edition, won by Spain after 104 games across five-and-a-half weeks in North America, it’s fair to conclude Maradona and Löw both had a point.

Cape Verde lead new faces

“Football is more than Europe and South America; football is global,” said Infantino after the 48-team format was announced in 2017, and the 2026 World Cup was undeniably a celebration of the sport’s diversity. Africa and Asia benefited more than other confederations when it came to greater qualifying quotas and all four debutants had their moments. Livano Comenencia’s equaliser for Curaçao against Germany was a group-stage highlight and Cape Verde were the tournament’s biggest underdog story, even if they didn’t win a game.

Adding the last 32 also gave six nations the opportunity to play knockout football at a World Cup for the first time, with Egypt and Canada recording their first such wins. With Infantino likely to spread the tournament’s record revenues across Fifa’s member associations, you could argue that the smaller nations – especially those drawing on a previously untapped diaspora – will only get stronger in future tournaments.

View image in fullscreen Egypt won their first World Cup knockout game, beating Australia on penalties. Photograph: Julio Cortez/AP

Gulf in class

With a bigger tournament came a wider disparity between opponents in the group stage. At the last 32-team World Cup in Qatar, Brazil versus Haiti was the biggest group mismatch, with a difference of 77 in their world rankings. In this tournament there were five group games with gaps of more than 65 places. Some of these were competitive – England 0-0 Ghana, Spain 0-0 Cape Verde. But there was little chance of a shock defeat for the big guns, let alone a humiliating group exit like those suffered by holders Spain in 2014 or Germany in 2018. A poor Uruguay were the only major early casualty this time around.

Whereas Costa Rica had the worst goal difference in 2022 (-8), there were five nations who either matched that or did worse in 2026. Iraq (-11) were the whipping boys in Group I – the closest to a group of death as the 48-team format could muster with France, Norway and Senegal, who all progressed in predictable fashion. The more pedestrian group stage did at least offer star names such as Kylian Mbappé and Lionel Messi a chance to gain some real momentum in a memorable race for the Golden Boot.

Flawed third-place system

After the drama of the 2022 group stage, where only two teams (about 6%) were officially out before the final round of fixtures, Fifa changed their plans for three-team groups for the expanded 48-team format and stuck with four-team groups, with eight third-place teams heading through to the last 32. This did not entirely bury the question of collusion between teams nor the fact that those playing later had a competitive advantage in knowing what result they needed to progress.

Knockout opponents could also change in an instant. When Riyad Mahrez put Algeria 3-2 up against Austria in the 93rd minute of the final game in Group J, it meant Algeria would go through as runners-up to play Spain in the last 32. When they conceded an equaliser in the 96th minute, it meant they would face Switzerland on the other side of the draw. Players and fans of third-place finishers like Scotland were also forced to hang around for several days before finding out they were, in fact, going home.

View image in fullscreen When Austria and Algeria met in Group J, the outcome (and therefore the last-32 lineup) was in doubt until the final seconds Photograph: Phil Noble/Reuters

With the shift from goal difference to head-to-head as a tie-breaker, there were five teams (about 10%) already eliminated before their final group game, the third-place system giving an illusion that everything would still be to play for.

What about 64 teams?

Infantino again stressed the importance of organising the World Cup “not just for Europe and South America” when he dropped the hint of an expansion to 64 teams. Adding an extra 16 nations – but only 24 more games – seems like a logical next step for Fifa if they want to do away with the third-place system and return to the top-two-go-through group format. There would at least be some jeopardy, although the disparity within the groups would be even greater.

Nations such as New Caledonia (ranked 151) and Indonesia (118) were involved in late-stage qualifying for the 2026 edition and could make it in with higher quotas. How would they fare against Spain or Argentina? And with the world’s 16 best teams all in the same pot, glamour group ties – which were already in short supply this time – would probably be a thing of the past. England 4-2 Croatia would not have happened with 64 teams.

Then there is the logistical issue of playing four games a day for a three-week group stage – with many matches taking place during the summer daytime heat in Spain, Portugal and Morocco. Of the 23 proposed venues, only the revamped Bernabéu and Camp Nou would have roofs. Further expansion will be a hot topic in the months to come, for sure.

Sports.title: Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert charged with misconduct by FA over spygate scandal
Sports.content:
Southampton’s manager, Tonda Eckert, is facing a lengthy suspension from all football activity after being charged with three counts of misconduct by the Football Association.

They relate to the Spygate scandal and involve breaching FA rules during covert missions to illicitly observe Championship training sessions involving Middlesbrough, Ipswich and Oxford last season.

The 33-year-old has until Tuesday to respond to the charges and may well fear the precedent set by Fifa when it banned Bev Priestman, the English-born former Canada women’s head coach and assistant England women coach, from football worldwide for 12 months.

In 2024 Priestman, then in charge of Canada, was found to have authorised the use of a drone to monitor New Zealand’s training during the Paris Olympics.

Southampton have already been punished for Spygate by the English Football League when in May an independent disciplinary commission found the Championship club guilty of three counts of football espionage.

That ruling stripped Eckert’s team of their right to appear in the playoff final in addition to ruling that they must start the coming Championship campaign handicapped by a four-point deduction. The EFL, though, has no power to issue sanctions against individuals in such instances, so the case against Eckert was handed to the FA, which launched a long-running inquiry.

At the start of July the governing body spoke to Eckert, a former analyst for the Germany national team, at length and have the power to issue a range of punishments, ranging from a warning to a heavy fine to suspension.

Yet whereas Priestman’s ban was worldwide, the FA only possess the power to prevent Eckert working in England. The governing body does, however, have the right to ask Fifa to apply any suspension internationally.

In 2023, the Italian FA succeeded with such a request when they demanded that the then Newcastle midfielder Sandro Tonali’s 10-month suspension for betting irregularities be applied worldwide. In Eckert’s case, an England-only ban would appear almost meaningless were he to be offered a job abroad.

Eckert has already apologised to Southampton fans and admitted he should have known that EFL regulations specifically outlawed spying. A coach who grew up within a European culture that tacitly tolerates observing rivals’ training sessions also spoke of the “bitter irony” that Southampton’s three spying missions had “no impact” on his team’s planning or performances.

William Salt, the intern first-team analyst, was caught filming Middlesbrough’s training session on a mobile phone before the first leg of a playoff semi-final won on aggregate by Southampton before their expulsion. He has since been offered a permanent post in the club’s academy. Salt has not been the subject of any FA charges.

Southampton’s owner, Dragan Solak, has vowed to stand by Eckert and has maintained he will not sack him. But a possible 12-month – or, as some sources are suggesting, six-month FA ban – could alter that stance.

In a statement on Wednesday Southampton said: “Tonda and the club will continue to cooperate fully and openly with the FA. Our focus remains on preparations for the 2026-27 season. The club remains fully supportive of Tonda and his staff as we work towards our ambition of returning to the Premier League.”

Eckert, who saw Middlesbrough take Southampton’s place in a playoff final won by Hull, recently told BBC Radio Solent: “I’ve held my hand up for this judgment on something I have authorised. I am responsible and I apologise for bad judgment.”

Back in 2019, the FA issued formal warnings to the then Leeds manager Marcelo Bielsa and a club analyst for spying on Derby, but English football’s regulations have since been tightened.

Sports.title: Financial ‘exceptions’ made for Pep Guardiola to become next Italy head coach
Sports.content:
Financial “exceptions” are in place to allow Pep Guardiola to become Italy’s next head coach, the president of the Italian Football Federation (FIGC), Giovanni Malago, has said.

Guardiola left Manchester City at the end of last season after winning six Premier League titles, three FA Cups, five League Cups and the Champions League during a hugely successful 10-year reign.

The Spaniard is free to take up another job, having also coached Barcelona and Bayern Munich, and has been linked with the Italy vacancy for some time, with it reported earlier this week that he has held talks with the FIGC.

Gennaro Gattuso resigned from the post in April after the four-time World Cup champions failed to qualify for a third tournament in a row.

“[Financial] exceptions have been made, exceptions that for example may concern the name that is so overbearing in these hours: Pep Guardiola,” Malago is quoted as saying by Gazzetta dello Sport. “Exceptions for obvious reasons that I am not here to explain, but it is not certain that this thing will go through.”

Roberto Mancini, who led Italy to Euro 2020 glory, and the former Azzurri midfielder Andrea Pirlo are other reported candidates for the vacancy.

Asked if Guardiola, Mancini and Pirlo were the only names on the shortlist, Malago added: “Absolutely not. We think about a certain profile and certainly these names fall into that category.”

Italian football ​has hit its ​lowest point in nearly 40 ​years, following an early wholesale exit from European club competitions last season ​and the ‌failure to reach ​the World Cup.

The ​appointment of a new national coach is viewed as the first step in overhauling a youth and talent infrastructure that has largely collapsed. Italy’s next fixture is the Nations League Group A match against Belgium on 25 September.

Sports.title: Football Daily | Chelsea’s financial shrug and Liverpool leaking players – what you may have missed
Sports.content:
TIME FOR A RECAP

After the eye-watering excess of the Geopolitics World Cup, we can return to the modest, measured land of the domestic game. While our attention has been elsewhere, Manchester City have splashed £116m on Elliot Anderson. Chelsea, not to be outshone, have splurged £117m on Morgan Rogers. Even Tottenham have parted with £230m to revamp their mildly traumatised squad. Manchester United, who went down to Wrexham in their first pre-season friendly in Helsinki, have kept things modest, buying Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans for the same £85m Spurs have thrown in the direction of relegation’s West Ham for Mateus Fernandes.

Liverpool, who blew all their dosh last summer, are one of three Premier League heavyweights under new management. Andoni Iraola, it seems, is more concerned with stemming the flow of departures from his inherited squad after Mohamed Salah, Andy Robertson and Ibrahima Konaté all slipped out. The smiley Spaniard gave his transfer strategy away this week and blurted: “I want to keep my good players.” Any big club with a short memory will be keen on Alexis Mac Allister, while Iraola is also keen to hold on to his experienced players. “We need the references like Virgil [van Dijk], Alisson, Joe Gomez,” he doubletaked from the USA USA USA, where Liverpool will take on exotic friendly opposition in Sunderland, Wrexham and Leeds.

Over at Chelsea, Xabi Alonso was last seen standing over the shoulder of club-record fee’s Rogers as he signed his contract, presumably to make sure he didn’t do a runner. The nine-figure outlay is an expensive way of keeping Rogers’ good mate Cole Palmer happy and a sort of financial shoulder shrug from a club who posted a £355m loss in the 2024-25 season. Chelsea have also spent more than £100m on Marco Palestra, Geovany Quenda and Emmanuel Emegha (all real players) this summer as they bid to reach the holy grail that is Tin Pot qualification. Pre-season takes them to Australia, Hong Kong, Indonesia and Malaysia – but Marc Cucurella won’t be there. He’s been shipped off to Real Madrid, raising funds for the polish needed to keep that glorious Copa Gianni shiny, Chelsea wondering if he still thinks about them.

Manchester City have moved on from the Pep Guardiola era by auctioning off the contents of his office for charity, including his whistle, notes, desk chair and coffee cups. Football Daily was outbid for his incense collection, which reached £1,294 this morning. Enzo Maresca can console himself with the arrival of Anderson, another of England’s brave bronze medallists, before City fly out to Hong Kong for a meeting with Inter in the Asahi Super Dry Trophy. That’s followed by dates with the K League All-Stars and Atlético Madrid in Seoul. “City is an incredibly well-run football club,” Maresca tooted, no doubt remembering his days at Stamford Bridge. Amid the GWC noise, Chelsea produced a statement blaming last season’s failings on “the disruption caused” by Maresca’s resignation in January. They referred to him as “the Head Coach” throughout with the sort of bitterness and rogue capital letters you’d expect from a Truth Social post. If Donald Trump has really fallen for soccer, maybe he’ll be there to gatecrash another trophy celebration in August. Roll on the Community Shield!

QUOTE OF THE DAY

double quotation mark I was pleased with a lot of things that I saw in the game. We could do better. We could have taken more responsibility to have the ball instead of just watching and reacting … efficiency is very important at this level. When you don’t kill, you get killed” – new Hearts boss Wouter Vrancken chooses to focus on the positives after the, erm, 4-0 tonking by Sturm Graz in the first leg of their Bigger Cup qualifier.

Not only were Hearts, Larne, Shamrock Rovers and Lincoln Red Imps all beaten in their second qualifying round first legs, they didn’t manage a single goal among them! Larne were were given no home comforts on the coast of Northern Ireland by Red Star Belgrade, who brought on Marko Arnautovic, the Austria veteran who retired from his national side after exiting the GWC at the hands of Spain. Sports.title: Putellas, Batlle and León are gone: what will be left of Barcelona after latest exodus?
Sports.content:
The joy of lifting all four trophies in 2025-26 has been short-lived for Barcelona’s women’s team as they face a second consecutive summer exodus.

If winning the Champions League is not enough to retain players then you have to wonder what is. Seven players have left the European champions so far with 19-year-old Renee van Asten from Ajax the only arrival.

To make matters worse some of the team’s best players are those departing with twice Ballon d’Or winner Alexia Putellas top of that list. Fellow Spain internationals Ona Batlle, Mapi León and Salma Paralluelo have also left.

The reason? As so often when it comes to football: money. The men’s La Liga financial fair play troubles continue to disrupt the club from top to bottom. At the time of writing the women’s team have 17 senior players – two goalkeepers, six defenders, six midfielders and three forwards – although they are in talks to sign the Brazil forward Kerolin from Manchester City.

Putellas was the biggest loss for the club, leaving her home of 14 years for Michele Kang’s London City Lionesses in the Women’s Super League. The fact that she left on a free transfer highlighted an internal management crisis at the club. Mapi León followed her Blaugrana captain to London City, also on a free transfer, where they will be reunited with three former teammates; Jana Fernández, María Pérez and Lucía Corrales.

The WSL is a popular destination for Barcelona players with 14 of their last 19 departures joining clubs in England. Batlle signed for Arsenal, where she will join up with the former Barcelona winger Mariona Caldentey. Salma Paralluelo has yet to announce where she will be playing next season, though PSG are the favourite to sign her after negotiations with Chelsea broke down.

Those 19 departures have come since 2024 and they include academy players who have made regular appearances for the first team. At the same time there have only been two signings and two academy players who have joined the senior side. The reserve goalkeeper Ellie Roebuck arrived in July 2024, but left after one season, while Laia Aleixandri joined on a free transfer from Manchester City in June 2025.

View image in fullscreen Ona Batlle has joined Arsenal. Photograph: David Price/Arsenal FC/Getty Images

With their pre-season training commencing on Monday 27 July the pressure is on to sign players to reinforce a squad that looks threadbare at best and dangerously thin at worst. The club have said that there will be signings – and that they will be announced soon – but whether they are seasoned pros or academy products remain to be seen.

Last season academy products Aïcha Camara and Clara Serrajordi were given first-team contracts with the club in a similar situation. In the past Barcelona have been able to promote high-quality players from within but now the problem is that key academy players are leaving as well. The goalkeeper Txell Font left for city neighbours FC Badalona, Adriana Ranera signed for Deportiva de A Coruña, Martine Fenger left for Hoffenheim and Alba Caño landed in the NWSL with Boston Legacy.

Some academy players did step up last season and arguably saved the club’s campaign. Serrajordi deputised in the midfield when Aitana Bonmatí or Patri Guijarro were out and Camara played a big role in the defensive line with Batlle picking up a month-long injury. However, as the best academy players have already been given first-team contracts there are fewer options to turn to this summer. Midfielders Carla Julià (19) and Rosalía Domínguez (17) seem to be current favourites to make the jump to the first team should the club prioritise signing in-house talent.

Last season Barcelona Femení made a profit of €1.955m (£1.67m), their best financial result since the 2023-24 campaign. That came off the back of the Champions League prize money being increased and the team collecting all three domestic trophies. However, with some of their biggest names departing they are unlikely to match that figure in 2026-27.

Losing Batlle will have a big impact on the defence, coming as it does a year after Fridolina Rölfö joined Manchester United. Van Asten, as mentioned, has signed from Ajax and Martina Fernández looks likely to return from Everton. The forward line appears even thinner, although the coach, Pere Romeu, has a particular style of football and can utilise midfielders such as Vicky López, Kika Nazareth and Sydney Schertenleib in attack.

It feels like this team is one major injury away from imploding. They got away with it last season – in fact, they won everything they could – but for how long can this carry on? A team hoping to defend their title as European champions can’t continue to rely solely on academy products for ever.
