The End of an Era: French Bases Leave Senegal

On 17 July 2025, France formally ended more than six decades of continuous military deployment in Senegal, handing back the last facilities in Dakar’s Maréchal and Saint-Exupéry districts. The withdrawal fulfilled a pledge by President Bassirou Diomaye Faye, elected in March 2024 on a platform of national and economic sovereignty, who had told AFP in November 2024 that France would have to close its military bases.

Prime Minister Ousmane Sonko had publicly criticised the bases in May 2024, linking the debate to the CFA franc currency regime and existing oil and gas contracts. By December 2024, Sonko formally announced the closure of all foreign military bases, making Senegal the first democratically elected West African state to terminate a French defence presence, following the coup-led expulsions in Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger.

A joint commission established in February 2025 oversaw the withdrawal and the restitution of facilities, with both governments pledging to negotiate a new defence and security partnership that accounts for all parties’ strategic priorities. The departure marks a symbolic and operational rupture in the architecture that had governed France’s presence in the region since a 1974 defence agreement allowed Paris to station forces on Senegalese soil.

A Letter of Intent: Naval Access Without Permanent Bases

On 15 July 2025, just two days before the final withdrawal, the Chiefs of Staff of the French and Senegalese armed forces signed a letter of intent establishing what Paris describes as a “temporary framework for the continuation of a special partnership that is balanced and mutually beneficial.” The document explicitly rules out permanent facilities while maintaining naval and airport access for French forces.

This arrangement allows France to rotate frigates and patrol vessels through Dakar’s port, use Senegalese airfields for logistics and crisis response, and continue joint exercises with the Senegalese navy. It effectively shifts the Senegal France defence partnership from a land-based garrison model to a maritime and air-access framework, consistent with Paris’s broader post-Barkhane repositioning across Africa.

The 2012 defence partnership treaty remains the legal backbone of bilateral military cooperation, covering training, equipment, exercises, and port and airport calls. The new letter of intent builds on that treaty while adapting to Dakar’s insistence on sovereignty, and a more comprehensive accord is still under negotiation as of early 2026.

Why Senegal’s Coastline Matters for Sahel Security

Senegal sits on the Atlantic flank of the Sahel, and Dakar’s port is a critical logistics node for access to Mauritania, Mali, and the wider Sahelian hinterland. French naval doctrine for West Africa has long relied on Mission Corymbe, a semi-permanent deployment of a warship in the Gulf of Guinea aimed at reducing maritime insecurity, piracy, and illicit trafficking.

With permanent bases gone but naval access retained, France can still use Dakar as a hub for regional maritime security missions, complementing its remaining footholds in Gabon and Djibouti. The coastline is also vital for protecting offshore oil and gas blocks, where Senegal has made significant discoveries, and for policing illegal fishing by European and Asian fleets.

Senegal’s own naval capabilities have expanded considerably: French shipbuilder Piriou delivered two OPV 58 S offshore patrol vessels in 2023, with a third expected, tailored for surveillance of the country’s exclusive economic zone and counter-piracy operations. These vessels are a flagship French naval export in the Gulf of Guinea and a concrete anchor for continued bilateral cooperation even as troops depart.

Space, Satellites, and the New Senegal France Defence Partnership

A less visible but strategically significant dimension of the evolving Senegal France defence partnership lies in space-based surveillance. In June 2025, the Senegalese Armed Forces Chief of Staff, General Mbaye Cissé, signed a five-year memorandum of understanding with the Senegalese Agency for Space Studies (ASES), creating a formal cooperation framework between defence and space sectors.

Senegal has also partnered with French company Prométhée Earth Intelligence, which develops Earth-observation nanosatellite constellations providing near-real-time, high-resolution imagery of Senegalese territory and surrounding maritime zones. Senegalese officers explicitly link space capability to maritime surveillance, border security, and the control of trafficking routes that connect Sahelian armed groups to the Atlantic.

This high-tech layer of cooperation — satellites, coastal radars, and secure communications — represents the new frontier of the bilateral relationship, replacing the old logic of garrisoned troops with intelligence sharing and domain awareness. It also opens commercial opportunities for French defence and aerospace firms at a moment when Paris is losing ground to competitors elsewhere in the region.

Turkey Moves In: The Great-Power Contest Heats Up

The reconfiguration of the Senegal France defence partnership cannot be understood in isolation from the wider great-power competition reshaping the Sahel and Gulf of Guinea. As France retreats, Turkey has moved aggressively to fill the vacuum, signing two military deals with Dakar in August and October 2025, including a memorandum on maritime search, rescue, and surveillance training.

In March 2025, under IMF supervision, Senegal signed a €317 million ($345 million) arms contract with Turkish firm ICC Yapi Yatirim to modernise its military over three years. The package includes two CASA C295 aircraft configured for transport and maritime patrol, and two Leonardo AW139 helicopters, directly overlapping with the capabilities France has traditionally supplied.

This supplier diversification mirrors a continental trend where African states seek maximum room to manoeuvre between declining French leverage, rising non-Western partners, and established Western financiers. The United States, which updated its own defence cooperation agreement with Senegal in 2016, also views Dakar as a valuable contingency access point on the Atlantic side of the Sahel, particularly for counterterrorism and evacuation operations.

What Each Side Wants: Sovereignty, Money, and Residual Influence

For Senegal, the new framework is about strategic sovereignty and economic leverage. General Mbaye Cissé has framed the withdrawal as a move “to affirm the autonomy of the Senegalese armed forces” while still contributing to regional peace, and President Faye’s government has linked the base closure to broader renegotiations of the CFA franc and hydrocarbon contracts.

Stronger control of the maritime domain gives Dakar more bargaining power over offshore oil and gas revenues, fishing rights, and the terms under which foreign navies operate in its waters. The government is also positioning Senegal as a hub for training, cyber-security, and maritime surveillance services for West Africa, drawing funding from France, the European Union, Turkey, and the United States.

For France, the letter of intent preserves a minimal but strategic footprint at a moment when its military presence in West Africa has shrunk to almost zero. Naval access to Dakar and close ties to Senegal’s navy and air force help Paris retain operational reach along the Atlantic coast, support French defence exports like the OPV 58 S vessels, and recast its narrative from “Francafrique” to a partnership of equals — a theme explored in depth in our pillar Africa: The New Scramble.

What to Watch Next

The letter of intent is explicitly temporary, and both sides are negotiating a more comprehensive defence and security partnership that will need to balance Senegalese sovereignty demands with French operational requirements. The outcome will signal whether the model of access without bases can become a durable template for France’s relationships with other African coastal states.

Investors and security analysts should also watch how Turkey’s deepening defence ties with Senegal affect French industrial interests, particularly follow-on contracts for patrol vessels, coastal radars, and satellite services. The competition between Piriou, Turkish shipyards, and potentially Chinese suppliers will shape the Gulf of Guinea’s naval procurement landscape for years to come.

Finally, the broader Sahel context remains volatile: the Alliance of Sahel States is building a 5,000-strong joint force, Russia and China are expanding their security footprints, and the United States is reassessing its own contingency access requirements. Senegal’s ability to navigate these currents while maintaining a working Senegal France defence partnership will be a defining test of the Faye administration’s foreign policy.

Connected Coverage Africa: The New Scramble

Frequently Asked Questions

Has Senegal signed a fully ratified defence accord with France focused on maritime security?

Not yet. The two countries signed a letter of intent on 15 July 2025 establishing a temporary framework for cooperation without permanent bases but with naval and airport access. A more comprehensive defence and security partnership is still under negotiation, building on the existing 2012 defence cooperation treaty.

Why did Senegal ask France to close its military bases?

President Bassirou Diomaye Faye was elected in March 2024 on a platform of national and economic sovereignty, and both he and Prime Minister Ousmane Sonko publicly criticised the presence of foreign bases as incompatible with Senegalese autonomy. The decision also ties into broader renegotiations of economic relationships, including the CFA franc currency and oil and gas contracts.

Which other countries are competing for defence influence in Senegal?

Turkey has moved most aggressively, signing a €317 million ($345 million) arms contract in March 2025 and two additional military deals later that year covering maritime surveillance and training. The United States maintains a defence cooperation agreement updated in 2016, while Russia and China are expanding their security footprints elsewhere in the Sahel and represent potential future partners for Dakar.

World.title: Cyberattack Forces Costa Rica’s Congress to Shut Down Its Systems
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Legislative Assembly was forced to disconnect its information systems yesterday after detecting an attempted cyberattack overnight, paralyzing congressional business for a full day and prompting opposition lawmakers to warn that any decisions taken without normal access to legislative documents could later be challenged.

Congress President Yara Jiménez told the plenary at the start of the session that the intrusion attempt occurred between Monday night and the early hours of Tuesday morning. She said security personnel detected an effort to get into the Assembly’s systems and, following established protocol, moved to shut down several digital services to keep out intruders and prevent the theft of information. “The protocol was to shut down the systems to prevent intruders from gaining access,” Jiménez said, adding that the continuity of public administration had to take precedence.

To keep the plenary running with its systems offline, the Legislative Directorate published the day’s agenda in a special edition of the official gazette, La Gaceta, so that the matters lawmakers would take up remained a matter of public record. Jiménez said she had requested detailed reports from the Assembly’s Security Management office and its Information Technology Department to establish the scope of the incident and the actions taken during the response. Officials from the Ministry of Science, Innovation, Technology and Telecommunications (MICITT) arrived at the Assembly in the morning to assist the technical evaluation.

The outage happened across the institution. The Integrated Legislative System, known as SIL, stores the digital versions of bills, updated texts, motions and institutional reports that lawmakers and staff rely on daily, and its loss left committees unable to consult basic documents. Seven committees were unable to meet as scheduled yesterday, and their sessions for today were left in doubt because agendas must be published at least 24 hours in advance.

No bills were voted on. The plenary itself proceeded only with its political-oversight segment before Jiménez, acting on a recommendation from the Technical Services Department, lifted the session in the late afternoon rather than risk debating legislation without the required public access to the relevant files.

The disclosure caught many lawmakers by surprise and drew sharp criticism over the delay in informing them. Several legislators argued they should have been told sooner and warned that interrupting the Assembly’s digital platforms could create procedural irregularities by limiting public access to official documents and proceedings. “In Costa Rica, public institutions have a legal and administrative obligation to report any type of attack or potential breach of public information,” Representative Claudia Dobles said during the session.

Members of the Frente Amplio, the Social Christian Unity Party and the National Liberation Party cautioned that agreements adopted without ordinary access to legislative documents could be exposed to later claims of nullity or unconstitutionality, and they urged Jiménez to release the final report from the Office of Information Security and Technology once the investigation concludes.

That report, they said, should establish the scope of the attack, determine whether any confidential or sensitive information was compromised, and set out the measures being taken to strengthen the Assembly’s defenses.

Later on, MICITT offered a more reassuring assessment, characterizing the episode as a “security event” detected on one of the Assembly’s servers that provides digital services to the public. The country’s Computer Security Incident Response Team, CSIRT-CR, said the activity was detected and contained thanks to existing controls, and that technical verification found no evidence that information hosted on the site had been compromised, altered or extracted.

On that basis, the incident was classified as a security event rather than an information-security breach, and the agency said it would continue supporting the Assembly’s technical review and the safe restoration of its services.

Authorities have not identified who was behind the attempt or disclosed a possible motive, questions that officials say will form part of the pending technical report. The incident lands as Costa Rican public institutions continue to harden their defenses following a series of cyberattacks on government systems in recent years.

World.title: Costa Rica Plans Integrated Train and Bus Network to Ease Traffic Congestion
World.content:
Costa Rica’s national railway institute is pushing to link the country’s trains, buses, and taxis into a single coordinated network, a plan its backers say could finally give commuters in the capital region a faster alternative to sitting in traffic.

The Instituto Costarricense de Ferrocarriles (Incofer) is promoting what it calls an intermodal public transport system, designed so that different modes of travel connect smoothly rather than competing for the same passengers. The aim is to shorten travel times and improve mobility across the Greater Metropolitan Area, the densely populated ring of cities spanning San José, Alajuela, Heredia, and Cartago where most of the chronic congestion is concentrated. Incofer is developing the scheme alongside the Cámara Nacional de Transportes (Canatrans), the national transport chamber that represents the country’s bus operators.

The plan is built around the Tren Eléctrico de Pasajeros, the electric passenger train that Incofer intends to make the backbone of public transport in the region. Under the proposal, buses would operate as feeder routes, carrying passengers from their neighborhoods to nearby rail stations, where they could transfer and continue by train to destinations elsewhere in the metropolitan area.

Taxis and other services would handle the shorter first- and last-mile connections at either end of a journey. Incofer and Canatrans argue that coordinating routes this way would cut the wasteful duplication that has buses and trains running parallel to one another today, and make transfers quick enough that public transport becomes a real option for people who now drive.

Technology is central to the pitch. The project envisions tools that would let a passenger plan a full trip across several modes at once, potentially including unified payment and real-time information on routes, schedules, and fares, so that moving from a bus to a train feels like one continuous journey rather than a series of disconnected legs.

Canatrans has framed the effort as a way to reduce dependence on private vehicles, which it identifies as one of the main drivers of the region’s gridlock. With Costa Rica recently ranked among the worst countries in the world for traffic, authorities hope that drawing more commuters onto a coordinated public network would ease that pressure over time.

The intermodal plan rests on a project that has moved unusually fast this year after decades of false starts. In May the Legislative Assembly approved the international financing for the electric train, tracked under file number 25.291, and President Laura Fernández Delgado signed the financing law shortly afterward. Incofer executive president Álvaro Bermúdez Peña called the approval a historic step toward a modern, efficient transport system.

The financing package draws on international lenders that include the Central American Bank for Economic Integration, the European Union, and the Green Climate Fund. As designed, the system would run along roughly 52 kilometers (32 miles) of double electrified track connecting the four Greater Metropolitan Area provinces, add a fleet of new electric trains, and lift daily ridership from about 16,000 passengers today toward a target of 100,000.

As of now, the intermodal component remains a framework rather than a finished plan. Neither Incofer nor Canatrans has published implementation timelines, the investment required to reorganize bus routes, or the locations of the transfer points where the connections would happen. Both institutions maintain, however, that no amount of new rail infrastructure will relieve congestion on its own, and that the trains only deliver on their promise if the buses and taxis around them are organized to feed passengers in and out.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Public Health Waiting Lists Hit 1.4 million, Audit Finds
World.content:
A newly surfaced internal audit at the Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social (CCSS) has intensified scrutiny of Costa Rica’s public healthcare system, and it has now drawn a formal demand for answers from the Legislative Assembly. Deputy Ángela Aguilar Vargas, of the Partido Liberación Nacional, has written to CCSS executive president Mónica Taylor Hernández requesting a detailed explanation of the findings and of the corrective measures the institution intends to take.

The document at the center of the dispute is the internal audit advisory cataloged as AS-ASALUD-0057-2026, dated June 3, 2026, which compiled the principal findings of a series of audits conducted between 2022 and 2025. According to that report, as of March 2026 the Caja carried 1,440,547 registered cases on its waiting lists.

That headline figure is easily misread by anyone accustomed to comparing it against a national health service abroad, so it warrants a careful reading: it is the combined total of three separate lists rather than a count of 1.44 million distinct individuals. A single insured person waiting for a specialist appointment, a diagnostic procedure and an operation can appear on all three at once, and official reporting uses the words “patients” and “cases” interchangeably.

The three lists break down as follows in the audit’s most recent snapshot. Roughly 204,622 people were awaiting surgery, some 362,356 were waiting for a specialty outpatient consultation, and the largest category by far, medical procedures, accounted for about 873,572 pending cases. The procedures list is where the backlog has grown most sharply, and it is the category that most distorts the topline number for readers who assume “waiting list” means “waiting for an operation.”

The audit’s central conclusion is not simply that the lists are long but that they are growing despite a dedicated plan to shrink them. Comparing December 2024 with March 2026, the report found the combined lists rose from 1,094,093 to 1,440,547 cases, an accumulated increase of 346,454 people, or 31.7 percent, over that roughly fifteen-month span. The auditors traced the persistent backlog to a shortage of medical specialists and nursing staff, the underuse of operating theatres, deficiencies in how the institution manages its own data, and problems of coordination across the hospital network.

Those failures are measured against a specific commitment. In May 2023 the CCSS board of directors approved what it called a roadmap to advance the management of waiting lists and of specialized health personnel, and it declared the matter an institutional emergency. The current audit concludes that the roadmap’s targets were not met, attributing to the administration a direct responsibility for the lack of effective results and pointing to weaknesses in the planning, execution and follow-up of the measures adopted.

It is on that basis that Aguilar has pressed the executive presidency for answers. In her letter she posed four questions: what corrective and complementary actions the administration will implement in response to the audit’s observations; what immediate steps it will take to relieve the bottleneck in specialized outpatient consultation; how it will ensure administrative accountability so that the shortcomings identified are not repeated; and which specific actions have already been set in motion on the audit’s recommendations, together with any preliminary results.

The deputy framed the stakes in human terms, stating in a translated remark that the deterioration shows the 2023 roadmap measures went unfulfilled, with serious consequences for users who face delays that harm their quality of life and allow their conditions to worsen.

The CCSS has publicly acknowledged the scale of the problem in recent months. Taylor has described the waiting lists as extremely difficult to reduce in the short term and has pointed to a strategy of strengthening emergency services to decongest hospitals, while the board earlier this year approved a new multi-year plan intended to distribute resources more evenly across the system. At the time of writing, the executive presidency had not issued a public response to Aguilar’s specific letter.

For the roughly five million people insured through the Caja, including foreign residents, retirees and residency applicants who pay monthly contributions and depend on the system for their care, the audit is less a single alarming statistic than a measure of how long the wait for specialist attention, diagnostics and surgery has become, and of whether the institution’s repeated promises to fix it are producing results.

World.title: Brandon Nakashima Wins First UTS Tournament in South America
World.content:
Brandon Nakashima claimed the title at the Ultimate Tennis Showdown’s first tournament in South America, defeating 17-year-old Brazilian Guto Miguel in a tightly contested final at Rio de Janeiro’s Maracanãzinho arena. The American completed a remarkable turnaround by beating Miguel 3-0 on Saturday, July 18, with quarter scores of 15-14, 17-14 and 15-13. Although the score appeared one-sided under the UTS system, all three quarters were decided by three points or fewer.

Nakashima earned $368,800 for winning UTS Rio, which was also his first appearance in the alternative tennis competition. “It was a great couple of days here,” Nakashima said after the final. “I really enjoyed my first experience here in Brazil and first UTS experience.” His path to the championship was far from straightforward. Nakashima opened the tournament with a 3-1 victory over top seed Francisco Cerúndolo before losing 3-2 to Miguel in Sudden Death during the round-robin stage.

The loss left Nakashima relying on quarter and point differentials to reach the semifinals as the fourth qualifier. Once there, he produced one of his best performances of the tournament, recovering from the loss of the opening quarter to defeat Nick Kyrgios 3-1. Nakashima won the final three quarters against Kyrgios by scores of 20-10, 17-12 and 20-10, ending the Australian’s bid for his first UTS title.

Miguel provided the tournament’s biggest surprise. The Brazilian teenager defeated Kyrgios, Nakashima and Cerúndolo during his run to the final, winning all three matches in Sudden Death. Miguel entered the event as a late replacement for Ugo Humbert but quickly became one of the central figures of the three-day competition.

He began by stunning Kyrgios 3-2, winning the first two quarters before surviving the Australian’s comeback. Miguel then defeated Nakashima by the same score and overcame Cerúndolo 3-2 in the semifinals after losing the opening quarter 23-11. Miguel had already enjoyed a breakthrough season after becoming the first Brazilian-born player to win the boys’ singles title at Roland Garros.

His victories over three established professionals in Rio offered another indication of his potential, even though Nakashima’s consistency proved too much in the final. Brazilian fans had initially expected João Fonseca to lead the home challenge. Fonseca defeated Tallon Griekspoor 3-1 in his UTS debut but was eliminated after Kyrgios swept him 3-0 in only 37 minutes.

Fonseca, Kyrgios and several other players finished the round-robin stage with one victory, leaving quarter and point differentials to determine the four semifinalists. Fonseca later defeated Corentin Moutet 3-1 in a classification match to finish sixth. Cerúndolo also recovered from an opening defeat, beating Cameron Norrie 3-0 to qualify for the semifinals. The Argentine eventually finished third after his Sudden Death loss to Miguel.

UTS Rio was held from July 16 through July 18 on an indoor hard court at the 11,000-seat Maracanãzinho. It marked the tour’s first appearance in South America and the second event of its 2026 season after an April tournament in Nîmes, France. The distinction is important: UTS had already staged an event in Latin America when Guadalajara, Mexico, hosted a tournament in 2025. Rio was the competition’s first stop on the South American continent.

Created by coach Patrick Mouratoglou, UTS replaces traditional games and sets with eight-minute quarters. The first player to win three quarters takes the match, while a 2-2 tie leads to Sudden Death, where a player must win two consecutive points. Players receive only one serve, fans may make noise during points and each competitor can use a bonus card that makes the next point worth three.

Rio also introduced a single eight-player round-robin table, with each player facing two opponents before the top four advanced to the semifinals. The event ultimately produced two significant results for UTS: a debut title for Nakashima and a breakthrough week for one of Brazil’s most promising teenagers.

World.content:
International News: Spain’s World Cup champions receive Royal welcome ahead of victory parade

By Zoila Palma: Spain’s World Cup-winning football team received a royal welcome Monday after returning home from their historic triumph in the United States.

King Felipe VI hosted the squad at Madrid’s Royal Palace, praising the players for what he described as an “epic” victory and calling them a “legendary and historic team.”

World.title: International News: Death toll rises to 53 in Guyana ferry disaster
World.content:
International News: Death toll rises to 53 in Guyana ferry disaster

By Zoila Palma: The death toll from a ferry disaster off the coast of Guyana has risen to 53, with hopes fading of finding more survivors after the passenger vessel capsized Saturday night.

Prime Minister Mark Phillips said that by Tuesday night, 76 people had been rescued alive, while dozens remained missing.

Officials said 179 people were believed to have been aboard the ferry, significantly more than the 133 passengers and crew listed on its manifest.

Authorities have launched an investigation into what caused the 87-year-old vessel, the MV Barima, to overturn, BBC reports.

The ferry had departed Georgetown on Saturday afternoon for Port Kaituma in northern Guyana.

The captain and another crew member were taken into custody after testing positive for cannabis, prompting officials to warn that anyone found responsible for negligence, misconduct or criminal wrongdoing would face the full force of the law.

World.title: 1,320 pounds of ribs a year, and the BDF chief never tasted one
World.content:
1,320 pounds of ribs a year, and the BDF chief never tasted one

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): According to purchase records for fiscal year 2023-2024, as reported by 7News, the Belize Defence Force was purchasing 1,320 pounds of baby back ribs annually. Yet the man at the top of the BDF, Brigadier General Anthony Velasquez, told the station he has never eaten BDF baby back ribs in his 32 years in the army.

Pressed by 7News on where all those ribs went, the Commander offered his explanation. “I said I’ve never eaten baby back ribs, which is true. I’ve never had, but that doesn’t mean that it’s not purchased, right?” Velasquez said. “We tell the Ministry of Defense, this is what we want. And we want baby back ribs and conchs and shrimp and lobster for special events. One special event we had was last week, Wednesday, when we had the recruit passing out and the change of responsibility.”

The general said leftovers do not go to waste. “After these events are over, we stock some of them as well, and then whatever remains in stock, we give to the soldiers, so we send it to the battalions, the units in P.G. and Belizario,” he explained, while conceding the circle of beneficiaries is limited. “Few soldiers get to enjoy these because the ones on camp get to enjoy it, not the ones being deployed. So it’s a small number of soldiers that actually get to enjoy these things.”

He added that surplus supplies feature in training for new military cooks, who prepare what he called a culinary delight that everyone at Price Barracks is invited to sample.

The most striking exchange came when 7News’ Jaleeza Roberts asked whether the Commander had personally seen anyone around him enjoying the ribs. “I have never seen. Yes, I have heard,” Velasquez replied. “I have spoken to some other commanders, and they have received, the unit commanders, the battalion commanders, they have received the baby back ribs and the conchs and everything else, and they have given it to their soldiers.”

The ribs question forms one thread of the broader examination of defence ministry procurement, matters currently the subject of a government-ordered audit, with no findings made to date. The Commander’s account stands as the BDF’s explanation of purchases he says the force itself requested for special occasions.

Whether that explanation satisfies a public now reading the ministry’s grocery lists line by line is another matter. What is certain is that in 32 years of service, through every rank to the very top, the man who commands the Belize Defence Force says the baby back ribs never once reached his plate.

What do you make of the general’s explanation, Belize? Comment below.

World.title: New broadcasting law would put online creators under licence
World.content:
New broadcasting law would put online creators under licence

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The rules of Belize’s information landscape may be about to change fundamentally. The proposed Broadcasting Act, 2026, released to stakeholders last week Thursday, promises sweeping changes that would bring online broadcasters, streaming services, and social media content creators under unprecedented government oversight and licensing requirements.

In the interest of full transparency, that includes outlets like this one. Online news pages serving Belizean audiences fall squarely within the proposed framework, so we report on this legislation as both journalists and stakeholders.

The landmark legislation officially expands the legal definition of broadcasting beyond traditional radio and television to cover internet-dependent digital platforms, Over-The-Top services, and what it terms National Online Broadcasters targeting Belizean audiences for commercial gain. Under the new framework, online outlets and digital content creators generating advertising or sponsorship revenue from Belizeans would no longer operate in a regulatory vacuum. They would be required to obtain an official licence, or secure an explicit exemption, from the Belize Broadcasting Authority.

Attorney-at-Law Marissa Longsworth, speaking to local media, explained how the exemption system is intended to work. “Exemptions are to be prescribed for national online broadcasters to consider that licenses should only be those that meet criteria such as commercial benefits of the broadcast, audience size, availability and accessibility to the broadcast, and frequency,” she said. “So the way this act will work is that once you broadcast online, you will fall within this act. The question comes whether you should be licensed for that purpose.”

Longsworth illustrated with a relatable example: a person going live on Facebook to some 900 friends, with perhaps 20 watching, on a private page. “If you report me to the BBA, the BBA will look at that and say, well, how many people did Marissa reach during that live? How many times did Marissa do a broadcast? Did she do a weekly podcast show? She has sponsors?” she explained. “Is there a commercial benefit being derived from her online podcast? That is a consideration. How frequent does she broadcast? That is a consideration. Who has access to her broadcast? Is it the general public? Is it a special group? Is it a very small group? That is a consideration.”

In short, the casual user going live for friends is not the target. The regular broadcaster with an audience, sponsors, and a schedule is.

The proposal raises questions that deserve a vigorous national conversation. How will licensing criteria be applied in practice, and by whom? What safeguards will ensure the framework regulates without restricting the press freedom that a healthy democracy requires? And how will the many Belizeans who have built livelihoods as online creators, from news pages to podcasters to entertainment channels, be affected?

Those questions arrive in the same week that a Belizean journalist earned a regional press freedom nomination, a reminder of both the strength of Belize’s media tradition and the stakes of getting this legislation right.

For now, the act remains a proposal in stakeholder consultation, and that consultation is where the details will be tested. Every Belizean with a page, a podcast, or a platform has reason to follow it closely. We certainly will.

World.title: International News: U.S. sends first humanitarian flight to Cuba under new $100 million aid package
World.content:
International News: U.S. sends first humanitarian flight to Cuba under new $100 million aid package

By Zoila Palma: The United States has sent its first humanitarian flight to Cuba as part of a new $100 million assistance commitment aimed at helping ordinary Cubans amid worsening shortages and economic hardship.

The U.S. State Department said Tuesday that the shipment marks the first delivery under the new aid package, which comes as Washington continues to increase pressure on Cuba’s communist government through sanctions and restrictions on oil shipments.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the assistance initiative in May, describing it as an unprecedented aid package intended to support the Cuban people without providing resources directly to the government.

The move comes alongside tougher U.S. measures against Havana, including efforts to restrict fuel supplies and impose additional financial pressure, Reuters report.

Cuban officials initially expressed skepticism about the offer and rejected U.S. demands for political reforms, while blaming Washington for contributing to the island’s power outages and shortages.

However, the Cuban government appears to have agreed to accept the assistance following discussions with officials from the Trump administration.

World.content:
Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth & Information’s Region One Director Ottis Brown addressing the region’s One Back-to-School Conference held at Grand Palladium Hotel and Spa in Point, Hanover, on Tuesday.Anthony Lewis

POINT, Hanover — The Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth & Information’s Region One Director Ottis Brown has sounded the alarm over what he alleges are numerous accounting breaches in primary schools within Kingston and St Andrew.

“The breaches are too many. Here is what is happening now, colleagues. We are getting documents from the Integrity Commission (IC) for principals to be investigated… Accountability is stepping up,” he said.

Brown made the revelation, Tuesday, during the second of a three-day back-to-school conference for Region One that was held at Grand Palladium Hotel and Spa in Point, Hanover.

“Stakeholders in the communities are writing to the ministry. They talk about what they observe in schools. They go to a school and they get no receipt for the money they pay. They call you and ask if they should get a receipt and what it should look like,” he told an audience of educators.

The regional director said primary schools are the main offenders.

“Do you know where we tend to find the bulk of the breaches now? The primary schools. It’s a serious problem,” said Brown.

While he conceded that there may be administrative issues such as inadequate staff that impact how money is handled, he said there can be no excuse for some of the behaviour seen.

“Some simple things. Why would you keep money in excess of a million dollars locked up in a room for two, three weeks, months, and so forth? The bursar not being there caused that? So what I’m saying: I know you need those people, and we are working on that, but don’t do things to set up yourselves in the process,” added the senior officer.

Brown used the opportunity to explain proper administrative procedures when handling school funds.

“I beg you, lodge the money in a reasonable time frame. Money must be lodged intact. Can somebody please explain what the FAA (Financial Administration and Audit) Act means when it says ‘money must be lodged intact’? ‘[It means as soon] as collected,” he emphasised.

He explained that if five $100-notes are collected, that exact configuration must be deposited into the account.

“Don’t use it to make any change for anybody who wants to pay somebody something. That is what they mean [by] to lodge the money intact. If you are guilty, don’t say anything. Just sit like nothing is wrong but pray a prayer in your heart. I’m giving you 30 seconds to ask God to forgive you,” stated Brown to an outburst of laughter.

“You saved the money, but the law says treat it a particular way,” added the senior officer.

During his address Brown also expressed gratitude to the Ministry of Education for providing the region with additional professionals to conduct audits of schools within the region.

“We want to publicly say thanks to the members of the central ministry team, our CEO, [and] the permanent secretary. We spoke and they have given us a large number of people to build out the finance unit in the region. I have about five or six additional staff members now so we can do more audits. Clap the central team for that,” he said magnanimously.

World.title: Danger in John’s Hall
World.content:
A bedhead and concrete block are among items used to alert commuters to danger on the John’s Hall road in St James..

MONTEGO BAY, St James — An old bedhead and the top of a broken table used to cobble together a crude guard rail serve as warning that there is danger on the road between John’s Hall and Spring Mount in southern St James. One section appears on the verge of collapse, much like a nearby house whose foundation was eroded by Hurricane Melissa, last October, and commuters are worried.

“I’m afraid but mi just have to drive on it, can’t do better,” a shopkeeper who identified herself as Sancia told the

Jamaica Observer Tuesday.

“If little rain fall it gone, because underneath it, it’s deteriorating,” she explained.

The gaping cavern in a section of the Spring Mount Road is just a few kilometres up the hill, impassable as residents eagerly await word from the Government on when it will be repaired. Now, they have added the danger at John’s Hall to their list of urgent issues.

When contacted, community relations officer for the National Works Agency (NWA), Western Region, Janel Ricketts said they are aware of this latest development at John’s Hall. Though none were seen by the Observer, she said signs are in place to help guide motorists.

“This too, like Spring Mount, is on the radar of the NWA but in terms of an update, I don’t have that right now,” she told the Observer.

For shopkeeper Sancia and others who use the road, help cannot come soon enough as the alternative route is longer and more costly. What was once a straight route from John’s Hall to Montego Bay has now become a meandering journey to Sunderland, around Blackshop, and through Patosi.

“And the hottest part is we dropping out right at the square down there and we don’t reach Montego Bay as yet. It’s going to be more money, more gas, more everything,” Sancia lamented.

She also highlighted challenges being faced by students in that area of the community.

“Children that live here now that have to go Maldon are paying double or triple fare because they have to take taxi from here go to Montego Bay and a next taxi go and vice versa,” Sancia explained.

“It bad for everybody: Parents, children, business owners,” she added.

A roadside vendor in John’s Hall who chose not to provide his name spoke of the downturn in business he has seen as commuters from southern St James have had to find new routes.

“It rough because the road block up that side so people can’t come down. They would stop and buy drinks, food stuff, shop stuff; that’s not happening again,” he said.

He also pointed to the impact it has had on other areas of life that used to generate income, such as sporting competitions.

“Football was a thing where the different communities partake in and now them can’t come,” he said.

“Spring Mount people a bawl now because nobody can’t come down. We just want to see the road fix, the two place; because without it we don’t have any real livelihood, nobody can’t come, nobody can’t go,” he said.

A motorist who gave his name as Richard said travelling to the area has been a financial challenge and, like area residents, he is also worried about the increasing deterioration at John’s Hall.

“With this breakaway now, we would have to find a next way to go in town, it’s really pressuring. I hope they do something fast, whether it’s construction to start the new road or they find something better that we can travel on. But do something better,” Richard appealed.

World.title: Stacious savours emotional return to Sumfest
World.content:
Stacious is all the rage on the Sumfest stage last weekend. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

When Stacious stepped onto the Reggae Sumfest stage on Saturday night as a surprise guest during Mavado’s set it was more than a welcome return for the dancehall artiste; it was an opportunity to be part of a moment that will be remembered as one of the festival’s most significant.

The entertainer joined Mavado during his historic showcase with fellow headliner Vybz Kartel, a performance that celebrated unity over division and marked a new chapter in one of dancehall’s most defining rivalries.

For Stacious, whose catalogue includes one of the most notable collaborations with Mavado in dancehall history, the occasion carried both personal and cultural significance.

“I can’t remember the last time I did Sumfest,” she told the Jamaica Observer following the performance. “I know I’ve done the show three times in the past, but I can’t remember when was the last time. It’s a good feeling being back.”

Her return came after years away from the festival’s stage, making the appearance all the more meaningful.

“I’m here tonight not just as an artiste, but as a fan of dancehall because Gully/Gaza did a run road, and now both deejays will come together in unity on one stage. It’s an honour to be a part of it,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

The sentiment echoed what many fans experienced inside Plantation Cove in St Ann as thousands watched two of dancehall’s biggest icons perform together, putting years of division behind them in favour of celebration.

For Stacious, the night also marked a long-awaited reunion with the man who helped produce, Come Into My Room, one of her most memorable collaborations.

“Mavado also hasn’t performed in Jamaica for a while and I’m here to witness the return of the Gully Gad, so it’s a great night,” she said. “Mavado and I haven’t performed together in maybe over 10 years, so it’s been a long time. The awesome thing is that it’s always good when we connect, and we enjoyed ourselves, which was most important.”

Stacious was among the female voices who helped shape dancehall during the late 2000s and early 2010s. Her surprise appearance on Saturday served as a reminder of that era while signalling that she still has plenty left to offer.

Away from the nostalgia, the deejay says she is focused on new music and reconnecting with supporters. She is currently promoting two singles, Tears and Velvet Sweetheart, the latter of which recently received the visual treatment and is now available for streaming across digital platforms.

Stacious is encouraging fans to subscribe to her YouTube channel and follow her social media pages to stay updated on upcoming releases, performances, and other career developments.

— Shereita Grizzle

World.title: US$18-m fuel shield
World.content:
STATE-OWNED refinery Petrojam has spent about US$18 million subsidising fuel costs to shield consumers from steeper price increases, with Chairman Metry Seaga saying the Government will eventually reimburse the company.

Seaga disclosed the figure during a panel discussion following Tuesday’s release of the second-quarter JCC/GK Capital Consumer Indices, while responding to questions about measures being taken to contain energy costs.

“To date, Petrojam has spent about US$18 million subsidising the cost of fuel,” Seaga said.

While acknowledging that the refinery has not done a good job of explaining how fuel prices are determined because of the complexity of the process, Seaga explained that Petrojam has been using a long-standing fuel price “smoothing mechanism” to cushion consumers from sharp swings in global oil prices. The mechanism was introduced to reduce volatility in fuel prices and lessen the inflationary impact of sudden increases in international oil prices.

According to Seaga, since the Middle East war began, domestic fuel-price increase reached as much as $40 per litre, leaving Petrojam to absorb significant costs rather than allowing domestic fuel price increases to immediately reflect international price movements which he said would have been “extremely inflationary”.

Under Petrojam’s pricing mechanism, weekly fuel price increases were initially capped at $4.50 per litre, before Cabinet approved an increase to $12.50. Petrojam calculates its prices using a US reference price and then applies costs within its control. When the calculated increase exceeds the cap, the refinery absorbs the difference rather than passing it on to consumers.

“The increase that the consumer saw last week of $12.50 is not a real number; the real number is significantly higher than that, but Petrojam has taken up any losses that are incurred,” he said. “Petrojam is doing everything it can, and the government by extension has to give us back that money, because the money has to come from somewhere.”

The JCC/GK Capital Consumer Indices found that rising energy costs continue to influence the behaviour of both businesses and households. Among businesses surveyed, 36 per cent said rising electricity costs were significantly affecting their operations, while another 29 per cent described the impact as moderate. In response, businesses said they were reducing energy consumption, investing in renewable energy solutions, increasing prices charged to customers, cutting operating expenses elsewhere, investing in energy-efficient equipment and delaying investment or expansion plans.

Seaga acknowledged not all businesses can pass higher energy costs on to customers. Pointing to Jamaica’s geography, and dependence on imported energy, he said businesses must accept that the country will remain exposed to global price shocks.

“We have to recognise from the get-go we are subject to price increases worldwide, and these are things businesses must plan for, including natural disasters,” he said. “What we have to do is know they are coming and be more efficient.”

Beyond businesses, consumers are also changing their behaviour in response to higher energy bills. The survey found that 51 per cent of respondents had reduced their electricity usage, while others said they were using fewer appliances or purchasing more energy-efficient appliances and light bulbs. Respondents also called for measures to reduce energy costs, with 56 per cent saying the government should lower electricity rates. Other recommendations included more stable fuel prices, lower taxes and duties on energy-efficient appliances, and easier financing for residential solar systems.

However, Seaga argued that households have viable alternatives to reduce their electricity bills.

“Majority of the people I know are telling me about their light bills being $12 and $15, so there’s no good reason that people should not be putting solar into their homes,” he said, noting that financing options are available.

Seaga also disclosed that Petrojam is exploring diversification into LNG, solar and potentially nuclear energy. He also hinted at the possibility of participating in oil development should commercially viable reserves be discovered in Jamaica, extending its involvement from production to the sale of fuel. However, Seaga noted that such plans would require significant investment.

World.title: Mission in Mexico
World.content:
Reggae Boyz Under-20 and Mount Pleasant Academy midfielder Jabarie Howell (foreground) is a key figure in Jamaica’s team to the Concacaf Under-20 Championship in Mexico, a qualifier for the FIFA Under-20 World Cup. The top four teams from the championship will qualify for the World Cup. (Photo: Concacaf)

Jamaica’s national men’s team haven’t qualified for a FIFA Under-20 World Cup in 25 years but Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) president Michael Ricketts is confident that the current squad can end the drought after significant investment in the qualification campaign.

The under-20 Reggae Boyz will leave the island on Friday for the 2026 Concacaf Under-20 Championship in Mexico, where they will look to secure one of four spots to next year’s World Cup in Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan. Rodolph Austin, who recently led Portmore United to their first Jamaica Premier League title since 2019, will lead the team along with Molynes United head coach Jermaine Thomas.

The pair oversaw Jamaica’s sweep through the qualifying tournament in Curaçao in February, with the team winning all five matches to reach the Under-20 Championship. They now face Honduras, Panama and Canada in Group C, with the top two advancing to the quarter-finals. A quarter-final victory would seal qualification for the FIFA Under-20 World Cup.

The team has been in a training camp at the Captain Horace Burrell Centre of Excellence at the UWI, Mona campus and have played friendlies against Jamaica Premier League clubs Cavalier, Mount Pleasant FC and Arnett Gardens in the past two weeks.

Since their historic berth in 2001 tournament in Argentina, Jamaica have missed out on the last 11 World Cups and have only advanced to the knockout stages of the Concacaf final round twice in nine attempts.

However, Ricketts told the Jamaica Observer that the JFF has made it a priority to give the team every opportunity to qualify, investing heavily ahead of the Concacaf Under-20 Championship in a bid to end the country’s drought.

“This year has been very busy for us and very expensive as well because of course the under-17s, under-20s on either side of the gender and of course the senior men’s and senior women’s have all been vying for a place in the World Cup tournaments,” he said.

“A structure has been put in place and it’s just now for us to execute. We really want to do well. I think we have a good set of young players and we are also hoping that they will make a transition and give some strength and support to our senior men’s team, but we would have given a lot more in terms of preparation.”

Ricketts says the JFF’s greater focus on its youth programmes over the past three years, along with improvements to its coaching structure, has given the federation greater confidence in qualifying for more World Cup tournaments.

“We are just very proud of our young coaches. Coach Austin and his deputy coach [Jermaine] Thomas have done an excellent job. We have a coaching programme that is probably second to none in the Caribbean and our coaches have done very well,” he said.

“Our TDS (Talent Development Scheme) programme is a huge success and it has evolved so much that our under-14 team won the Caribbean Challenge Series convincingly. Then a year after we stepped up in class, as they would say in racing terminology, and we went to Concacaf and we won that tournament as well and then afterwards we qualified for the U-17 World Cup.”

He added, “So it’s work in progress. Hopefully, all of this will translate into some success at the Under-20 level and, like I’ve said, the coaches have done well, the management structure has been at a premium and so we are optimistic and we are really expecting to qualify for the World Cup.”

Coach Austin named his 21-man squad last week with Cavalier standout Kimarly Scott, Mount Pleasant Football Academy star Jabarie Howell and Manchester United defender Dante Plunkett among the highlights of the squad. Che Gardner, son of Reggae Boyz legend Ricardo “Bibi” Gardner, has also been called up for the first time, having impressed for Stockport United in England’s third division.

The young Reggae Boyz take on Honduras in their opening game on Sunday before battling Panama next Wednesday and Canada next Saturday. All games are set for the Estadio Universitario BUAP in Puebla, Mexico.

Goalkeepers — Johnoi Steadman (Steths Elite), Justin Murray (Glenmuir High), Joshua Grant (Naples FC)

Defenders — Jaquan Brown (Portmore United FC), Duwayne Burgher (Waterhouse FC), Cai McLean (Inter Miami FC), Dante Plunkett (Manchester United), Brandon Bent (Miami FC), Santana Headley (Portmore United), Damario McIntosh (New England Revolution)

Midfielders — Jahmarie Nolan (Toronto FC), Raequan Campbell-Dennis (Toronto FC), Owen Jumpp (Mount Pleasant FA), Jermaine Young (Casa Pia AC), Jahmani Bell (Houston Dynamo FC), Jamone Lyle (Waterhouse FC), Jabarie Howell (Mount Pleasant FA)

Forwards — Kimarly Scott (Cavalier FC), Giovanni Taylor (Arnett Garden FC), Che Gardner (Stockport County FC), Sean Leighton (Phoenix Chapleton Maroons)

World.title: Child’s body found in Trelawny; two injured by irate residents in mob attack
World.content:
TRELAWNY, Jamaica — Police are now on a scene where the body of a child was found with her throat slashed in Tyre district near Troy in south Trelawny, residents say.

Residents told the Jamaica Observer that about 6:00 pm, the child’s body was found in bushes and an alarm was raised.

Residents say the child was raped before her death.

“A farmer went to look for his cow when he stumbled on the little girl’s body,” a resident who requested anonymity said.

Another resident said following the gruesome discovery there was a mob attack on a man who citizens accused of killing the child. His father was also wounded in the attack.

The men were reportedly taken to hospital. Their condition is not known at this time.

Efforts to get a comment from the police late Tuesday were unsuccessful.

— Kasey Williams

World.title: JLP condemns ‘vile’ alleged NaRRA voicenotes featuring PNP executives
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — The Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) says it has taken note of voicenotes leaked on traditional and social media in which two PNP executive members are allegedly heard confirming the PNP’s preparedness to implement delay tactics and use baseless allegations to smear “patriotic Jamaicans”.

In a statement on Tuesday, the JLP said media reports have indicated that the voicenotes were sent in a PNP executive WhatsApp group on May 27, 2026, shortly after Major General Antony Anderson was announced to head the National Resilience and Reconstruction Authority (NaRRA).

In the first piece of leaked audio the statement quotes, a PNP executive member whom it says may be heard stating:

“Bear in mind that the NaRRA is what the JLP sees as its glory and its saviour for a fourth term. So they see NaRRA as a saving grace and they are going to do everything in their power to try to get things done, which means bypassing, like all parish council, which, you know, we probably would do delay tactics, and they don’t get it, which is why they did it that way. But safety standards and these things is a concern. So let’s continue to play our ball game of politics.”

In the second piece of audio, which has gone viral in the public domain, a member of the PNP executive is heard referencing Major General Anderson’s appointment to lead NaRRA and saying:

“The concern I’m raising is that Anderson’s track record is not one full of blemishes that it will be so easy to attach certain things to him. The corruption argument is not going to be attached to him so easily, right? In my humble opinion, I think they’ve outsmarted us and put in this man to be a CEO and whatever reality is, we need to ensure that the average Jamaican is saying we don’t care who he is and him could have full integrity like, whoa, he could have been whatever. He’s the man who sorted out all of the hurricane relief that got it to Jamaica, whether we know it or not. So I would love for us to be able to put that information together, package it for the ground so that the average Jamaican can get that information.”

JLP Officer Corps member, Daryl Vaz, who co-chairs the Melissa Recovery and Relief Committee, says the revealing voicenotes disclose the PNP’s preparedness to implement delay tactics to slow down or block important national projects which NaRRA will pursue and to use baseless allegations to smear patriotic Jamaicans.

“What is particularly shameful is that the audio reveals that, despite the unprecedented natural disaster which devastated thousands of Jamaican lives and despite lamenting that the recovery effort should be faster, the PNP, at the highest level in their party, at the level of their executive, has been caught discussing ‘delay tactics’, which their executive member confessed they would probably implement. This behaviour by the PNP is most disgraceful but not surprising because we have seen these delay tactics implemented by the PNP before, to the detriment of Jamaicans.”

Vaz described the PNP executive member’s commitment to continue playing the political ball game concerning NaRRA as scandalous.

“Let us pause for a moment and recall that the Government has fast-tracked legislation to help rebuild communities and Jamaican lives in the aftermath of the devastating Category 5 Hurricane Melissa, and here is a PNP executive member caught on tape committing to ‘playing the ball game of politics’ with the people’s livelihood and the wellbeing of their communities. The obstructionist posture of the PNP on the issue of NaRRA and the Government’s bid to assist Jamaica to recover strongly and in a speedy manner is an utter disgrace,” he said.

He noted that the lamentation by another PNP executive member that corruption cannot be easily attached to Major General Anderson is also despicable and revealing, and confirms the PNP’s willingness to weaponise corruption without a credible basis and attempt to smear patriotic Jamaicans.

World.title: ‘Highway robbery’
World.content:
New toll fees affecting motorists using the North-South Highway are expected to take effect at the end of the month.

“HIGHWAY robbery” is how Noel Williams, president of the Kingston Chapter of Jamaica Union of Travellers Association (JUTA) Tours, has described the impending toll road rate increases, which transport operators fear could impact their operations. The increases prompted more calls on Monday for the Government to step in.

JUTA representatives, in collaboration with Jamaica Cooperative Automobile & Limousine (JCAL) Tours Limited and other transport organisations, gathered at the Jamaica Pegasus hotel in New Kingston for a meeting on Monday, hoping to get an audience with representatives of the Ministry of Transport and the Toll Authority of Jamaica to share pressing concerns.

But despite being invited, according to Williams, there were no representatives from either group.

Williams told the Jamaica Observer that their no-show was a clear indication of the scant regard which they have for transport operators.

“We are saying to the Government and the Toll Authority, that we cannot any longer absorb this toll increase, because we are of the opinion that this is the most expensive toll anywhere in the world,” Williams said, expressing that many operators already find it difficult to pay fees for certain categories of vehicles on the toll and cannot manage any upward adjustment at this time.

The new toll fees, to affect motorists using the North-South Highway, are expected to take effect at the end of the month.

The Government has published the proposed new rates with a capped toll of $2,610 each way for Class 1 vehicles. Operators of Class 2 vehicles would pay $5,220 one way, while the proposed toll for Class 3 vehicles, including larger trucks, is $7,830.

Williams recommended that the move be put on pause for a year, to allow for consultation among stakeholders.

“I think this is highway robbery by the Toll Authority, and the Government sits there completely complacent and they do nothing about it. With that said, we are asking the Government to have dialogue with the Toll Authority. We are having a serious issue already with what we are paying for one coaster bus to go from Kingston to St Ann and back. One round trip [now] costs bus operators $15,000. We will be asked to pay $15,680 when the new rate is introduced. If we are to do that, then we have to keep on passing on these increases to the passengers, who already have been complaining about what we are charging now,” he said.

The president said that numerous letters have been written to policymakers, but they have never responded.

He specifically referred to some representatives of the Toll Authority as being very disrespectful.

“We sent letters to the Toll Authority about another bus we have in the system, which is the new type of Hiace bus. It has a longer front than the older one, and hence when these buses go to the toll, they have to pay the same money as what the coaster pays,” he said.

“And when you question it, they are telling you that it’s because of the length of the bus. Nothing is put in place to accommodate the service that we provide in terms of transportation. And also the toll road barely has any lights. With all of this, we have to be paying so much money…

“We are definitely calling on the Government to sit and have a look at the situation and to renegotiate the contract so as to benefit the Jamaican people. A lot more people would use the toll as well, if it was much cheaper, but these people are just thinking about collecting money… they’re not thinking about us.“

Williams lamented that those operators who opt to take the alternative route from Kingston to St Ann cannot do so because those roads are deplorable. He appealed to the Government to have these alternative routes fixed.

“Right now, I believe it is a breach of people’s constitutional rights because they have been literally forced to use the toll, which is costly. The original roads are there, but they are not comfortable for people to drive on.

Meanwhile, Lorraine “Oscar” Finnikin, president of the All Voice Taxi Association, was among transport association heads present at the meeting.

He told the Observer that he attended to show solidarity with the JUTA president.

“They have tried their best over the years to not pass on the cost to their passengers but as it is now, they don’t have any choice,” he said.

“There are a lot of overhead expenses facing the public passenger vehicle sector. One is the cost of gas due to the situation in the Middle East, then there are overall expenses through maintenance, operational costs and service parts. With the increase in the toll fees, it has reached a stage where it is just too much for the sector to bear anymore.”

In a statement last Thursday, Minister of Transport Daryl Vaz acknowledged the concerns expressed by motorists, but explained that the concerning toll rates were yet another example of the former People’s National Party Administration entering into a less than favourable toll deal, which does not yield any tangible advantages for the Jamaican populace.

Vaz said the toll agreement binds current and future governments to its terms, but said the Government was moving to have discussions towards arriving at a more favourable and affordable toll cost for Jamaicans.

“However, the binding agreement entered by the former administration has put us in a position where the concessionaire has to agree to whatever we suggest in order for it to be implemented,” Vaz said.

He also said suggestions that Government pay off the toll operators in an effort to discontinue the unsustainable rise in rates, were impractical.

The Concession Agreement for the North-South Highway (Caymanas to Ocho Rios) was executed in June 2012 under a 50-year Build-Finance-Operate-Transfer arrangement.

World.title: EU sieht sich von Trumps neuen Generika-Zöllen nicht betroffen
World.content:
Im Rahmen der gemeinsamen Erklärung „haben sich die Vereinigten Staaten verpflichtet, Generika von den 15-prozentigen Zöllen auszunehmen; daher gilt weiterhin die Meistbegünstigungsklausel (MFN), was einem Zollsatz von 0 Prozent entspricht“, erklärte der stellvertretende Chefsprecher der Europäischen Kommission, Olof Gill. Er fügte hinzu, dass innovative Arzneimittel aus der EU weiterhin einem Zollsatz von 15 Prozent unterliegen.

„Dies zeigt deutlich, dass die gemeinsame Erklärung der EU und der USA ihre Wirkung entfaltet, indem sie Stabilität und Vorhersehbarkeit gewährleistet und einen wichtigen strategischen Sektor vor Störungen und Zollerhöhungen schützt“, betonte Gill. Die Vereinbarung an sich ist zwar nicht rechtsverbindlich, doch jeder Verstoß gegen ihre Bestimmungen würde wahrscheinlich eine Welle gegenseitiger Zollvergeltungsmaßnahmen auslösen.

Trumps jüngste Drohung kommt zu einem Zeitpunkt, an dem seine Regierung nach einem rechtlichen Rückschlag zu Beginn dieses Jahres eilig versucht, ihre Zollmauer wieder aufzubauen, da die vorübergehenden Zölle in Höhe von 10 Prozent am Freitag auslaufen sollen. Obwohl Washington beteuerte, dass die neuen Untersuchungen die im transatlantischen Abkommen festgelegte 15-Prozent-Schwelle nicht überschreiten würden, bereitet sich die EU dennoch auf weitere Untersuchungen vor, die sich auf Zwangsarbeit, Überkapazitäten im verarbeitenden Gewerbe und möglicherweise auch die Steuer auf digitale Dienstleistungen beziehen.

Risiken durch Arzneimittelknappheit

Die EU-Generika-Lobby „Medicines for Europe“ erklärte, die Maßnahmen könnten „erhebliche Arzneimittelengpässe in den gesamten Vereinigten Staaten“ auslösen. Patentfreie Arzneimittel aus Europa „sollten gemäß dem Turnberry-Abkommen unter allen Umständen von Zöllen ausgenommen bleiben“, so der Branchenverband.

Der Schweizer Generikahersteller Sandoz erklärte am Mittwochmorgen, es sei „noch zu früh, um die möglichen Auswirkungen einzuschätzen, da noch weitere Einzelheiten zur Umsetzung und zum Umfang der Maßnahme erforderlich sind“. Ein Sprecher von Sandoz fügte hinzu, das Unternehmen werde den Dialog mit den politischen Entscheidungsträgern darüber fortsetzen, wie die Erschwinglichkeit und der Zugang zu Medikamenten in den USA verbessert werden können.

Die Bedrohung für Generika erhöht den Druck auf die Pharmabranche, nachdem die Trump-Regierung Deutschland wegen seiner Preisgestaltung bei Arzneimitteln mit neuen Abgaben gedroht hatte.

World.title: Offener Widerstand gegen Weidel
World.content:
Share on LinkedIn

Share on WhatsApp

Share on X

Share via email

Im größten AfD-Landesverband Nordrhein-Westfalen tobt ein offener Machtkampf, der der Bundesspitze zunehmend entgleitet. Pauline von Pezold und Frederik Schindler analysieren im Detail, wie das radikale Helferich-Lager die Listenwahl sabotieren wollte. Sie besprechen, warum Landeschef Martin Vincentz sich juristisch gegen Alice Weidel wehren wollte und wie das Tabu des Widerstands gebrochen ist.

Zudem diskutieren die beiden die fehlenden Berührungsängste der AfD-Spitze zur rechtsextremen Szene. Schindler und von Pezold beleuchten, wie Spitzenpolitiker wie Ulrich Siegmund dem verurteilten Neonazi Sebastian Schmidtke freundschaftliche Interviews geben. Dabei gehen sie der Frage nach, warum die Unvereinbarkeitsliste der Partei in der Praxis offensichtlich ignoriert wird.

Nach dem Rücktritt von Jens Spahn geht es zudem um die gezielte Instrumentalisierung der Debatte um Leihmutterschaft. AfD-Funktionäre nutzen die ethische Diskussion als Deckmantel benutzen, um homosexuellen Paaren grundsätzlich die Eignung zur Erziehung von Kindern abzusprechen.

„Inside AfD“ ist der POLITICO-Podcast über die umstrittenste Partei des Landes. Trotz Radikalisierung und Beobachtung durch den Verfassungsschutz wächst die AfD weiter. Wie ist das möglich? Was treibt ihre Anhänger, Strategen und Gegner an? Wie funktioniert das Innenleben der Partei? Und was bedeutet ihr Aufstieg für das politische System Deutschlands?

Antworten liefern immer mittwochs Pauline von Pezold von POLITICO und Frederik Schindler von WELT — unaufgeregt, aber kritisch.

World.title: EU says Trump’s new generic drug tariffs won’t hit its exports
World.content:
Under the joint statement, “the United States committed to exempting generic medicines from the 15% tariffs; therefore MFN [most-favored-nation] treatment continues to apply, corresponding to a 0% tariff rate,” said the European Commission deputy chief spokesperson Olof Gill. He added that EU innovative drugs continue to be subject to a 15 percent tariff.

“This clearly shows that the EU–U.S. Joint Statement is delivering by preserving stability and predictability, and protecting a key strategic sector from disruption and tariff increases,” Gill stressed. The deal as such is not legally binding, but any breach of its terms would likely unleash tit-for-tat tariff retaliation.

Trump’s latest threat comes as his administration is scrambling to rebuild its tariff wall after a legal setback earlier this year, with its temporary 10 percent tariffs due to lapse Friday. Although Washington insisted that the new probes would not breach the 15 percent threshold enshrined by the transatlantic deal, the EU is still bracing for more investigations, targeting forced labor, excess capacity in the manufacturing sector and possibly also digital services tax.

Drug shortage risks

The EU generics lobby, Medicines for Europe, said the measures risked triggering “significant medicine shortages across the United States”. Off-patent drugs from Europe “should remain exempt from tariffs under all circumstances” under the Turnberry agreement, the trade group said.

Swiss generics manufacturer Sandoz said Wednesday morning it was “too early to assess the potential implications, as further details on the implementation and scope of the measure are still required.” A Sandoz spokesperson added the company would continue dialogue with policymakers on how to improve affordability and access to medicines in the U.S.

Threats to generic medicines increase pressure on the pharmaceutical sector, after the Trump administration threatened new levies on Germany over its drug pricing policies.

Washington alleges that Berlin’s laws result in the U.S. paying a disproportionate share of research and development costs for innovative drugs. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said last week that he was also in talks with France over its pricing practices.

“The pharmaceutical sector is critically important on both sides of the Atlantic, with highly integrated supply chains, strong investment and research ties, and broadly balanced trade flows. Preserving these links is essential both for patient access and for sustaining innovation,” added Gill, the Commission spokesperson.

World.title: Macron convinces environment minister to stay on
World.content:
Tensions between Monique Barbut and the government came to a head over an agriculture bill. | Magali Cohen/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images

Monique Barbut had resigned earlier this week claiming the “forces opposing” her green transition agenda had become “too powerful.”

PARIS — French President Emmanuel Macron asked his Minister for Ecological Transition Monique Barbut to stay in her role after she resigned on Wednesday morning.

"The French president refused her resignation," government spokesperson Maud Bregeon announced at a press conference. "They agreed on three fundamental pillars that will guide her action: forests, water and environmental health … on which she agreed to remain fully invested."

Barbut's office told French news agency AFP that she had agreed to remain in her post "at the request" of the president, citing "the urgent need to take action against the consequences of climate change."

World.title: Britain’s new defense chief Streeting says Israel has ‘fallen short’ in Gaza
World.content:
The defense secretary has previously said — in WhatsApp messages to former U.S. ambassador Peter Mandelson before Streeting took up his current job — that “Israel is committing war crimes before our eyes,” and is committing “rogue state behaviour” in the West Bank.

Asked about these messages Wednesday, Streeting refused to repeat them. But he said: “I’m not going to pretend I didn’t make those comments.”

His remarks highlight the continued ripple effects on the left of British politics over Israel’s protracted campaign in the Gaza Strip, which followed the deadly Oct. 7, 2023 attacks by Hamas. The new defense secretary nearly lost his parliamentary seat of Ilford North at the last general election after a large turnout among pro-Palestinian constituents, and has been projected to lose it by some pollsters.

Streeting also refused to say whether he believes Britain should continue to buy Israeli weapons as those are “not my decisions alone.”

“I’ve expressed very clearly my concerns about Israel’s actions in Gaza and the West Bank,” he said, adding that he believes “very strongly in Israel's right to defend itself, to defend its values, its freedom, and its democracy, just as we do every single day.”

Britain’s new Prime Minister Andy Burnham has tried to make a break with his predecessor, Keir Starmer, who was condemned by some in his own party for his staunch support for Israel in the immediate aftermath of October 7 – including a broadcast interview in which he appeared to say that Israel had the "right" to cut off water and energy to Gaza.

World.title: Huawei ban to cost the EU up to €40 billion, says industry
World.content:
The true cost of ripping up and replacing telecom equipment from Chinese manufacturers Huawei and ZTE — which the Commission proposed banning as part of a new EU Cybersecurity Act — is hotly contested, as is whether telecom operators should be compensated.

GSMA on Wednesday priced the removal of high-risk vendors from mobile networks at €16 to €22 billion, including costs from fixed networks at €5 billion and from transport networks at €9 to €12 billion.

The trade body also said there would be an additional cost of €8.5 billion from 2027 to 2030 because there would be less competition among manufacturers of telecom equipment, leading to higher prices.

Some experts dispute the figures. “GSMA estimates are gross, not incremental,” said Hosuk Lee-Makiyama, director at think tank ECIPE. If the study deducted “replacement costs that would have occurred anyway,” it would arrive at roughly the same figures as the Commission, he argued.

The Commission did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

World.title: Is everyone on the Burnham bus?
World.content:
Andy Burnham wants to talk about his new bus fare cap but, as Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy point out, there isn’t much chance of talking about anything else without the Commons sitting.

They go through how the bus fare plan is funded. Chancellor John Healey says it will be “no burden to British taxpayers”, but the small print raises questions about how the scheme will be funded.

At the Farnborough Air Show, there is the opportunity to talk defence spending – and fresh questions about how to fill the funding gap from Keir Starmer’s pledges.

Plus, Sam and Anne round up the latest ministerial movements.

World.title: The EU’s Russia sanctions crunch
World.content:
Today is a make-or-break moment for the EU’s 21st sanctions package targeting Russia.

After EU countries failed to agree on the ins and outs of the agreement last week, ambassadors are meeting again today in Brussels to finally clinch the deal. But can they hash out the remaining thorny issues?

Next: European Parliament is trying to reengage with China after a seven-year diplomatic freeze. But despite the defrosting of relations, it’s clear lawmakers are unsure of what their stance toward Beijing should be.

And finally, as Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” hits cinemas, a Hollywood culture war hits Greece.
