World.title: People are living longer, but not healthier, study finds
World.content:
Life expectancy has risen dramatically over the past century — reaching 73.8 years — thanks to steep declines in infectious diseases, maternal and child mortality, and advances in the prevention and treatment of chronic conditions.

 

However, the years gained are not necessarily lived in good health, a new study, published in The Lancet Public Health, found. With gains in life expectancy outstripping improvements in healthy life expectancy across almost all 204 countries and territories analysed, the authors argue that health systems need to shift their focus from simply extending lives to improving the quality of those extra years.

Globally, people spent an average of 14.5% of their lives in poor health in 2023, with longer life expectancy increasingly accompanied by non-fatal illnesses and disabilities, researchers found.

Countries where people lived the longest also saw more years spent in poor health, suggesting that longer life expectancy is extending the period of illness and disability across adulthood rather than delaying it until the final years of life.

In 2023, people in the wealthiest countries spent 15.7% of their lives in poor health, while the sub-Saharan African super-region had the smallest morbidity gap, at 9 years.

The Netherlands saw the largest absolute increase, with the proportion of life spent in poor health rising from 13.2% in 1990 to 15.7% in 2023.

The greatest morbidity gaps — the duration or proportion of life spent in poor health — were in the United States, Australia and Canada.

By contrast, people in Nauru, the Solomon Islands and Laos experienced the smallest morbidity gaps, spending the fewest years of their lives in poor health.

What is driving this gap?

The authors found that non-fatal conditions accounted for 57.4% of the global morbidity gap, as they increase the time people spend living with disability or reduced health.

The main drivers among these conditions were musculoskeletal disorders such as low back pain, mental disorders, sense organ diseases such as age-related hearing loss and unintentional injuries.

In lower-income countries, nutritional deficiencies, respiratory infections, tuberculosis and neglected tropical diseases were also among the leading contributors.

The study also identified multiple risk factors, including high body mass index, child and maternal malnutrition, tobacco use, high fasting plasma glucose and air pollution.

Drug use and high alcohol use were among the ten leading risk factors contributing to the morbidity gap only in the high-income super-region, whereas unsafe sex emerged as a leading factor solely in sub-Saharan Africa.

What does a healthy future look like?

According to the authors, the findings raise questions about the sustainability of social care and the allocation of resources between prevention, treatment, and innovation. As the percentage of life spent in poor health has steadily increased since 1990, there is an urgency to focus on healthy ageing — the process of developing and maintaining the functional ability that enables wellbeing in older age, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

“Our findings suggest that future gains in population health will come not only from helping people live longer, but from helping them live healthier,” said senior author of the study Christopher Murray, who is a director of the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) at the University of Washington School of Medicine.

“Progress in healthy [ageing] should be measured not only by lifespan, but by healthspan, with greater investment in prevention, long-term disease management, and chronic care to reduce years lived in poor health,” Murray said.

Economic modelling indicates that improving health by targeting ageing could offer larger financial gains than increasing life expectancy by eliminating specific diseases, authors of the study argued.

“Improving healthy [ageing] will require greater focus on the conditions and risk factors that drive years lived with disability,” said Catherine Bisignano, co-author of the study. “Addressing these earlier through prevention and better long-term care could have meaningful social, health system, and economic impacts.”

To that end, the study calls for sustained investment in prevention, rehabilitation, mental health services, and chronic care, as well as improved access to assistive technologies and integrated long-term care models.

World.title: Trump threatens to bomb Tehran back for every Iranian attack in Hormuz
World.content:
President Donald Trump on Wednesday pledged that the US would bomb Iranian civil infrastructure every time Tehran fires at ships in the strategic Strait of Hormuz.

 

"From this point forward, any time the Islamic Republic of Iran shoots at a ship in the Strait of Hormuz, whether it be by missile, rocket, drone, or any other device or weapon, the United States will bomb and destroy one bridge or power plant," Trump wrote on his Truth Social network.

Trump said this included Iranian facilities "located next to, or in, the capital city of Tehran."

Trump's threat came shortly before he headed to an airbase for the return of the remains of three US troops killed in Iranian attacks on US military facilities in the Gulf.

The US president said he was going to "honour our heroes and they're indeed great heroes."

"All of them said, very strongly, that we can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon, so we're going to honour them... For me it's one of the hardest things to do as president but it has to be done," he added.

Trump rejected polls that show the Iran war is unpopular with US voters ahead of midterm elections in November, with rising oil prices fueling a spike in the cost of living.

The war has already cost Washington $37.5 billion (€32.8bn).

"Americans don't want high gasoline prices but they're not against the war, that just came out loud and clear," Trump said.

Attacks shake Iran and Jordan

Washington has stepped up strikes against Iran since a preliminary ceasefire deal collapsed amid fighting over the strait, carrying out 11 straight days of attacks on the Islamic republic.

Iran has retaliated by firing at US military facilities in the Gulf.

Jordan’s military said it intercepted four Iranian missiles over Aqaba on Wednesday, while two others fell in “uninhabited areas”.

Plumes of smoke could be seen overhead in videos filmed by people in the nearby Israeli city of Eilat. Jordan said it also intercepted four Iranian drones.

Iran has avoided striking Israel since hostilities resumed last month, apparently hoping to keep it from reentering the war.

But the attack on Aqaba, within sight of Israel’s Eilat, raised concerns over a further widening of the conflict after an agreement to halt hostilities collapsed.

Another missile alert sounded in Bahrain, and Saudi Arabia warned residents of the Persian Gulf city of Dammam to seek shelter. Saudi authorities later said the danger had passed, without elaborating.

Iran's state-run IRNA news agency reported explosions across several provinces. Iran's Health Ministry says US strikes over the past 11 days have killed 53 people, including six women and three children, and wounded nearly 600 people.

Iran's IRGC insisted its retaliatory attacks would continue.

The US military said Wednesday's dignified transfer service at Dover Air Base in Delaware was for two service members killed in an Iranian attack on a base in Jordan and a service member killed during a controlled detonation of a drone in Iraq.

A third service member remains missing from the Jordan attack.

Trump has vowed to avenge the deaths of all US troops "many times over" and stepped up threats to target civilian infrastructure. The total number of US deaths since the start of the war is 18.

The US president also repeated threats on Tuesday to strike what he said was a secret Iranian nuclear complex called Pickaxe Mountain. Iran denies the existence of any facility at the site, which it calls Kolang mountain.

World.title: Nicolas Maduro returns to court in US drug trafficking case
World.content:
Venezuela's ousted president Nicolas Maduro is due to appear before a New York court on Wednesday for his third public hearing since US forces captured him in a nighttime raid in January.

 

In a court filing late on Tuesday, prosecutors and defence lawyers proposed a June 2027 trial date, which Judge Alvin Hellerstein could confirm at Wednesday's procedural hearing.

Meanwhile, outside the court, demonstrators have held signs in support of the ousted president and his wife.

Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores have been held in a Brooklyn jail since the US military operation, awaiting trial on drug trafficking, firearms and other charges.

People protest in support of former Venezuela President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores outside of Manhattan federal court, Wednesday, 22 July, 2026, in New York. AP Photo

Both have pleaded not guilty. They face possible life sentences if a jury finds they conspired to send cocaine into the United States.

“I am not guilty. I am a decent man, the constitutional president of my country,” Maduro said at his arraignment in January.

US President Donald Trump's administration has described the raid as a "surgical law enforcement operation" in a criminal case first brought six years ago. However, Maduro has described himself as a "prisoner of war" and his capture as a kidnapping.

Prosecutors allege that Maduro conspired to traffic thousands of tonnes of cocaine into the United States by colluding with Venezuelan law enforcement officials to assist drug kingpins.

Maduro’s lawyer, Barry Pollack, has said he expects to contest the legality of Maduro’s “military abduction.”

The lawyers have said there are complex legal defenses that the court must address before a trial can begin.

Maduro and Flores have not asked to be released on bail.

World.title: Hungary's prosecutor resigns under pressure in political win for Magyar
World.content:
Hungary's Prosecutor General has resigned, bowing to pressure from Prime Minister Péter Magyar, who is seeking to remove key officials appointed under Viktor Orbán.

 

In a statement, Gábor Bálint Nagy said he was stepping down to safeguard the integrity and independence of the prosecutor office, condemning what he described as political pressure placed upon it.

"The prosecution service must not become an instrument in the struggles of political actors, nor can it be a stage for day-to-day political interests or power games," Nagy said, adding that he no longer wished to be part of a conflict "built on false premises and serving political ends."

Magyar welcomed the resignation, saying: "With this, the country has freed itself from another Orbán puppet."

Since his landslide election victory in April, Magyar has called for the removal of senior officials appointed during Orbán's time in office. Over the weekend, President Tamás Sulyok also signed a constitutional amendment ending his own mandate.

Nagy had also come under criticism from lawyers representing a group of Ukrainian cash couriers, who accused him of acting on political orders.

In early March, two vans carrying large quantities of cash and gold bound for Oschadbank's headquarters in Kyiv left Vienna before being stopped near Budapest. The crew were detained, questioned and expelled from Hungary, while the cash and gold were confiscated.

Lóránt Horváth, the lawyer representing Oschadbank and the seven detained Ukrainians, told Euronews that those responsible for the operation should themselves have faced prosecution.

"The chief prosecutor supervising and directing this investigation was appointed by the previous government, so it is also possible that he is providing political support, or a safety net, to his former bosses in some way," Horváth said.

The Prosecutor's Office has denied any political motive behind the operation. Nagy had led the office since last year.

World.title: What are the ‘catastrophic’ pesticides that led France’s environment minister to try and quit?
World.content:
France's Minister for the Ecological Transition has tried to resign after lawmakers approved a bill allowing bee-harming pesticides to come back into use.

 

"Contrary to the commitments that had been made to me, the government prevented any debate on the removal of this measure," Monique Barbut said in a statement posted on LinkedIn.

She said that the reversal was "one environmental setback too many" however President Macron did not accept her resignation, and "assured her of his support," her office told news agency AFP.

Barbut - also former executive secretary of the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification - will stay due to the "urgency to address the consequences of climate change," her team added.

What are the two pesticides that led Monique Barbut to try and resign and how dangerous are they?

Acetamiprid and flupyradifurone: ‘Catastrophic’ pesticides

The French parliament approved a controversial agriculture bill reintroducing two pesticides critics say harm bees.

The legislation gives France's health and safety agency, Anses, the authority to conditionally authorise the use of acetamiprid and flupyradifurone. The pesticides are allowed in the European Union, but individual countries can limit their use.

Proponents say French sugar beet, apple and hazelnut farmers need the insecticides - forbidden in France since 2018 and 2019 respectively - to help them compete with their European counterparts.

While research has found that acetamiprid can poison honeybees, affecting their foraging capacity and memory, a 2024 study suggested flupyradifurone could be lethal to some bees.

"In 2016, France chose to ban acetamiprid in the name of the precautionary principle, based on the scientific evidence available at the time," Barbut said. "Ten years later, far from dispelling concerns, scientific studies continue to raise doubts about its effects on human health and the environment."

Pesticide Action Network Europe have long campaigned for acetamiprid to be banned not only on the basis of its impacts on bees but also on humans: “New scientific evidence shows that neonicotinoids like acetamiprid can favour breast cancer, due to its endocrine disruption property, and may lead to infertility. They can also affect our brain. Neonicotinoids cross the placental barrier and the brain barrier, putting unborn children at risk.

“Acetamiprid has been detected in umbilical cords, breast milk and even in children's cerebrospinal fluid. It has been shown to concentrate at high levels in mice fetuses' brains upon mother exposure.”

Flupyradifurone was approved in 2015. “It was presented by producer Bayer as an alternative to the other, more bee-toxic neonicotinoids. This proves to be new wine in an old bottle, since, in fact, it can be considered just another neonicotinoid,” according to Pesticide Action Network Europe.

How did acetamiprid and flupyradifurone get approved in the French parliament?

The vote came after the Constitutional Council, France's highest court, last year struck down a provision in another bill trying to reintroduce acetamiprid, saying it posed risks to human health, after more than two million people signed a petition against it.

Most leftists in the lower house voted against the reintroduction of the two pesticides, but backing from the far right and many centrists meant it passed. The left has said it would appeal to the Constitutional Council if the Senate approved the measure.

The left is expected to refer the matter to the Constitutional Council, and Green MP Daniel Salmon has slammed “a reckless and destructive headlong rush, with complacent measures that deny the scientific evidence”.

For his part, centrist senator Franck Ménonville describes the text as a response to “the hypocrisy of producing less in France in order to import ever more products that do not comply with our standards”.

"The government and its allies are trampling on science, health, the environment, and the will of the people," Greenpeace said after the National Assembly passed the bill.

Henri Clement, of the French Beekeeping Union, told regional media outlet Ici Gard Lozere the measure was "absolutely catastrophic".

Agriculture Minister Annie Genevard has defended the bill as necessary to address discontent among farmers after protests this winter. She has stressed health authorities would only approve use of the pesticides in certain areas for limited periods "on the condition there is no impact on human health or on the environment, there is an emergency situation" and "there is no alternative".

World.title: Countdown to the ballot: Zambia gears up for August elections
World.content:
This week on Spotlight on Africa, we're heading to Zambia, where general elections are set to take place on the 13th August. Voters will go to the polls to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs. Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema has already picked up endorsements from within his own camp, the UPND Alliance, the coalition that's held power since 2021. So what's at stake, and who's in the running?

Advertising

This week on the podcast, we're heading to Zambia, which is gearing up for elections next month and is now in full campaign mode. Two of our RFI colleagues, Yang Mei and Igor Strauss, travelled to Zambia recently for in-depth reporting on four years of Hakainde Hichilema's rule, and his chances of re-election.

In power since August 2021, "HH", as he's most often called, is a businessman, farmer and politician, and the seventh president of Zambia.

General elections are due to be held in the country on 13 August 2026 to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs.

The year ahead for African democracy: who is going to the polls in 2026?

Hichilema has received endorsements from some members of the UPND Alliance, including from the leaders of the Party of National Unity and Progress and the Movement for Multi-Party Democracy.

According to an opinion poll conducted by a University of Zambia demographer, Hichilema is set to be re-elected, leading with 60 percent of the vote, while the combined opposition would take 35 percent.

Zambia's Hichilema sworn in, becoming rare opposition president in southern Africa

Our colleagues Yang Mei and Igor Strauss bring us some of the interviews they gathered on the ground, so join us as we hear from ordinary Zambians, as well as from leading journalist Joseph Mwenda, editor-in-chief at News Diggers, who has led multiple investigations into the current government's relations with China; and from Robert Mwale, an economist and Lead Public Finance and Economic Governance Researcher at the Centre for Trade Policy and Development (CTPD).

Among the issues at stake are a lack of freedom of expression, but also a legacy of economic growth, driven in no small part by China's heavy involvement in the economy.

Thanks to our reporters, Igor Strauss and Yang Mei, for their work and insight, and thank you for listening.

This is the last episode of the 2025–26 season. We'll be back in September with another one.

Spotlight on Africa is produced by RFI's English language service. This episode was mixed by Erwan Rome.

World.title: Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended
World.content:
On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

Advertising

On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

A decade ago, factions within the Turkish military, composed of rebellious officers and followers of the Islamic cleric Fethullah Gulen, launched a dramatic attempt to topple President Erdogan.

"I remember, as a soldier, those who started the coup," recalls Murat Aslan, an army officer at the time. "I had no idea that there were members of this organisation (Gulen followers); they were very secretive."

Erdogan tightens his grip

Now a security analyst at SETA, a pro-government think tank, Aslan describes the failed coup as a turning point that reshaped the course of Turkish democracy.

"The message was very clear. Turkish society collectively rejected it," said Aslan. "Thousands took to the streets; that's more than challenging, because you see tanks rolling and people trying to stop them, trying to capture the soldiers with their rifles. It takes more than courage." More than 250 people died resisting the coup.

In the aftermath, Erdogan imposed emergency rule and expanded his presidential authority through a sharply contested national referendum. "This military intervention actually consolidated the Erdogan-led government," Aslan added.

Turkey's military, relations with US to survive failed coup, ruling party vice-president

Hundreds of soldiers and officers faced prosecution as the government declared an end to the army's long history of political interference. Since 1960, the military had orchestrated three coups, the most recent in 1980.

A decade of purges and closures

In the wake of the failed takeover, tens of thousands were purged from state institutions, many never returning even after being cleared.

More than a thousand NGOs were shut down during two years of emergency rule. Milena Buyum, senior Turkey campaigner for Amnesty International, acknowledges the grave threat to democracy posed by the attempted coup: "The state has a responsibility to ensure the safety and security of its citizens and to investigate criminal acts like the ones carried out that night," said Buyum.

Turkey's Erdogan warms to Russia after West coup response

However, Buyum warns that many of the measures introduced under the state of emergency have since been written into ordinary law, permanently curtailing fundamental freedoms: "The right to freedom of expression, freedom of assembly and association: the impact on civil society was felt very sharply and starkly in the immediate aftermath of the coup, but that impact continues," said Buyum.

Ankara's alliances

The failed coup also drove a wedge into Turkey's long-standing alliance with the United States. "Ankara saw the hand of the United States behind the failed coup attempt," claims Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, who leads the Ankara office of the German Marshall Fund.

Even before the attempted coup, Erdogan's relations with President Barack Obama had been tense. Obama's belated support, offered only after the coup had failed, fuelled Ankara's suspicions of US complicity, particularly as Washington refused to extradite Fethullah Gulen, whom Erdogan blamed for orchestrating the plot. Gulen denied the accusation until his death in 2024.

Turks in France divided on failed coup

Unluhisarcikli observes that US-Turkish relations remained strained for years, while Erdogan gravitated towards Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose rapid show of support stood in sharp contrast to Washington's hesitation.

"Putin was among the first leaders, I believe even the first, to extend political support to the elected government in Ankara, and in those days I believe that support mattered greatly to President Erdogan," Unluhisarcikli said.

Rumours still persist in Turkey today that Moscow warned Erdogan on the day of the failed coup. Unluhisarcikli says it was only with the election of President Donald Trump, who shared Erdogan's animosity towards Obama and Joe Biden, that US-Turkish relations began to thaw, a shift highlighted at this month's NATO summit in Ankara. Yet the wave of mass arrests during the summit, enabled by post-coup emergency powers, served as a stark reminder that the shadow of the failed takeover still looms over Turkey.

World.title: DW correspondent Alican Uludag released, ordered not to leave Turkey
World.content:
Alican Uludag was freed Wednesday, a day after being taken back into custody on new charges. The arrest had come just two months after he was released pending trial in a separate case.

Deutsche Welle correspondent Alican Uludag was released Wednesday under judicial supervision after spending approximately 25 hours in police custody.

He was taken into custody Tuesday on suspicion of inciting hatred and hostility and publicly spreading misleading ​information the Turkish prosecutor's office ‌said.

At the time of his latest detention, Uludag was already on conditional release after being detained in February on charges including insulting President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Germany criticizes renewed detention

Before his release Wednesday, a German government spokesperson said Berlin was "highly irritated" by Uludag's renewed detention.

According to Reuters news agency, the spokesperson said Turkish authorities were acting in violation of press freedom, which Turkey had committed itself to upholding by joining the Council of Europe and signing the European Convention on Human Rights.

Following Tuesday's arrest, DW Director General Barbara Massing described his re-arrest as "deeply concerning" and added, "we expect his rights to be fully respected and demand a fair trial in accordance with the rule of law."

Journalists protest outside courthouse

Uludag's latest detention drew criticism from Turkish press organizations, which gathered outside the Ankara courthouse before the proceedings Wednesday.

A small group of demonstrators carried signs and chanted, "Journalism is not a crime," while calling for his immediate release.

Some members of Turkish press organizations gathered outside the Ankara courthouse to criticise the case against Uludag Image: ANKA

Uludag was released, but the court warned him not to leave the country and ordered him to report to police four times a week.

Sinan Tartanoglu, head of the Ankara branch of the Turkish Journalists' Union, said the case reflected broader pressure on reporters in Turkey.

"There are many journalists in prison and many under investigation," Tartanoglu was quoted by DW's Turkish Service as saying. "We want to be able to report the news, publish our social media posts and express our criticism freely."

Uludag has repeatedly denied the charges against him.

World.title: Germany: Merz replaces key figure following surrogacy row
World.content:
Thorsten Frei, a close confidant of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is taking over the role as parliamentary group leader for the conservative CDU/CSU bloc. The position is a powerful one.

The leaders of Germany's governing conservatives wasted no time: Just a few days after Jens Spahn resigned as parliamentary group leader following a scandal over surrogacy, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) named its candidate to succeed him: Thorsten Frei.

The 52-year-old, currently serving as head of the chancellery and considered a close confidant of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is now set take over one of the most important positions in German politics, leading the Bundestag members of both the CDU and its Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union (CSU).

Frei can only officially take office once he has been elected by the parliamentarians. To that end, the 208 CDU and CSU lawmakers are scheduled to interrupt their summer recess on July 29 to convene a special session in the Bundestag. Frei's successor at the chancellery is also expected to be named by then.

Working behind the scenes wasn't Frei's strength

Friendly, likable, approachable, and a good mediator — that's how Thorsten Frei is often described in Berlin's political circles.

A trained lawyer, he has been married to a teacher for 20 years and has three children. He lives in the city of Donaueschingen in the southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg in the Black Forest, where Frei was also mayor for nine years before entering federal politics.

At the chancellery, his job was essentially to cover Friedrich Merz's back, a kind of first officer to the ship's captain who is responsible for ensuring that the chancellor's affairs run smoothly, that obstacles are cleared out of the way, and that the chancellor is properly briefed on the day's appointments.

It was a role that, some critics have said, did not really suit Frei, who was sometimes accused of preferring to give interviews himself rather than quietly coordinate the chancellor's affairs.

Back in the spotlight

But as parliamentary group leader, Frei will be freer to take center stage. His task will be to explain his party's positions in speeches in the Bundestag parliament and media interviews. Above all, he will have to secure majorities for the government's policies and ensure that the members of his parliamentary group are as united as possible.

This is not seen as an easy task. Since the current government took office in May last year, outgoing group leader Jens Spahn sometimes struggled to maintain the government's 18-seat majority.

The parliamentary group leader must also negotiate with the conservatives' coalition partner, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), something that Spahn had recently been seen as good at. In short: The chancellor governs, while the parliamentary group leader ensures his political support.

When the CDU/CSU was in opposition from 2021 to 2025, Frei held the office of parliamentary secretary of the group, an administrative task that involves overseeing day-to-day coordination of the parliament's agenda, organizing committees, and ensuring that group members are present for important votes. At the time, Frei worked closely with Merz, then the leader of the opposition and parliamentary group leader.

After the February 2025 election, Frei reportedly coveted the group leader job, but had to make way for the more famous Spahn, a former health minister under Angela Merkel.

A case of double standards

Spahn had been in office for about 14 months when he resigned last Saturday (July 18). He and his husband, Daniel Funke, had announced that they had become parents with the help of a surrogate mother in the United States. However, surrogacy is prohibited in Germany, and the CDU is a party that has repeatedly voted to support this ban.

Spahn was accused of hypocrisy. By bypassing a law that some saw as a cornerstone of his party's moral values, Spahn was seen as having created a credibility problem not only for himself but also for his party.

The Social Democrats are satisfied

The nomination of Frei as Spahn's successor has been met with approval by the coalition partner, the SPD. "I have worked very well with Thorsten Frei in the past," said Dirk Wiese, parliamentary secretary of the SPD parliamentary group in the Bundestag, in Berlin. "We were both deputy parliamentary group leaders for domestic and legal policy in the last grand coalition, and I got to know him there as a very knowledgeable colleague who is easy to negotiate with and who always has a very detailed grasp of the issues."

Wiese said he looked forward to working with him in the future, once the CDU/CSU leadership bodies have given their approval.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Germany's growing interest in Africa: A win for both sides?
World.content:
Germany is deepening its footprint across Africa, as Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul embarks on his third trip to the continent in 2026. His top-level talks will focus on security, skills development and investment.

Wadephul is currently visiting Nigeria as part of a multi-country trip across Africa, after a major stopover in Mauritania, and before making a call on South Africa.

The trip follows up on prior journeys to Africa by Germany's top diplomat, who visited Ethiopia and Kenya in January, and Morocco in April.

Wadephul says these repeated travels to the continent are a strategic necessity as part of Germany's expanding engagement with Africa.

"This is my third trip to Africa now. Why? Africa is a continent of both destiny and opportunity for Europe," he told reporters, highlighting the continent's economic potential while also pointing out persistent security challenges.

In Nouakchott, Wadephul met with Mauritanian President Mohamed Ghazouani Image: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

Mauritania: Security, migration and counterterrorism

Wadephul's stop in Mauritania focused on various interlinked issues such as security cooperation, migration management and regional stability.

Geopolitical analyst Fidel Amakye Owusu said that Germany was interested in "Mauritania because of migration," highlighting the growing use of Atlantic migration routes by people desperate to reach Europe.

The German foreign minister's visit came just days after the UN refugee agency reported at least 144 deaths along this route near the Mauritanian coast.

Wadephul's visit, however, also focused on opportunities for deeper security cooperation with Mauritania; his delegation visited the Mourchidates, an all-female Islamic spiritual guide group trained and deployed by the state to counter extremism.

DW's Silja Fröhlich, who accompanied Wadephul on the trip, noted that the foreign minister's interaction with the Mourchidates was one of the main highlights: "In Mauritania, he was visibly moved by women working with the UN to prevent extremism and violence — women who, despite living in a deeply patriarchal society and often carrying personal ties to the very conflict they are confronting, are determined to protect their communities," she explained.

Support for such a grassroots initiative is also a reflection of Germany's intent on bolstering community‑based approaches to preventing radicalization.

Germany hopes to intensify its involvement — and investments — in Nigeria Image: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

Nigeria: Economic partnership and youth‑driven innovation

As part of the second leg in Nigeria, Wadephul has met with various entrepreneurs, creatives, influencers, filmmakers and students.

"We are looking for new global partners. This is the very reason that I am here: that we are looking to Africa and to the countries in Africa. I view Nigeria as some kind of a powerhouse, a striving nation, growing faster and faster and with a lot of creative ideas," the foreign minister commented, describing Nigeria as an African powerhouse, particularly in the creative industries.

Vocational education, skills development and collaboration in science, technology and innovation have been highlighted as key areas for future cooperation, with discussions also centering on expanding economic and commercial partnerships and attracting greater German investment into priority sectors.

Nigeria's Ministry of Foreign Affairs Ministry in a statement said that the country "looks forward to productive engagements that will further consolidate the existing friendship, and open new avenues for collaboration in support of inclusive economic growth, regional stability and shared prosperity."

Local content creator Shalom Onyuinye said that Wadephul's recognition of Nigeria's growing cultural momentum around the world marked a significant shift in the global perception of Africa's most populous country.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul wants to support and boost Nigeria's creative enterprises Image: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

South Africa: Germany's closest economic partner in Africa

Wadephul's trip across the continent is due to conclude in South Africa — Germany's most significant economic partner in Africa, with more than 600 German companies operating there.

German direct investment in South Africa reached €7.99 billion ($9.1 billion) in 2023, with South African investment in Germany totaling €2.6 billion, according to Germany's Federal Foreign Office.

Analyst Owusu thinks that South Africa's advanced and diverse economy as well as its role as Africa's chief manufacturing hub make the country attractive to foreign investors; he also noted that German investment could generate substantial benefits in the long run — for both sides.

However, against the backdrop of recent xenophobic attacks across the country, the German foreign minister is expected to insist on shared democratic values between the two nations.

This upcoming leg of Wadephul's trip will also likely focus on industrial cooperation, energy transition partnerships and strengthening Germany's ties with South Africa's business and political leadership.

Germany's FM stresses Europe's 'need' for skilled workers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany's growing interest in Africa

Wadephul's visit to Africa also builds on a partnership established last year, when Germany and the African Union (AU) launched their first‑ever strategic dialogue on foreign and security policy at the AU headquarters in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

This new framework aims to deepen cooperation on global security crises and multilateral engagement, for which Germany has pledged funds exceeding €100 million in total.

"Especially at a time of major global geopolitical upheaval, reliable cooperation with our African partners is essential," Wadephul remarked at the launch of the initiative.

The German foreign minister stressed at the time that Europe and Africa were "closely interconnected politically, economically, and in terms of security, and face many of the same challenges," stressing that "a strong Africa is in Germany's interest."

Silja Fröhlich contributed to this article

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

World.title: Female coaches want more representation in African football
World.content:
Female head coaches will be a rare sight at the Women’s African Cup of Nations. However, there are some promising signs.

When it kicks off in Morocco on July 26, the Women's African Cup of Nations (WAFCON) promises to provide great goals, games and memories as 16 teams compete for the continental title. While the focus will be on the stars on the pitch, there may also be some attention on the fact that very few of the head coaches are female.

Cameroon's appointment of Valentine Nguel just weeks before the tournament, brought the number of WAFCON nations with female coaches to four — along with Zambia, Kenya, and South Africa. Still, the vast majority of coaches are men. Other teams have appointed female assistants in order to comply with a rule passed by FIFA earlier this year, which requires women's teams to have at least one female coach on the bench.

Africa may be moving slowly in the right direction with two head coaches of 12 at the 2025 WAFCON (16.7%) to four of 16 (25%) in 2026, but there is still a long way to go.

Desiree Ellis has been named Africa's women's coach of the year four times. Image: Nour Aknajja/Sports Inc/empics/picture alliance

South Africa leads the way. Desiree Ellis is one of the world's most successful female coaches and led South Africa to the 2022 title. The four-time African Women's coach of the year would like more countries to follow the example set by hers.

Helping female coaches

"Our federation took a stand long ago that all female teams will be coached by females," Ellis told DW.

"That needs to happen and federations need to be brave and appoint female coaches. They need to not just appoint them but give them support, otherwise they are not going to succeed."

South Africa is one of 14 members of the Council of Southern Africa Football Associations (COSAFA). Even before the FIFA regulation announced in March, this regional organization already had a rule in place making it mandatory for women to form part of the coaching teams.

"This is to force federations to provide more opportunities for female coaches, and we can see that in South Africa, it's yielded good dividends," Ellis said.

Jackline Juma says female coaches in Africa are not given the same support as their male counterparts Image: Talanta FC

Jackline Juma is head coach of Kenya's U-20 women's team and would like to see something similar set up all over the continent.

"We don't have many female coaches in charge of African female teams… It's because they still don't trust women, don't give them chances, the support is not as much as for male coaches," Juma told DW.

She believes that such attitudes mean help is needed.

"At least, get restrictions when it comes to club licensing so that for female football teams, priority should be given to female coaches as head coaches so this would give us a good number of female coaches rising up."

Juma suggests that the first assistant coach should also be female with men allowed to fill out the coaching staff after that.

Setting pathways

More jobs coupled with role models like Ellis can inspire a new generation of female coaches and Vicky Huyton, who founded the Female Coaching Network in 2014, told DW that while just 20% of female national teams have female coaches, they account for 90% of major championships.

Inspiring young girls is, however, just the beginning of what can be a long and difficult journey to the upper reaches of the sport. While there are some countries that have made strides, some federations still have much to do in this field to enable coaches to reach their full potential.

"I am contacted quite often by amazing female coaches in Africa –various countries, Uganda, Kenya, Nigeria." Huyton told DW.

"Often they say 'I have a passion, I have a want, but I have nowhere to go.'"

Huyton would like to see a clear pathway in place for all young coaches.

"They don't know how to take that route and that's not necessarily the coach's fault, that's the federation or governing body who aren't reaching out to these women and saying 'if you want to be national team coach, this is what you have to do.' I honestly think that in some sports even the governing bodies don't know how to get them there."

Huyton admits that all around the world there is a long way still to go but that there is a fundamental lesson that Africa can learn from Europe.

"From a level-one grassroots coach volunteering once a week, what does that pathway look like to go all the way to a national team coach?" she asked.

"It's really important to understand what the journey looks like. People think that women don't want to coach…it isn't true."

Sarina Wiegman has coached both the Netherlands and England to Women's Euros titles Image: Priscila Bütler/SPP/IMAGO

Reasons for optimism

The lack of representation at the top level is not confined to Africa. Men are a common sight on the benches of women's games all over the world, including Europe. At the Women's Euro 2025, just seven of the 16 teams had female coaches, an increase from past tournaments but still fewer than half.

England's national team may be European champions and led by a woman, but female coaches are still a minority in the country's Women's Super League, regarded by most as the strongest domestic competition in the world.

In Africa, progress is being made and while it is slower than many would like in terms of women rising to senior positions, there are reasons to be optimistic, according to Ellis.

"Now, you have Lamia [Boumehdi] who has just won CAF (Confederation of African Football) coach of the year, being appointed as U20 coach of Morocco," Ellis said.

"You have Adelaide [Koudougnon] qualifying Ivory Coast for the first time to the U17 tournament, you have Carol [Kanyemba] of Zambia going to back-to-back World Cups with the U17s, you have Mildred [Cheche] going to the U17 World Cup with Kenya. There are a lot of future coaches coming up."

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

World.title: Iran war: Trump threatens bridges over Hormuz Strait attacks
World.content:
Skip next section Signs of ships avoiding second choke point off Yemen after Houthi warnings: tracker data

07/22/2026 July 22, 2026 Signs of ships avoiding second choke point off Yemen after Houthi warnings: tracker data

Houthi supporters rallied in Sanaa in support of the announcement of a maritime blockade earlier this week [FILE: July 20, 2026] Image: Mohammed Hamoud/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

Houthi threats to ships headed to or from Saudi Arabia's western shoreline could further impact commercial shipping, data trackers are warning.

The Houthis, who have de facto control over much of Yemen, have declared a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia and told ships to avoid the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the gateway to the Red Sea on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula from the Strait of Hormuz. It provides access to western Saudi coastal cities like Jeddah and Yanbu.

Data provider Kpler said shipping in both waterways was "under pressure," saying traffic in both straits had fallen sharply.

Ship broker Clarksons issued a similar warning, saying four vessels had registered new courses on Wednesday, avoiding the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and heading north through the Suez Canal towards the Mediterranean instead.

"The threat of Houthi hostile actions against Saudi Arabia ... has begun to have an overall effect on tanker activity," Clarksons wrote. "There are reports of several tankers, having ​loaded in Saudi Arabia's Yanbu port in the Red Sea, that have shifted course towards the Suez Canal rather than sail south towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, while ​others are holding their positions waiting for further instruction."

For ships headed to places like India, Pakistan, Indonesia or Australia, doing this would add well over 10,000 nautical miles (more than 20,000 kilometers) and weeks at sea to the typical travel distance.

"Anything that restricts shipping through the Red Sea would be problematic for the same reasons that the Strait of Hormuz is problematic," US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on the sidelines of a regional summit in the Philippines on Wednesday.

Pakistan's Foreign Ministry on Wednesday warned that the actions "threaten regional security, undermine freedom of navigation, challenge the rules-based maritime order and jeopardize uninterrupted flow of global commerce."

The Reuters news agency cited an advisory from the European Union's Aspides naval mission in the Red Sea as saying that ships with links to Israel, the United ​States or Saudi Arabia ‌were at a higher risk of being attacked by the Houthis and were advised to avoid voyages through the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden until the threat level decreases.

World.title: What's holding up the Gaza stabilization mission?
World.content:
A multinational stabilization mission is supposed to ensure the reconstruction of Gaza. Without political consensus among Israel, Hamas and the Arab states, its implementation remains uncertain.

Morocco recently signed an agreement to participate ​in the International Stabilization Force (ISF) in Gaza.

This agreement "reflects the shared determination to contribute, through concrete ​humanitarian and security actions, to the ​establishment of a climate of peace and security in the region," Morocco's state news agency MAP reported in July. According to the report, Morocco's contribution includes military personnel, police and gendarmerie forces and a field hospital.

Morocco is the first Arab country to join the planned international security mission for the Gaza Strip. Indonesia, Kazakhstan, Kosovo and Albania are also part of the force, while Jordan and Egypt have agreed to supporting roles only.

However, it remains to be seen whether the ISF can ever be deployed on the scale originally envisioned by its initiators.

The force, which is linked to the "Board of Peace" established by US President Donald Trump, is intended to do far more than simply secure humanitarian aid: It's seen as the security cornerstone of the planned post-war order for Gaza.

No traditional UN peacekeeping mission

The International Stabilization Force is tasked with securing the reconstruction process, protecting humanitarian aid deliveries, and training new Palestinian security forces. In the long term, it is intended to support a political transition.

However, in contrast to traditional United Nations peacekeeping missions, it will be organized outside the usual UN command structures even though the UN authorized the force. This structural difference makes the ISF one of the most ambitious — and one of the most challenging — international projects for the Gaza Strip.

"The involvement of international actors requires at least a minimum level of political stability," Gil Murciano , executive director of the Israeli Institute for Regional Foreign Policies, told DW. The real problem, he said, is not the mission itself, but the lack of a political framework in which it needs to operate.

Marcus Schneider, head of Germany's political Friedrich Ebert Foundation's Regional Project for Peace and Security in the Middle East in Beirut, is also skeptical about the mission's prospects for success.

"Israel wants to secure military freedom of action, while potential troop-contributing countries are primarily interested in a traditional peacekeeping mission," he told DW, adding that "these differing expectations pretty much rule each other out."

This view is echoed by the International Peace Institute (IPI). According to a recent analysis , a stable, legitimate Palestinian administration is needed first; otherwise, the ISF risks becoming yet another international transitional project.

As long as reconstruction is tied to a political framework, the population of Gaza remains in limbo Image: Dawoud Abu Alkas/REUTERS

Israel, Hamas, and the Arab states still differ on Gaza's future

In particular, Israel, Hamas, and the Arab states have differing views on what role the ISF should play. From Israel's perspective, security is the top priority.

"The Israeli government has made its position very clear: as long as Hamas does not agree to disarm, the reconstruction of Gaza should not begin," Murciano said. This ties reconstruction to a political condition that has not yet been agreed upon.

In Schneider's assessment, the actors involved are pursuing different political goals. While Israel wants to preserve its military freedom of action, many potential troop-contributing countries expect a clearly defined mandate with manageable risks. However, these expectations are currently difficult to reconcile.

The stance of Hamas — which is designated as a terrorist organization by the US and the EU, among others — further complicates the planning. Although the organization has signaled a willingness to withdraw from the civilian administration of Gaza, it has so far refused to fully disarm.

From Israel's perspective, this means that a key prerequisite for the mission's deployment remains unmet; at the same time, many international actors argue that reconstruction and political stabilization should not wait until all security issues have been resolved.

Is the Board of Peace Trump's private UN? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The role of the Arab states in Gaza

Arab states play a key role in Gaza's future as they are considered the most important financial backers for reconstruction. They could also lend the mission the necessary regional legitimacy. However, many governments want to avoid sending troops and billions in aid to Gaza without a solid political roadmap.

Morocco's commitment is seen as an important signal, even though it does not change the fact that other major regional powers have so far remained cautious.

The Washington-based think tank Arab Center Washington DC highlights this dilemma. While many Arab states are, in principle, willing to support the reconstruction of Gaza, participation in an international stabilization mission would be possible for them only within the framework of a credible political process, a report stated.

Gaza's reconstruction as a prerequisite for security

The real challenge lies in solving this stalemate, predicts Murciano. "Reconstruction itself is an essential component of security," he said. Anyone who separates the two processes risks further entrenching the political stalemate, he added.

Whether the ISF will ever be able to assume its intended role remains uncertain. While planning is well advanced, the mission still lacks the political conditions needed for deployment.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Congo: Ebola deaths increase to 1,000
World.content:
The fatality rate of the latest Ebola virus outbreak since mid-May is far higher than in previous outbreaks. No vaccines or treatments exist for the new strain.

The World Health Organization (WHO) on Wednesday published an overview of new data documenting the rapid spread of the current Ebola outbreak in Congo.

Democratic Republic of Congo Ministry of Health data documenting cases traced between May 15 and July 19 shows that 2,473 people in Congo and neighboring Uganda have been infected by the latest Bundibugyo strain of the virus, with 999 documented deaths in Congo, and two in Uganda.

The spread — the fastest ever recorded for Ebola — has continued unabated as no vaccines or treatments exist for this new strain of the virus.

Until now, the deadliest outbreak — which raged from 2013 to 2016 and infected 28,000 people, 11,000 of whom died — took some eight months to reach the grim 1,000 death mark.

Ebola spreading faster than officials can track

Health officials in Congo say some 80% of new cases have emerged through unknown transmission chains, suggesting it is spreading far faster than authorities can track.

In DRC, fighting Ebola means fighting misinformation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Overall, 82% of contacts linked to confirmed cases are being traced by authorities. This is well below the 90%-95% rate WHO officials say is needed to contain the virus.

The highly-contagious Ebola virus is spread via bodily fluids, such as blood, semen and vomit, and is often fatal.

To date, infections in the central African nation of 116 million have been recorded in five of Congo's 26 provinces. The epicenter of the current outbreak lies in Ituri province, which borders Uganda and South Sudan.

Healthcare workers forced to flee

The severity of the situation is being compounded by attacks on health workers as well as the generally poor working conditions that these individuals face.

Many healthcare workers have been forced to flee affected areas in fear for their own safety, and others say they have not been paid in months.

Speaking in Ghana on Tuesday, Director-General of the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Jean Kaseya told attendees at the Africa Health Summit that international efforts to stop the spread of the virus must be intensified.

"If we don't stop this outbreak, it could become one of the worst Ebola outbreaks the world has ever documented," Kaseya said.
