World.title: Can India become the next semiconductor hub after Taiwan?
World.content:
India is investing billions to build a domestic semiconductor industry as major industrial powers seek to diversify supply chains beyond Taiwan.

More than 90% of the world's most advanced semiconductor chips are made in Taiwan, an island at the center of ongoing rivalry between the US and China.

Any disruption to Taiwan's chip industry would likely send shockwaves through the global economy, with modern semiconductors used to make everything from smartphones and electric vehicles (EVs) to aircraft and military systems.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, chip shortages forced automakers to halt production — exposing how dependent the world had become on a handful of manufacturers in East Asia.

The result has been a global race to build more resilient semiconductor supply chains. The US, Japan, South Korea and also the EU have all launched multi-billion-dollar programs to attract chipmakers.

India is now mounting its biggest push yet to become part of that network and enter the global arena as the next electronics powerhouse.

India's chipmaking ambitions

Last week, the Indian government approved a $13.2 billion (€11.4 billion) semiconductor program labeled Semicon 2.0. The project builds on the $9 billion India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) launched in 2021 and aims to develop the entire chip ecosystem — from chip design and fabrication to advanced packaging, specialty materials, equipment manufacturing and workforce training.

US giant Micron Technology has established a semiconductor assembly and test facility in India Image: Jonathan Raa/Sipa USA/picture alliance

Thousands of engineers working for companies such as Nvidia, AMD, Qualcomm and Texas Instruments already design some of the world's most sophisticated chips from research centers in the Indian cities of Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Noida.

But analysts warn India has been lagging behind in large-scale manufacturing. In the semiconductor industry, this is the area that brings both economic value and strategic importance.

"India already has the expertise to design sophisticated semiconductor chips," said V Kamakoti, director of the Indian Institute of Technology in the city of Madras.

"Indian engineers working for both domestic companies and multinational firms have successfully designed and delivered complex chips," Kamakoti told DW. "The bigger challenge is manufacturing them."

So far, India's progress has been concentrated in chip packaging and testing rather than manufacturing the chips themselves.

Kamakoti said the next step is building a domestic fabrication ecosystem that can turn those design strengths into large-scale production.

Taiwan's AI surge fuels global power, amid growing risks To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hopes of a $100 billion market by 2030

Micron Technology, a US memory chip maker, Kaynes Semicon and CG Semi, two Indian semiconductor assembly and packaging companies, have begun commercial production under the first phase of India's semiconductor program.

Indian Minister for Electronics and Information Technology Ashwini Vaishnaw says the next phase is intended to move more of the semiconductor value chain into India.

"Convincing global companies is no longer that difficult," said ISM chief executive Amitesh Kumar Sinha, pointing to the 12 approved fabrication and packaging projects, three of which are already in commercial production.

The government wants to build a domestic semiconductor market worth between $100 billion and $110 billion by 2030 and meet up to three-quarters of India's electronics demand through locally designed and manufactured chips.

A costly industrial leap

Becoming a major chip manufacturer, however, is one of the toughest industrial challenges any country could take on.

A leading-edge fabrication plant can cost more than $20 billion, requires uninterrupted electricity, vast quantities of ultra-pure water and an extensive network of suppliers producing specialized chemicals, silicon wafers and precision equipment.

Chip market contest: Who will win the race? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Kamakoti argues that India should first prove it can manufacture mature 28-nanometer (28 nm) chips reliably at scale before attempting the most advanced 3 nm processors used in high-end smartphones and AI systems.

"28 nm [chips] will meet the majority of India's needs. Once that succeeds, we can gradually move to more advanced technologies," he said.

Riding the AI boom

India's ambitions are being helped by forces beyond its control.

In a time of geopolitical tensions and the rapid growth of AI, companies are rethinking their supply chains and demand for semiconductors is expected to rise sharply over the coming decade.

Sambit Sahu, a semiconductor industry veteran with more than three decades of experience at Qualcomm and Intel, says India must build capabilities across the semiconductor value chain from chip design and intellectual property to fabrication and manufacturing.

"The rapid growth of artificial intelligence will drive demand for semiconductors for years to come, creating a window of opportunity for India," Sahu told DW.

"Building a semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem will be expensive and technically challenging, but with sustained investment and supportive policies, India could emerge as an important manufacturing hub over the next decade."

High-tech boom and expensive housing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, not everyone is convinced India can narrow the manufacturing gap quickly.

A senior semiconductor industry executive, who preferred to stay anonymous, says India is likely to remain stronger in chip design than fabrication for the foreseeable future.

"India has built world-class capabilities in chip design, but manufacturing is a different challenge," he said. "The biggest opportunities in the near term are in packaging, testing and mature-node manufacturing."

Semicon 2.0 marks India's most ambitious attempt yet to enter the semiconductor race.

Whether it succeeds will depend less on the billions India has pledged and more on its ability to turn those commitments into factories, skilled workers and a competitive manufacturing ecosystem.

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: El precio del gas en Europa supera los máximos de marzo y complica el acopio de reservas para el invierno
World.content:
El riesgo de crisis energética asoma de nuevo en su versión más amenazante para Europa con el encarecimiento del gas natural, materia prima clave para la economía de la región. Europa ha encajado hasta ahora el golpe del conflicto en Oriente Próximo, pero la prolongación de la guerra está añadiendo de nuevo presión sobre el precio del petróleo y del gas natural licuado, que hoy supera en Europa los máximos que había marcado en marzo, al inicio de la guerra en Irán. El futuro del TTF en el mercado de Ámsterdam, referencia para el mercado europeo, ronda hoy los 62 euros por megavatio-hora —máximos de enero de 2023— y se dispara el 40% en lo que va de mes. Su encarecimiento apunta a complicar el acopio de reservas de cara al próximo invierno en la UE, ahora a niveles que rondan el 50%, por debajo del 64% del año pasado.

El ascenso del precio del gas natural se ha acelerado con la reanudación del conflicto entre Estados Unidos e Israel contra Irán, que ha dejado en papel mojado el preacuerdo de paz alcanzado en junio y que ha provocado la parálisis del suministro de materias primas energéticas desde el golfo Pérsico. Qatar de hecho exportaba antes de la guerra a través de Ormuz el 20% del gas natural que se consume en el mundo, cubriendo el 10% del consumo en Europa, el 30% en China y el 40% en la India. La UE no es, por tanto, especialmente dependiente del gas natural procedente de Oriente Próximo pero la fuerte demanda de Asia —región muy vulnerable al suministro desde Ormuz y que ha restringido el consumo de energía— está presionando al alza el precio del gas natural de forma generalizada. “Asia está comprando gas natural licuado allí donde puede, ha perdido mucho suministro y esa competencia supone un problema para Europa”, explica Jorge León, experto en materias primas de Rystad Energy.

A la falta de suministro desde Ormuz se añade además la cuenta atrás para eliminar las importaciones de gas natural ruso decidida por la UE y que está previsto entre en vigor el próximo 1 de enero de 2027. La prohibición ya tiene en alerta al sector gasista europeo y Naturgy ha advertido hoy en su presentación de resultados que Europa puede sufrir escasez de gas este invierno tras las nuevas sanciones a Rusia. La compañía ya trabaja con el peor escenario, en el que tendrá que cortar en enero su aprovisionamiento de gas ruso, que supone más del 15% de su cartera.

En un escenario en el que el suministro de gas desde Oriente Próximo sigue siendo limitado, a lo que se añade la previsible restricción total al gas ruso, surge la preocupación sobre la capacidad europea de reponer sus reservas de combustible antes de que llegue el invierno. El nivel de almacenamiento de gas de la UE es ahora inferior al 54%, frente al 64% del año pasado y a una media de cinco años del 69%, según datos de ING. La Agencia Internacional de la Energía advirtió este martes en un comunicado que si bien el aumento de flujos de gas natural licuado desde otros mercados, en especial desde Estados Unidos y Canadá, ha compensado alrededor del 70% de la pérdida de suministro a través de Ormuz, nuevos retrasos en la reanudación del suministro desde la zona amenazan con mantener los precios en tensión durante más tiempo. Y lanza un especial aviso hacia la UE: “Esto lo notarán todos los importadores de gas natural licuado, incluida Europa, mientras busca reabastecer su reserva de gas para el próximo invierno”.

La vulnerabilidad de Europa en materia energética se puso crudamente de manifiesto en 2022 con la invasión de Ucrania por parte de Rusia. Aquel año el precio del gas natural en Europa superó el nivel sin precedentes de los 300 euros por megavatio-hora y si bien el nivel actual de precios no es ni mucho menos comparable —al tiempo que la UE ha reducido drásticamente su dependencia de Rusia y diversificado sus fuentes de energía—, el encarecimiento del gas natural es motivo de inquietud y un factor claramente inflacionista.

Goldman Sachs apunta en un informe publicado esta semana a la “mayor vulnerabilidad de Europa ante una ola de frío en invierno”. El banco estadounidense acaba de elevar su previsión para el precio del gas natural en Europa, con el riesgo de que el TTF suba hasta los 65 euros por megavatio-hora, un nivel próximo al actual, en un escenario base en el que la normalización de las exportaciones desde el golfo Pérsico se retrasan a octubre, desde el mes de julio previsto anteriormente. Sin embargo, en un escenario en que esa normalización no llegue hasta 2027 y solo de forma gradual, el futuro del TTF de diciembre de este año podría dispararse por encima de los 100 euros por megavatio-hora.

World.title: Galán pide rebajar la fiscalidad de la luz y eliminar el IVA para los hogares, en línea con Reino Unido
World.content:
La energética ganó 4.336 millones en el primer semestre, un 22% más, y superó los 7.000 millones de inversión, principalmente en el negocio de Redes

El presidente de Iberdrola, Ignacio Sánchez Galán, se ha mostrado partidario de rebajar las cargas fiscales que gravan la factura de la luz, en línea con las recomendaciones de la Comisión Europea y la decisión del nuevo primer ministro británico, Andy Burnham, de suprimir el IVA de la luz para los hogares. Así lo ha declarado en la conferencia de analistas que ha mantenido este miércoles para presentar las cuentas semestrales de la compañía, que se han saldado con un beneficio neto reportado de 4.336 millones, un 22% más que en el mismo periodo del año pasado.

Según palabras de Galán, “la manera más fácil y rápida de reducir el precio de la electricidad al consumidor consiste en eliminar las cargas y los impuestos que se le aplican” y recordó que casi el 50% de la factura eléctrica tiene que ver con tributos y cargas, “algo infinitamente superior a lo que soportan los combustibles fósiles”.

El ejecutivo de Iberdrola ha insistido en achacar toda la responsabilidad del apagón del 28 de abril de 2025 a una “planificación inadecuada” y a una “mala gestión” del operador del sistema, Red Eléctrica (REE), y ha subrayado la necesidad de avanzar hacia una separación más clara entre sus funciones como operador del sistema y transportista en alta tensión, en línea con las advertencias de la Comisión Nacional de los Mercados y la Competencia (CNMC). “Existe un conflicto entre el papel que desempeña el operador del sistema y el del transporte, que es una compañía cotizada en Bolsa y que podría sobreestimar las necesidades de infraestructuras para priorizar inversiones donde los retornos sean mayores”, añadió.

En este sentido, recalcó que este modelo de separación funcional ya se aplica en otros mercados donde opera la compañía, como Estados Unidos o Brasil. En su opinión, la operación reforzada que aplica REE desde entonces corrobora que hubo una mala gestión: “Queda muy claro que después del apagón, Red Eléctrica ha decidido modificar la operación del sistema para poder programar las unidades con más seguridad”, indicó.

Apuesta por las Redes

Volviendo a las cuentas de esta primera mitad del año, Iberdrola obtuvo en el primer semestre del año un beneficio neto reportado de 4.336 millones de euros, lo que supuso un 22% más respecto al mismo periodo del año pasado, según ha informado la compañía a la Comisión Nacional del Mercado de Valores (CNMV). El beneficio neto ajustado (que excluye las plusvalías por la venta de centrales térmicas en México) ha crecido un 8%, hasta los 3.565 millones.

El beneficio neto de explotación (ebitda) ajustado de Iberdrola alcanzó los 8.050 millones, un 8% superior al primer semestre del año pasado, siendo el principal motor el negocio de Redes, con un aumento del ebitda de Generación y Clientes del 1% interanual. Sin el impacto del tipo de cambio, señala Iberdrola, el ebitda ajustado habría aumentado el 9%.

En cuanto a las inversiones, estas aumentaron un 25% en el periodo, hasta los 7.000 millones de euros, de las que un 70% se concentraron en Reino Unido, Estados Unidos y Brasil (incluidos los minoritarios de Neoenergía). Un 14% de las inversiones se quedaron en España y dos tercios del total fueron a Redes. El grupo instaló 1,6 GW con un importante avance en eólica marina. Y como consecuencia de todo ello, la base de activos regulados (RAB) aumentó un 11%, hasta 55.000 millones.

Con una producción mundial de 61.319 GWh, que aumentó ligeramente, un 0,7%, de los cuales, 45.900 GWh correspondieron a renovables, Iberdrola sigue impulsando la eólica marina, cuya producción aumentó en los seis primeros meses del año un 23%, hasta 4.310 GWh. En España sigue destacando la producción de las centrales de ciclo combinado de gas, que aumenta un 38% en el periodo, hasta 2.958 GWh, por la operación reforzada que aplica el operador del sistema, Red Eléctrica (REE), que consiste en la programación masiva de este tipo de plantas, que son síncronas y controlan tensión.

La energética tiene una capacidad instalada en España de 32.513 MW, que se mantiene estable, con un aumento del 1,8% en el semestre, y las ventas de energía le supusieron en el trimestre 22.469 millones de euros frente a los 22.100 millones del año pasado. Asimismo, cuenta con proyectos maduros para añadir hasta 15.500 MW de potencia entre 2025 y 2030, frente a los 9.500 MW del plan estratégico 2025-2028.

El dividendo de Iberdrola se sitúa en 0,685 euros por acción, de los cuales, 0,427 serán abonados el 27 de julio, hasta 4.500 millones de euros, con un aumento del 12%. Iberdrola mantiene sus previsiones para el año, con un crecimiento estimado del beneficio neto ajustado superior al 8% en el ejercicio. A este respecto, su presidente ha asegurafo que Iberdrola podría “dar buenas noticias después del verano”, en alusión a las previsiones de beneficio. “Hoy ya estamos trabajando para seguir superando nuestras previsionespara los próximos años, gracias a la aceleración de las inversiones orgánicas en redes en Estados Unidos, Reino Unido o Brasil, y también en generación, principalmente en Estados Unidos, con mejoras adicionales en eficiencia y de proceso que tienen que ver con la inteligencia artificial”, dijo.

Ventas y compras

Con una capitalización bursátil de 147.591 millones, el beneficio por acción de la sociedad es de 0,622 euros. La deuda neta de Iberdrola aumentó en 3.790 millones, hasta 53.972 millones, por las nuevas inversiones y la depreciación del real brasileño y el dólar. La compañía cuenta con una liquidez de 21.500 millones, suficiente para 22 meses de necesidades de financiación.

En la primera mitad de este año, Iberdrola cerró la operación de venta de sus activos de gas en México y la compra de las participaciones de los minoritarios en Brasil, con unas plusvalías netas de 953,3 millones de euros.

La energética anunció este mismo martes la compra del 80% de la distribuidora eléctrica finlandesa Caruna, por casi 2.500 millones de euros, y la asunción de deuda que le supondrá un desembolso total de unos 5.000 millones de euros. Sobre la operación de compra de la finlandesa, que supone el 21% de la distribución del país nórdico, el presidente de Iberdrola destacó que responde a la estrategia de otras compras en el pasado en mercados como Reino Unido, Estados Unidos o Brasil, de ser “inversores a largo plazo, industriales, no inversores especulativos”.

Según sus palabras, “nosotros vemos oportunidades que no ven otros, y que nos permiten materializar estas operaciones”. Aunque indicó que se trata de una transacción “relativamente pequeña” en comparación con las cifras de inversión del grupo: entre 40.000 y 50.000 millones de euros anuales.

World.title: Karin Hindsbo, directora de la Tate: “Si buscas el consenso a toda costa, caes en la parálisis”
World.content:
Karin Hindsbo, directora de la Tate de Londres, el lunes pasado en su despacho en la Tate Modern.

El audio de esta noticia utiliza una voz sintética generada por Inteligencia Artificial y podría tener algunas inconsistencias.

La responsable del museo londinense ha impulsado la presencia de mujeres y artistas no occidentales en sus salas, a riesgo de molestar en estos tiempos polarizados. “No podemos dejar que el miedo nos domine”, asegura

Karin Hindsbo (Gentofte, Dinamarca, 52 años) recibe en su pequeño despacho de la Tate Modern, dentro de la famosa central eléctrica de ladrillo situada a orillas del Támesis que, hace algo más de 25 años, se convirtió en uno de los grandes museos de arte del mundo. Sobria y seria, se sienta ante una hoja llena de apuntes y responde midiendo cada palabra. Solo se sale del guion al recordar su pasado grunge, a propósito de una exposición sobre los noventa que el museo inaugurará en otoño.

En marzo, esta danesa asumió la dirección de todo el grupo Tate, mientras se resuelve un concurso público para el que Hindsbo es una de las favoritas, tras haber dirigido la sede de la institución para el arte moderno y contemporáneo desde 2023. Al frente del museo, esta historiadora del arte, hija de la periferia residencial de Copenhague, ha impulsado la presencia de mujeres y de tradiciones no occidentales. Este verano, coinciden en sus salas tres grandes muestras dedicadas a Frida Kahlo, Ana Mendieta y Tracey Emin.

Pregunta. En los últimos tiempos, los museos se han abierto a artistas marginados por el canon. Sobre todo, mujeres. Ahora que ese gesto ya se ha normalizado, ¿cuál cree que debe ser el siguiente paso?

Respuesta. Es un proceso que no termina: siempre habrá artistas ignorados. La Tate lleva un cuarto de siglo ampliando el canon y mostrando que la modernidad no fue un invento europeo, sino un proceso en el que participaron artistas de todo el mundo a lo largo del siglo XX. Seguiremos desafiando las ideas preconcebidas. Me interesan los artistas que mezclan disciplinas, que alternan la tecnología con la performance o la poesía, y también las tradiciones indígenas. Habrá más cosas en esta línea.

P. La Tate Modern acaba de cumplir 25 años. ¿Cómo ve el museo en el futuro?

R. Es fundamental mantener el arte en el centro, pero también hay que prestar atención al artista y su proceso de creación. Eso puede propiciar un diálogo más directo con los visitantes. Es importante volver al elemento humano en el arte.

P. Durante mucho tiempo, la historia del arte ha considerado que la vida privada del artista era una anécdota que no merecía atención. ¿A usted sí le importan la biografía o la intimidad de un creador?

R. Sí, porque esa dimensión personal es lo que hace que el arte nos resulte cercano. Las obras suelen surgir de un espacio profundamente íntimo. En el centro de todo, siempre hay un ser humano que está creando. Es importante entender de dónde surgen sus motivaciones.

“En toda Europa, el apoyo privado se ha vuelto necesario. Las subvenciones públicas ya no son suficientes para cubrir los costes”

P. En esta sociedad polarizada, ¿un museo debe buscar un terreno común o crear conflicto?

R. No es posible lograr un consenso absoluto, ni creo que sea nuestra función conseguirlo. Cuando se busca ese consenso a toda costa, se corre el riesgo de caer en la parálisis institucional. No debemos convertirnos en instituciones reactivas, que se reposicionen ante cada crítica por miedo a molestar, ni dejar que el miedo nos domine. Tenemos que escuchar las críticas y aprender de ellas, pero también ser capaces de convivir con los ataques y aceptar la incomodidad que puedan generar.

P. El mundo del arte se sostiene a menudo sobre sueldos bajos y condiciones precarias. ¿Qué se puede hacer?

R. Cuando llegué a la Tate quise prestar atención a la cuestión salarial. La colección es uno de los elementos fundamentales de cualquier museo, sin olvidar otro de la misma importancia: las personas que trabajan con ella. Un museo debe cuidar a su equipo todo lo que pueda. Londres es una ciudad muy cara y, con la inflación de los últimos años, el salario se ha vuelto aún más importante. Aun así, admito que seguimos lejos de donde deberíamos estar.

P. Defiende la entrada gratuita universal a las colecciones de arte. ¿Sigue siendo viable?

R. El Partido Laborista introdujo la gratuidad en 2001 y ahora es el propio laborismo el que debate la posibilidad de eliminarla para los visitantes internacionales. Me opongo a ello. Museos como la Tate o el British Museum conservan obras procedentes de todo el planeta. Me parece lógico que cualquier visitante pueda contemplarlas.

P. La Tate también fue pionera al asociarse con espónsores como Hyundai o Uniqlo. ¿Cómo condiciona su oferta?

R. No cambia en absoluto lo que exponemos ni lo que coleccionamos, y nunca debería hacerlo. Son grandes compañeros de viaje que aportan un mecenazgo a largo plazo. Acabamos de renovar con Hyundai durante 10 años, lo que nos permitirá seguir adelante con los proyectos en la Sala de las Turbinas, que tanto gustan a nuestro público, aunque alguna vez también lo odien [risas]. Es innegable que, en toda Europa, ese apoyo privado se ha vuelto necesario. Las subvenciones públicas ya no son suficientes para cubrir los costes.

La directora de la Tate, Karin Hindsbo, el 13 de julio en la sede de la institución, en Londres. Manuel Vázquez

P. El éxito democrático de los museos ha creado otro problema: hay demasiados visitantes. ¿Qué se puede hacer?

R. No es nuestro caso. Tenemos un espacio muy grande y podemos recibir a muchos visitantes. No hemos llegado a la saturación. Pero es cierto que, en algunas exposiciones muy populares, la afluencia puede afectar a la experiencia.

P. El Louvre ha impuesto un máximo diario de 30.000 visitantes. Cuando se acaban las entradas, no entra nadie más. ¿Sería favorable a hacer lo mismo?

R. Si alcanzáramos nuestra capacidad máxima, tendríamos que hacerlo. También hay un componente de seguridad, tanto para las obras como para los visitantes. Si en algún momento se vieran comprometidos los límites de aforo, tomaríamos medidas. Pero, de momento, es suficiente con ampliar horarios para las exposiciones con más éxito.

P. ¿Qué artista vivo será recordado como uno de los grandes, aunque hoy todavía no lo sepamos?

R. Tracey Emin. Aborda experiencias compartidas por muchas mujeres, como los abusos, sin camuflarlas. Cuando estudiaba ya era una gran fan suya. Me atraían su crudeza y su insistencia en ser artista en un mundo en el que todos le decían que no era lo suficientemente buena.

P. ¿Y a qué museos mira cuando necesita inspiración?

R. El Hamburger Bahnhof de Berlín está haciendo un trabajo extraordinario. Siempre que voy encuentro algo nuevo y salgo inspirada. También me gustan los grandes museos clásicos. Entrar en el Kunsthistorisches Museum de Viena para ver a Brueghel siempre te aporta algo. Por supuesto, está el Museo Nacional de Oslo, que dirigí durante seis años. Y este otoño llevaré a mi hijo al Prado por primera vez, porque le encanta Goya.

P. Es danesa, estudió en Berlín, dirigió durante seis años el Museo Nacional de Noruega y ahora encabeza una gran institución británica. ¿Se siente europea?

R. Mucho, aunque no sepa definir por qué. Pero es importante que tengamos una Europa fuerte y que colaboremos más, viendo lo que está sucediendo en el mundo. Hablo tanto de las instituciones artísticas como de las demás.

“A veces hay que saber sentarse en el asiento trasero en lugar de ocupar todo el rato el del conductor. Hay reuniones donde decido ser la que menos habla”

P. ¿Qué ha cambiado desde que llegó a la Tate?

R. Para mí ha sido importante dar un paso atrás, permitir que otras personas brillen y que sus ideas sean escuchadas. Eso exige un esfuerzo: trabajamos en un sector en el que parece importante que un director manifieste su visión todo el rato. Hay que ser capaz de crear otro espacio de trabajo y aprender a ocupar un segundo plano.

P. Vamos, que tiene el ego bajo control.

R. Creo que sí. A veces hay que saber sentarse en el asiento trasero en lugar de ocupar todo el rato el del conductor. Hay situaciones en las que debes liderar y defender una posición. Pero, en ciertas reuniones, decido ser la persona que menos habla. Lo hago adrede.

P. ¿Es ese el famoso liderazgo feminista del que tanto hablamos, pero que no siempre vemos?

R. Sí, o en todo caso yo lo veo como el liderazgo del futuro. Estoy convencida de que es el camino a seguir.

World.title: Ivory and a rhino skull among 5,800 items handed to RVO
World.content:
Some 5,800 prohibited objects including elephant ivory have been anonymously handed in to the Netherlands Enterprise Agency (RVO) over the past year, a more than fivefold increase on the previous year.

“Never before has so much been handed in,” says The Hague-based RVO, including “moving boxes with a thousand [pieces of] ivory jewellery, a rhino skull with a gunshot wound, crocodile leather bags, musical instruments and an elephant’s leg.”

The objects also included taxidermy animals such as a long-eared owl, peregrine falcon and turtles. Pictures on broadcaster NOS show ivory binoculars and crocodile leather bags.

The sale and trade of elephant ivory are strictly regulated under European CITES laws (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species), with permits required for the possession and trade of protected plants or animals.

Most of the items, which can be handed in at a drop-off bin in The Hague or even by post, are destroyed to prevent them from (re)entering the illegal trade. The RVO says it uses a small number of the items for research and education.

World.title: Thuisbezorgd hides costs and fakes discounts: consumer group
World.content:
The food delivery platform Thuisbezorgd.nl hides compulsory charges and advertises fake discounts, the Dutch consumer association Consumentenbond said on Tuesday, calling on the company to stop and to compensate affected customers.

Mandatory costs should be clearly shown before a customer starts ordering, the association said, but Thuisbezorgd’s app and website do not reveal compulsory “service” charges – for items such as bags, plastic packaging and sauce – until part-way through or at the end of an order, adding an average of €2 to €4 to the bill.

The association also said the company broke rules on special offers. Under Authority for Consumers and Markets (ACM) rules, a struck-through sale price must be the lowest the seller charged in the previous 30 days. In one case, the association found Indian snacks that had previously cost €3.75 being offered “on sale” from €7.50 to €6.

“We have been in talks with Thuisbezorgd since March, but the platform is still confronting customers with hidden costs and fake discounts,” said Consumentenbond director Sandra Molenaar, noting the company has more than six million users in the Netherlands.

Because the practice has probably been going on for years, the association estimates the hidden costs run into the hundreds of millions of euros in total. A Thuisbezorgd spokesperson said the company did not recognise the association’s accusations.

The Consumentenbond said it had also found hidden costs at Uber Eats, which made changes in June, though no fake discounts. The findings are part of a wider campaign against hidden charges and misleading offers that also named Bol and Amazon last week.

The association can press companies to change but cannot impose penalties; that is a matter for the ACM, which has fined firms including Leen Bakker, G-Star and Jysk in the past.

Three men have been arrested over the theft of a shipment of smartphones with an estimated street value of around €5 million from the Schiphol area, the Royal Military Police (Koninklijke Marechaussee) have said.

The suspects are two 24-year-old men from Amsterdam and a 39-year-old from Zoetermeer.

The shipment went missing on June 18, prompting an investigation, led by the Noord-Holland public prosecution department, into an organised crime group.

One of the suspects works for a transport company at Schiphol and is thought to have passed confidential information to the group, the military police said. Further arrests have not been ruled out.

World.title: Two trams collide on Rotterdam’s Erasmus Bridge, 15 injured
World.content:
Fifteen people were injured, one of them seriously, when two trams collided on the Erasmus Bridge in Rotterdam on Wednesday morning, the regional safety board has said. One of the trams was derailed by the impact.

The crash happened at around 11.10am, regional broadcaster Rijnmond reported. Footage shows one tram coming to a halt as it drove onto the bridge from the direction of the city centre, before a second tram approached from behind and ran into it, apparently without braking.

The seriously injured person was trapped and had to be freed before being taken to hospital. The safety board initially reported 18 injured and two seriously hurt, but later revised the figures.

Transport company RET said it could not yet say what caused the rear-end collision, adding that it was shocked by the footage and that its thoughts were with the victims and passengers. Two cars were also damaged, the fire service said.

The power to the overhead lines was switched off and the bridge closed to traffic, halting tram services on lines 3 and 5.

World.title: Man jailed for 15 months over threats to Groningen butchers
World.content:
A Groningen court has sentenced a 23-year-old man to 15 months in prison for sending death threats to butchers in the province and neighbouring Drenthe.

Prosecutors requested a four-year sentence, saying he had a terrorist motive. But the court ruled there was insufficient evidence for such a charge, saying instead he acted out of radical environmental and animal-rights beliefs.

Because four months of his sentence are suspended, the man, known as Bas V., will be released immediately, having already served his time in pre-trial detention. He is bound by a three-year probationary period.

The crime

Last September, Bas V. sent threatening emails to 12 butcher shops demanding they close. “You get one warning, nothing more. If the shop isn’t closed tomorrow, I will come with a machete and stab everyone to death,” read the email.

The court stated: “The texts on his phone say something about his mindset, but not that he wanted to disrupt society with them.”

Bas V., who admitted to sending the emails, was arrested after seven of the butchers filed a complaint. Police found a machete in his home and notes on his phone saying he also needed a pistol with a silencer to “kill people responsible for the humiliation of animals,” according to broadcaster NOS.

The national broadcaster also says that Bas V. was found by experts to have a gaming addiction, a cannabis addiction, ADHD and autism, and will be placed in a protected living facility to receive treatment.

World.title: House prices rising fastest in Groningen, slowest in Amsterdam
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

House prices are climbing fastest in Groningen and slowest in the Randstad, figures from the national statistics office CBS and the Land Registry showed on Tuesday.

Homes in Groningen province cost 7.9% more in the second quarter than a year earlier – the biggest rise in the country – while in Noord-Holland prices went up just 2.4%.

House prices rose 4.2% nationwide, the tenth quarter running that they have climbed, though more slowly than the 5.2% jump in the first three months of the year. After Groningen, the steepest rises were in Drenthe, Gelderland and Friesland, all above 5%.

Of the four biggest cities, The Hague rose most, at 4.5%, while Amsterdam barely moved, up 0.8%. Fewer homes sold than a year earlier in both Amsterdam and Rotterdam.

Nearly 59,000 homes changed hands across the country, 2.7% more than the same quarter last year.

World.title: Dutch government warns against travel to the Middle East
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

As the conflict between the US and Iran escalates, the foreign affairs ministry has tightened its advice for people wanting to travel to the region.

With Iran targeting US allies in the Middle East in response to American attacks, the Dutch government has advised against travelling to Qatar, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates – which includes the popular holiday destination of Dubai – unless absolutely necessary.

That falls under the ministry’s orange travel advisory, which discourages all travel unless there’s an emergency, such as the death of a family member.

The travel advice for Bahrain has moved up to red, meaning the ministry says the Dutch embassy cannot offer help. “Whatever your situation is, don’t travel there,” the ministry said. “It’s too dangerous.”

The US, UK, Canada and Australia have also updated their travel alerts for Gulf countries in recent days.

Check the ministry’s website for the latest travel advisories.

World.title: Explosive attacks fall as task force targets young offenders
World.content:
Attacks using explosives fell by more than 17% in the first half of this year, the first substantial drop since the wave of explosions peaked in 2024, according to the government’s Offensive against Explosions (OTE) working group.

The number of explosions or attempted explosions decreased from 705 during the first half of 2025 to 581 during the same time, putting the OTE on track to achieve a 10% decrease this year.

But explosions remain a serious safety threat – and it’s mostly young people who use them to commit crimes. Almost half of all arrested suspects were minors, reports NU.nl, with fewer than one in six suspects older than 30. A large proportion of offenders are under the age of 25.

“Every attack is one too many,” said Carola Schouten, mayor of Rotterdam and chairwoman of the OTE. “But it is good to see that the number of attacks is starting to decrease nationwide… This requires continued attention and joint commitment on all fronts.”

Young offenders

Specifically, the task force is focusing on reducing the number of young offenders, finding and prosecuting those who hire them and their intermediaries and limiting the availability of explosives – in this case mostly powerful, illegally trafficked fireworks, often procured from neighbouring countries like Germany or ordered online.

“This is done, among other things, by disrupting the production, transport, storage and trade in such explosives,” said the OTE, which is also setting up a joint Europol task force with Germany and Sweden, and lobbying with France and Sweden for tighter EU rules on powerful fireworks.

But given the young age of offenders, prevention is the name of the game. The OTE has begun a pilot focusing on conflict mediation among young people, while parents, caregivers and those who work with them are being given support to make “young people more resilient to (online) temptations to crime”.

World.title: Germany deploys soldiers to Poland to help reinforce eastern borders
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Germany has deployed soldiers to Poland to help reinforce defences on NATO’s eastern flank in response to the threat of Russia. While Poland already hosts various allied forces, the presence of German troops is particularly symbolic given the two countries’ difficult history. “United, we will prevail,” wrote the General Staff of the Polish Armed Forces (SGWP), announcing the deployment. “This is what allied cooperation looks like in practice, which translates into greater military readiness and strengthens NATO’s defensive potential.” Polscy i niemieccy żołnierze razem wzmacniają granicę z Rosją. Takie rzeczy możliwe tylko za Tuska ☺️ pic.twitter.com/oNBME2gBsv — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 22, 2026 Last December, the Polish and German defence ministries revealed that a “mid-double-digit number” of German troops would be deployed from mid-2026 until the end of 2027 to support implementation of Poland’s East Shield operation, which seeks to bolster defences along the borders with Belarus and Russia. They said that the German personnel would mainly engage in engineering work, such as digging trenches, laying barbed wire and constructing anti-tank barriers. Today, Poland’s SGWP confirmed that “several dozen” German troops, including “highly specialised engineering forces” along with their equipment, had since June been temporarily deployed to “support the Polish armed forces in expanding defence infrastructure on NATO’s northeastern flank”. It emphasised that the East Shield project is “purely defensive in nature” and comes in “response to threats stemming from, among others, Russian aggression against Ukraine”. While the armed forces did not reveal the location of the deployment, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk indicated in a social media post that it was on the Russian border. Poland has a 210-km frontier with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. German public broadcaster Deutsche Welle reports that the activities of the German sappers are focused in particular on improving defences around the so-called Suwałki Gap, a strategically important stretch of land around the Polish-Lithuanian border between Belarus and Kaliningrad. “Together, we are ensuring Europe’s security,” said Lieutenant General Alexander Sollfrank, the Bundeswehr’s operational commander, announcing the deployment today. “Through our engagement in Poland, we are strengthening NATO’s defence capabilities and underscoring the alliance’s unwavering commitment to ensuring peace through unity and credible deterrence.” Poland and Germany have signed a bilateral security agreement that will see the two neighbours and NATO allies increase cooperation in areas such as military mobility, logistics infrastructure, maritime security in the Baltic Sea, and cybersecurity https://t.co/6BPX2WxvxH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 17, 2026 SGWP, which shared footage of Polish and German forces installing anti-tank barriers, said the work aims to “hinder and delay an aggressor’s actions in the event of a threat”, thereby “increasing the time for a response from the Polish armed forces and the entire [NATO] alliance”. It also seeks to “create conditions for the efficient reception, deployment and use of NATO forces on Polish territory”. SGWP welcomed “the involvement of the German contingent as a practical expression of allied solidarity and the result of consistently developing military cooperation between Poland and Germany”. It also noted that the cooperation would help the two sides improve their ability to operate jointly, including “developing the competencies necessary for conducting a joint defence operation”. However, it emphasised that the current deployment is focused on training and engineering, with no combat component, and that the German troops are unarmed. SGWP also emphasised that the East Shield operation remains entirely a Polish national programme. The leaders of eight countries on the EU's eastern flank have met in the first summit of its kind to discuss closer security cooperation. Finland and Poland announced that they would jointly lead an initiative, Eastern Flank Watch, to bolster defences https://t.co/fxRHpkM6w9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 16, 2025 The deployment of German troops to Poland comes shortly after the two countries signed a defence cooperation agreement in which they pledged to increase cooperation in areas such as military mobility, logistics infrastructure, maritime security in the Baltic Sea, and cybersecurity. The agreement is a sign that the two countries now stand “shoulder to shoulder, as equals”, declared German defence minister Boris Pistorius. Poland is also currently seeking a new permanent US military base on its territory, after President Donald Trump recently pledged to boost American troop numbers. Last week, Tusk also announced that Poland will host military exercises involving France and the UK this autumn. Poland will host military exercises later this year with France and the UK to prepare for providing future security guarantees to Ukraine, says PM @donaldtusk. He also declared Poland's willingness to permanently host more troops from its European allies https://t.co/couian4FrP — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland launches first of 11 planned “community forests” around major cities
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s climate and environment ministry has inaugurated the first of 11 planned “community forests” around large cities, with the aim of giving residents a place for recreation and contact with nature while also helping to fulfil the government’s pledge to reduce logging. Plans for the forests were announced in 2024, and the first has now been established around Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city. Ten other major urban centres, including Warsaw, Kraków, Poznań and Łódź, are set to follow. Dotrzymujemy słowa. Powołaliśmy pierwsze lasy społeczne w Polsce, to lasy ochronne wokół Wrocławia. Kolejne miasta przed nami. @MKiS_GOV_PL pic.twitter.com/RxhsMZShj9 — Paulina Hennig-Kloska (@hennigkloska) July 21, 2026 “This is a historic moment and the beginning of a new approach to forest protection – with residents in mind first and foremost,” said climate and environment minister Paulina Hennig-Kloska at an inauguration ceremony outside Wrocław on Sunday. “Community forests are places where residents can relax, play sports and simply spend time close to nature,” she added. “At the same time, they are crucial to our security and quality of life: they retain water, regulate the climate, purify the air and protect the soil.” An area covering 13,000 hectares (32,124 acres) has been designated as a community forest around Wrocław. Forest management there will now be aimed at “maximising the forest’s social functions”, says the ministry, while timber harvesting is also restricted. The area will be divided into three zones, including “natural forests”, where nature will be left to take its course, and “near-natural forests” with minimal intervention. However, the largest zone, amounting to over 8,000 hectares, will be “social forests”, which the state forestry agency says “will be managed in a way that ensures the comfort of those who use the forest and its benefits related to wellbeing, physical exercise and recreation”. Hennig-Kloska noted that, in the latter area, educational trails as well as hiking and cycling paths would be established. However, given that such facilities already exist in many forests, it remains unclear how the new community forests will differ. The ministry is now conducting consultations and analysis on establishing community forests around ten other designated urban centres: Bielsko-Biała, Tricity (Gdańsk-Gdynia-Sopot), Katowice, Kielce, Kraków, Łódź, Poznań, Szczecin, Toruń-Bydgoszcz and Warsaw. On Sunday, Hennig-Kloska said that the “next in line” to have their community forests established are Kielce and Bielsko-Biała, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Shortly after coming to power in December 2023, the current government announced that it would halt planned logging in some forests. The former Law and Justice (PiS) administration had faced criticism for overseeing an increase in logging, especially in Białowieża Forest. The current government also launched plans to create Poland’s first new national parks in over two decades. However, PiS-aligned President Karol Nawrocki last year vetoed that move, arguing that it would “block the economic development of the region” and threaten Poland’s security. World.title: Poland joins EU satellite project developing European alternative to Starlink
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has joined a European Union project developing a secure satellite internet service that would provide an alternative to networks such as Elon Musk’s Starlink. Warsaw has committed €656 million (2.8 billion zloty) to the IRIS² programme, with the money coming from Poland’s EU post-pandemic recovery funds. In return for joining the project, Poland will gain access to the secure satellite communications network for government institutions, the armed forces and emergency services, while the growing Polish space industry will be eligible to compete for contracts linked to the development of the constellation Today Poland🇵🇱joins the EU🇪🇺space programme #IRIS² w/additional €656 mln. 🇵🇱 is on a remarkable space journey to build a strong space economy & secure connectivity for the defence of Poland, the Eastern Flank & 🇪🇺. IRIS² brings greater unity & strength for the entire Europe. pic.twitter.com/TwS59vpXtm — Andrius Kubilius (@KubiliusA) July 21, 2026 “This is a big day for Poland, the eastern flank and the entire European Union,” declared the EU’s defence and space commissioner, Andrius Kubilius, at a signing ceremony in Warsaw on Tuesday. “By investing in space, Poland is investing in its security, its economy and its future.” Speaking alongside him, Poland’s interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said that IRIS² would help “ensure our security and strategic independence” while “demonstrating that Poland aims to be a leader in the European space industry and remain at the centre of EU security efforts”. “No single country is able to build such a [satellite] constellation so efficiently, which is why we are joining this major project – to be part of it and one of its managers,” he added. The IRIS² programme aims to deploy a constellation of nearly 300 satellites in low and medium Earth orbit, providing encrypted, interference-resistant communications for governments, defence agencies, emergency services and selected commercial users across the EU. First announced in 2022, the project is part of the EU’s efforts to reduce dependence on non-European satellite operators amid growing concerns over cybersecurity, hybrid threats and the resilience of critical infrastructure following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. “It is super important for Europe to have a sovereign capacity, and Starlink will never do that,” said Eva Berneke, CEO of Eutelsat, one of the companies involved in the project, quoted by Politico Europe. The project is expected to cost €10.6 billion, including €6.5 billion in public funding and around €4 billion from private investors. IRIS² is expected to become operational in 2030. 🇪🇺 The IRIS program is Europe's replacement for Starlink. The constellation will consist of over 300 satellites to serve Europe alone. Security and sovereignty! Like Galileo, it could surpass its US counterpart. Fewer satellites, smarter coverage. Eventually more could be added pic.twitter.com/Uswmuotw7F — Mariska den Eelden 🇪🇺🇳🇱 (@eeldenden) February 22, 2025 As part of its contribution to IRIS², Poland will finance six large satellites in medium Earth orbit (MEO) and six smaller satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO). It will also build a ground gateway station in Warsaw to connect the satellites with GovNet, the country’s secure government fibre-optic communications network. Earlier this year, the Polish government approved the use of money from its share of the EU’s post-pandemic reconstruction fund to cover its contribution to IRIS². Sięgamy gwiazd!! Polska przystępuje do europejskiego programu budowy bezpiecznej łączności satelitarnej 🛰️📡! W ten sposób zaspokoimy wszystkie potrzeby łączności służb i administracji państwowej. IRIS² zapewni nam bezpieczeństwo i niezależność. Dziękuję @KubiliusA za współpracę pic.twitter.com/c8u2QH0Wyn — Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) July 21, 2026 Once the system is up and running, Poland’s police, border guards and other emergency services would be able to use the network during natural disasters, power outages and other emergencies when terrestrial communications infrastructure is unavailable. The system would also make it possible to provide temporary connectivity for civilians through emergency hotspots, says Poland’s interior ministry. Polish companies will now also be able to compete for contracts covering satellite manufacturing, telecommunications equipment, software and ground infrastructure, expanding the country’s role in Europe’s space industry. “It is estimated that each zloty invested in the project will generate a five-zloty return through new jobs, innovation and the development of domestic technologies,” the ministry said in a statement. Warsaw has been chosen as the location for a new European Space Agency security centre, as Poland takes another step in its ambitions to become a bigger player in the space sector The facility will be the @esa's first outside its 11 founding member states https://t.co/WnHIbrW3ze — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 13, 2026 Poland has placed great emphasis on developing its space industry in recent years, with the aim of becoming a major European player in the sector. Last week, the European Space Agency (ESA) announced that it will open a new security centre in Warsaw. One of its areas of operation will be satellite communication, including the use of satellite imagery to monitor critical incidents such as natural disasters. Prime Minister Donald Tusk also revealed that Poland and the ESA are working on the first Polish spacecraft, which would provide servicing, refuelling and other services for satellites Last year, Poland launched its first national military satellite. A Polish firm, Creotech Instruments, signed Poland’s largest ever contract with the ESA, a €52 million deal to build and launch a constellation of Earth observation satellites. Astronaut @astro_slawosz's recent trip to the International Space Station highlighted the Polish space industry's growing importance. World.title: Archaeologists uncover synagogue in Warsaw Jewish cemetery destroyed by Germans in WWII
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Archaeological work at a Jewish cemetery in Warsaw has uncovered the foundations of and many objects from a former synagogue and funeral home that was destroyed by the Nazi-German occupiers in 1943. The finds were made at the cemetery on Okopowa Street, which, at around 33.5 hectares in size and with some 250,000 people buried there, is the second largest in Poland, after the Łódź Jewish cemetery, and one of the biggest anywhere in the world. Following the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising of 1943, the Germans liquidated the ghetto, sending most of its remaining inhabitants to the gas chambers and destroying the buildings that remained there, including the synagogue and burial houses. In June this year, archaeological work began at the site of the former synagogue, commissioned by Warsaw’s Jewish community, which owns and manages the cemetery. The two-storey building, designed by architect Adolf Schimmelpfennig, a Pole of Dutch Lutheran descent, was constructed in 1877 and existed until 15 May 1943, when it was destroyed with explosives. The archaeological work aims to “uncover, document and preserve the remains of this historic complex, maintaining the memory of this place and passing it on to future generations”, says the office of the conservator of monuments for Masovia, the province in which Warsaw is located and which is supervising the work. Archaeologists have so far discovered numerous items that offer “silent testament to the daily life of the community that was connected to this site for decades”, says the conservator. They include ceramic floor and wall tiles, glass bottles and tiles from stoves used at the funeral home. “Every discovered brick, fragment of flooring or piece of furniture helps reconstruct the history of one of the most important buildings in historic Warsaw,” adds the conservator. Among the finds is an item that relates to a well-known and tragic story from the war, a door plaque from the office of the then-director of the cemetery, Abram Pozner. Pozner brought members of his extended family to the funeral home at the start of the war, where they were initially able to remain in relative safety, away from the horrors of the ghetto that the occupiers forced Jews to live in. As life became ever more brutal and dangerous for Jews, Pozner created an underground hideout within the cemetery. The Germans eventually found the bunker and killed most of those hiding there. However, two of them managed to survive imprisonment in German labour camps, one of whom, Avraham Carmi, remains alive today and lives in Israel. The current archaeological work is expected to be completed by the end of July, after which the foundations will be re-covered with earth. Warsaw’s Jewish community then hopes to restore the previous building, adapted to current conditions and needs, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. “The goal is to determine whether the funeral home could be rebuilt on these remains, or whether it would make more sense to display them as a monument within a newly constructed building, and also whether erecting a building on this site is even realistic,” cemetery director Witold Wrzosiński told the newspaper. Archaeologist Szymon Lenarczyk, who has led the work at the site, says he has proposed that the structure of a future building should feature an underground room where discovered artefacts can be displayed. Before World War Two, Warsaw was home to around 350,000 Jews, a third of its population and more than any city in the world other than New York. However, the vast majority were killed in the Holocaust, meaning that only a small Jewish community remains today. World.title: Kraków launches €43m “pre-design” tender for planned metro system
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A planned metro system in Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has moved a step closer after the authorities launched a 188 million zloty (€43 million) tender for “pre-design” of the project. City authorities say the plans – which will include a feasibility study, environmental report, geological research, and assessment of the project’s impact on existing buildings – are a major milestone in the development of what would be only Poland’s second underground railway network. #Krakow #metro #projektowanie #przetargi 🚇Kraków ogłasza przetarg na opracowanie dokumentacji przedprojektowej dla budowy metra. W ramach uruchomionego postępowania powstaną m. in. dokumenty, analizy i decyzje, które pozwolą przygotować dokumentację niezbędną do finalnego… pic.twitter.com/0jcYL4HGRq — Kraków (@krakow_pl) July 13, 2026 The idea of building a metro in Kraków has been discussed for decades and, in 2014, 55% of residents who took part in a referendum voted in favour of the project. However, only in 2024 did the city’s then-mayor, Aleksander Miszalski, announce plans to build a system. In September last year, the city unveiled the metro’s planned route, with two lines travelling through the city’s historic centre from its southwestern and southeastern suburbs to its eastern outskirts. In May this year, Miszalski, who had made developing the metro part of his election campaign in 2023, was removed as mayor in a recall referendum. But the project has nevertheless continued, with the municipal authorities last week announcing a tender for pre-design of the metro. The work will include confirmation of the planned structure of the system as well as the location of stations, tunnels and other infrastructure. The city has allocated 188 million zloty for the pre-design in its budget for 2026 to 2031. Studies of feasibility and impact are particularly important given that the planned route of the metro envisages it skirting around Kraków’s Old Town, which is a UNESCO World Heritage site that contains many historical structures. The tender follows months of preparatory work, initial market consultations, analyses and discussions with experts, said Maria Wojtacha, director of Kraków’s public works department. “Although this process doesn’t yet mean that construction has begun, it is one of the most important steps that the city can take individually,” Wojtacha added. “Our goal is to prepare Kraków for the next stage – the ‘design and build’ phase.” The experiences of other recent major infrastructure projects in Poland, such as a major new airport and transport hub and Warsaw’s second metro line, show that environmental and tender procedures need not slow investments down, said Marek Grochowicz of the city’s strategy and European funds department. However, it is clear that the earlier timeline for Kraków’s metro outlined is slipping. Last September, the city said that it hoped construction would begin in 2030 and that the system would be finished by 2035. However, the current acting mayor, Stanisław Kracik, announced last month that construction is unlikely to start until between 2040 and 2045. Even the current tender for “pre-design” work envisages a timeline of up to 50 months for that work alone. Warsaw has announced 56m zloty for “pre-design” work on a fourth metro line. The mayor says improving public transport is an "absolute priority". But his rival in next month's elections says the mayor is digging up forgotten plans as part of the campaign https://t.co/lg3zkNeW2E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 15, 2024 Rafał Solecki, head of Kraków’s department of strategy and European funds, also made clear last week that “construction of the metro exceeds the financial capabilities of the local authorities”, and that therefore financial support from the national government and the EU will be necessary. “The metro should be treated as a national strategic investment, similar to large railway, road, aviation and metropolitan projects implemented in other parts of the country with state participation,” he added. The city also announced that it has received a proposal for a consortium of seven local universities and research institutions to provide scientific and expert support for the metro project throughout its preparation and implementation. “Building a metro in a historic city is an extremely complex undertaking, requiring special attention to the protection of cultural heritage,” said Andrzej Szarata, rector of Cracow University of Technology. “Therefore, the support of the scientific community…is of paramount importance.” Kraków has been named Europe's best city break destination by members of @WhichUK. World.title: Attempted illegal border crossings from Belarus to Poland down over 98% this year
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland says that the number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants over the border from Belarus fell from around 15,500 in the first half of last year to less than 250 in the same period this year – a drop of over 98%. It also now claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally. “The effectiveness of [border guard] officers and the Polish armed forces discourages migrants from taking risks,” says Poland’s interior ministry. Bezpieczeństwo na granicy z Białorusią w pierwszej połowie 2026 r. w liczbach: 📉 Ponad 65-krotny spadek prób nielegalnego przekroczenia (ok. 235 vs ponad 15,5 tys. w pierwszym półroczu 2025 r.) 🛡️ 0 udanych prób nielegalnego przekroczenia granicy 💯 Skuteczność ochrony: 100%… pic.twitter.com/1lTXV56JdW — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) July 18, 2026 Since 2021, large numbers of migrants and asylum seekers – mainly from Africa and Asia – have tried to irregularly cross the border from Belarus to Poland with the help and encouragement of the Belarusian authorities. In 2021 alone, just under 40,000 attempted illegal crossings were recorded. While Poland subsequently strengthened border infrastructure and sent thousands of additional officers to bolster security, attempted crossings remained high: there were just under 30,000 in each of 2024 and 2025. However, those figures have now fallen dramatically in the first half of this year, when Poland’s border guard recorded only 235 crossings, compared to 15,500 in the equivalent period for 2025. Meanwhile, the interior minister says that the number of successful crossings by migrants – i.e. those who managed to get across the border and were not apprehended – has fallen to zero so far this year, down from around 1,700 in 2025, 5,000 in 2024 and 12,000 in 2023. However, when presenting such figures on successful crossings, the ministry does not indicate how it calculates them, given that successful crossings are often inherently undetected. Most of those who manage to cross do not remain in Poland, instead heading westwards, in particular to Germany. “The statistics clearly show that the 3 billion zloty (€692 million) investment in the security of the Polish-Belarusian border has delivered the intended results – we are effectively protecting our country from illegal migration organised by the Belarusian regime with the support of the Kremlin,” declared the ministry. Poland says that “specialists from the Middle East” have been brought to Belarus to dig tunnels under the border for migrants to cross into Poland. Four such tunnels have been discovered this year, including one last week that was used by 180 migrants https://t.co/4ConkQnj8z — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 16, 2025 Among the measures taken to protect the border are a 5.5-metre-high steel fence as well as an electronic monitoring system that detects attempts to cross and dispatches officers to the scene. In 2024, following the death of a soldier who had been stabbed by a migrant attempting to cross the border, Poland also loosened the rules on the use of firearms by officers posted there. Since last year, it has banned asylum claims by people who cross from Belarus. Last August, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen visited Poland’s border with Belarus, where she thanked the Polish authorities for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” orchestrated by Belarus and Russia. Germany’s interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, also praised Poland’s “impressive” efforts “to stop illegal migration” and said that it was vital for the EU to offer financial and logistical support. EU chief @vonderleyen has thanked Poland for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” during a visit with PM @donaldtusk to the border with Belarus. She emphasised the “urgency” of protecting the EU’s frontier from the “predator” Vladimir Putin https://t.co/O9bhmLha44 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2025 However, while Poland has managed to significantly reduce the number of attempted and successful border crossings, there is evidence that Belarus has switched its focus to Latvia, another EU member state with which it shares a border. Last week, Latvian interior minister Jānis Dombrava told Euronews that his country has now “become the main target” for Belarus’s migrant trafficking, instead of Poland and Lithuania. On Thursday, Latvia recorded 111 attempted illegal crossings from Belarus, compared to two in Lithuania on the same day and zero in Poland the previous day. World.title: Poland welcomes Zelensky’s five-point plan for resolving dispute over WWII massacres
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has cautiously welcomed an announcement by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of a five-point plan intended to alleviate the diplomatic crisis triggered by his earlier decision to name a military unit after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which led massacres of Poles during World War Two. In a statement on Friday evening, Zelensky announced that, following a meeting on Kyiv’s policy towards Poland, “the priorities are clear: all of us in Europe need good-neighbourly, equal, and mutually beneficial relations built on respect”. He reiterated Ukraine’s gratitude for Poland’s “significant support” since Russia’s full-scale invasion and announced that his administration had “agreed on several key steps” in response to the current tensions. I held a meeting on our policy toward Poland. The priorities are clear: all of us in Europe need good-neighborly, equal, and mutually beneficial relations built on respect. Poland provided significant support to Ukraine after the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, and we are… pic.twitter.com/5dNFQYqi1n — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) July 17, 2026 “First, there will be decisions on the diplomatic track,” said Zelensky, though without indicating what this would mean in practice. “Second, all archives of the Security Service of Ukraine and the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine concerning the tragic events in Volyn during the 20th century will be opened.” The latter is a reference to the historical issues that are at the heart of the dispute. The historical region of Volhynia, which is now mostly in Ukraine, was part of Poland in the interwar period. There, and in some neighbouring areas, the UPA, a nationalist partisan formation, led massacres of around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, during World War Two, when the region was under Nazi-German occupation. Poland recognises those massacres as a genocide. Ukraine vehemently rejects that label, and also points to anti-Ukrainian measures in the region by the interwar Polish state as well as massacres of Ukrainians by Polish groups during the war. As his third pledge, Zelensky announced that there would be “decisions to grant a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”. From 2017 to 2025, Ukraine prohibited searches for and exhumations of Polish massacre victims on its territory, where it is believed that tens of thousands remain buried in unmarked mass graves. In a diplomatic breakthrough, such work was allowed to resume last year. However, Ukraine has so far only approved a small number of requests for searches and exhumations, prompting some complaints from Poland. Poland has for the first time used DNA testing to identify the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII. “After more than 80 years, families are receiving the answer they have awaited for generations,” says the culture minister https://t.co/c1gM3kQ83s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026 As a fourth point, Zelensky said that his team had “discussed possible formats for expanding dialogue between the societies of Ukraine and Poland”, though again without providing details as to what this would involve. Finally, he said that he had agreed with the head of the Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINP), Oleksandr Alfyorov, to expand the institute’s capabilities and funding, so that it can “properly represent Ukraine’s interests”. Alfyorov caused anger in Poland earlier this year when he said that the Volhynia massacres are viewed in Ukraine as “just a local historical episode” and suggested they did not constitute a genocide. That prompted a rebuke from Poland’s own Institute of National Remembrance (IPN). Poland's state historical institute has criticised remarks by the head of its Ukrainian counterpart about massacres of Poles by Ukrainians in WWII. He said they are regarded in Ukraine as a "local episode" and suggested they do not constitute a genocide https://t.co/MAi6RhpRDL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 11, 2026 In response to Zelensky’s announcement, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that he “accepted the words and decisions with satisfaction and hope”. He reiterated that Poland is “ready for a serious and friendly dialogue on the matters that unite us and those that divide”. However, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, a deputy prime minister, emphasised that it was important now for “the announcements regarding the opening of archives, exhumations and dialogue to turn into concrete actions”. “Today, Poland and Ukraine have a common enemy: Russia,” added Kosiniak-Kamysz. “That is where the threat lies. Sowing discord between our nations serves the interests of the Kremlin.” Z satysfakcją i nadzieją przyjmuję słowa i decyzje @ZelenskyyUa, dotyczące relacji między naszymi państwami, które muszą być oparte na wzajemnym szacunku i prawdzie. Jesteśmy gotowi do poważnego i przyjaznego dialogu w sprawach, które nas łączą i tych, które nas dziś dzielą. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 17, 2026 Meanwhile, a senior aide to Polish President Karol Nawrocki – who deepened the crisis by last month stripping Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour – also cautiously welcomed Zelensky’s announcement. “Facing the historical truth is the only way to build further relationships,” Bartosz Grodecki, the head of Nawrocki’s National Security Bureau (BBN), told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “The Ukrainian president’s decision to open the entire archives of the Security Service of Ukraine and the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine concerning the events in Volhynia, as well as additional permits for search and exhumation work, is a step in this direction,” he added. Long-simmering tensions between Poland and Ukraine over WWII massacres have finally boiled over, prompting a diplomatic crisis.@danieltilles1 looks at how we got here and what it may mean for the two countries and Europe more broadly https://t.co/a8tiYJJHRr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 22, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland up 30% this year
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland was 30% higher in the first half of this year compared to the same period in 2025, newly reported police data show. The figures come following a number of recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians – who are Poland’s largest immigrant group – as well as ongoing diplomatic tensions between Kyiv and Warsaw. 🔴Coraz więcej ataków na Ukraińców w Polsce – wynika z danych @PolskaPolicja https://t.co/6ZnKFILbdL — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) July 17, 2026 The new data, which were reported by the Rzeczpospolita daily, show that police received 180 reports of hate crimes against Ukrainians in the first half of 2026, which was around 30% higher than in the same period last year and around 35% more than in 2024. If the same trend continues, there would be around 360 such reports by the end of the year, more than the 275 recorded in 2025 and 267 in 2024. However, Rzeczpospolita notes that the figures relate to reported incidents of hate crimes, rather than confirmed cases. On the other hand, experts point out that many such incidents are never even reported to the police. “It is generally assumed that hate crimes are underreported,” Jacek Kucharczyk, head of the Institute of Public Affairs, a think tank, told the newspaper. “Some victims don’t want to report a crime because they’re simply afraid.” Ukrainians are by far Poland’s largest foreign national group, with around 1.6 million living in the country. While Poland welcomed Ukrainian refugees in 2022, there has been growing negative sentiment towards them recently, indicated in polls and through anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from prominent politicians. In particular, two far-right opposition parties, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have used anti-Ukrainian rhetoric, while the largest opposition group, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has recently taken a tougher line towards Ukraine. Kucharczyk told Rzeczpospolita that the “toxic atmosphere” around Ukrainians is now spreading from political rhetoric into real-life consequences, as seen in the new police data. He added that Russia also seeks to stoke and exploit such sentiment. An 18-year-old Ukrainian will stand trial in Poland accused of working on behalf of Russia to stir tension between Poland and Ukraine by painting dozens of inscriptions in public places glorifying the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, which massacred Poles in WWII https://t.co/0w0gVYiGpp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 16, 2026 In May, five Polish teenagers were detained in Warsaw over a violent attack on a group of young Ukrainians. The city’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, blamed the anti-Ukrainian rhetoric of right-wing politicians for “encouraging thugs” to carry out these kinds of attacks. Tensions with Ukraine have since ramped up even further, amid a diplomatic dispute sparked by President Volodomyr Zelensky’s decision to name a military unit after a Ukrainian nationalist group that led massacres of Poles during World War Two. Earlier this month, two Polish far-right activists were charged over an incident in which they confronted a Ukrainian woman who runs a business that offers assistance to other Ukrainian immigrants. Last week, a man was detained after being recorded hurling xenophobic obscenities at Ukrainian children on a bus in the city of Bielsko-Biała. That latter incident prompted Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, to call on “Polish politicians to stop inciting hatred against Ukrainians”. Ukraine’s foreign minister has called on "Polish politicians to stop inciting hatred against Ukrainians” after an incident in which a man was filmed shouting xenophobic obscenities at Ukrainian girls on a bus in Poland. The perpetrator has been detained https://t.co/AfGCNqtJbj — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 13, 2026 Figures from Poland’s government, which is a coalition ranging from left to centre right, have also condemned recent incidents of hate towards Ukrainians. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called last week’s incident in a bus “disgusting” and warned of the potential “disastrous consequences” of inciting national hatred. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński promised that the state would deal with “any form of aggression”, but also blamed the right-wing opposition for stirring antipathy. However, PiS spokesman Rafał Bochenek accused the government of “cynically exploiting” the incident in Bielsko-Biała “for political purposes”. He said it was, in fact, Tusk and Kierwiński who were “responsible for the brutalisation of public life in Poland”. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s ambassador to Poland, Vasyl Bodnar, hailed the fact that “the entire political class” in Poland had condemned the incident on the bus and expressed hope that the recent wave of attacks is a “temporary symptom” that “will pass”, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Two Polish far-right activists have been charged over an incident in which they confronted a Ukrainian woman who runs a business providing services to immigrants.
