World.title: Romanian City Holds Out Against Authorising LGBTQ+ Pride March
World.content:
Oradea’s unauthorised Pride March in 2025. Photo: Photo: Ovi D. Pop/Oradea Pride.

Just over 250 kilometres separate Romania’s western city of Oradea from Budapest in Hungary, but until recently the two cities shared another distinction: both had refused to allow Pride marches.

Hungary’s capital hosted a Pride event this year despite government opposition. Oradea is now the only major city in the European Union where local authorities continue to deny permission for a Pride march, after refusing to authorise the 2026 event on Wednesday.

“The City Hall has decided not to approve the event. All 115 possible routes proposed by the organisers are concentrated in the city’s central area … These routes are unavailable because they overlap with other authorised events, or are affected by major public infrastructure works,” municipal spokesperson Octavian Haragoș said, as quoted by the local news outlet ebihoreanul.ro.

The municipality did not explain why alternative routes outside the city centre could not be considered. The decision followed weeks of delays by the city council in ruling on the organisers’ request, where conservative councillors and religious groups dominated the debate.

Human rights groups condemned the decision, arguing that it violates the constitutional right to peaceful assembly.

“We consider this decision completely unacceptable because it effectively blocks people’s constitutional right to peaceful assembly,” Victor Ciobotaru, director of ACCEPT, Romania’s leading LGBTQ+ rights organisation, told BIRN.

“Under Romanian law, local authorities cannot ban a public march. Their role is to identify practical solutions to ensure that such events can take place safely and under appropriate conditions, not to prevent them altogether,” Ciobotaru added.

Citing the same legal argument, ARK Oradea, the organisation behind the city’s Pride Parade, said the march would go ahead on July 25 despite the municipality’s refusal to authorise it.

“Our march will take place … As a sign of solidarity and concern for the situation in Oradea, representatives of nine diplomatic missions accredited to Romania, as well as representatives of the Ombudsman Institution, will be present in Oradea to monitor the unfolding of events,” ARK said, adding that the presence of diplomats reflects growing international concern over restrictions on freedom of assembly and LGBTQ+ rights in Romania.

This marks the fourth consecutive year that Oradea’s authorities have refused to authorise the Pride Parade.

Last year, however, an unauthorised march was still held through the city centre, attended by several hundred mostly young people. There were brief scuffles between some participants and the police but the situation did not escalate.

Authorities later imposed fines totalling 19,800 lei (about 3,900 euros) on organisers and participants in the unauthorised march

Romania has made progress on LGBTQ+ rights since joining the European Union in 2007 but continues to rank among the bloc’s weakest performers in terms of legal protections and social acceptance.

Consensual same-sex relations have been legal since 2001, but same-sex marriage and civil partnerships are not recognised, despite a 2023 ruling by the European Court of Human Rights requiring Romania to provide legal recognition and protection for same-sex couples.

Public attitudes toward LGBTQ+ people remain largely conservative, particularly outside major cities. Pride marches have been held annually in Bucharest for two decades, however, and in several other cities, generally under police protection and without major incidents.

Human rights organisations have urged Romania to strengthen anti-discrimination protections and fully implement European human rights standards, arguing that it is lagging behind in terms of the country’s commitments as an EU member.

World.title: EU, OSCE Missions Criticise Kosovo’s Demolition of Serb-Owned Villas
World.content:
Demolition of villas near Ujman/Gazivoda lake in north Kosovo on July 21, 2026. Photo: BIRN

International missions in Kosovo expressed concern on Wednesday over the police’s demolition of 11 villas belonging to local Serbs near Lake Ujman/Gazivoda in the Serb-majority north of the country.

Kosovo authorities said the houses were built illegally on land owned by the public water management company Iber-Lepenc, near the Ujman/Gazivode Lake. The operation began on June 26.

The European Union Office in Kosovo said that it regretted Tuesday’s demolitions, noting that, “the affected residents had already initiated court proceedings within the 15-day deadline provided in notices issued by the public enterprise Iber-Lepenc to vacate the land”.

The EU called for an “immediate halt to any further demolitions, forced removals or takeovers until concerns relating to due process, proportionality, property rights, human rights and effective remedies are adequately addressed.

“Irreversible enforcement measures in the context of pending proceedings and contested property claims raise serious rule-of-law concerns,” the statement added.

The OSCE Mission in Kosovo said that, “any action affecting property rights, including the demolition of illegally constructed buildings, must be carried out strictly within the applicable legal framework, with full respect for due process”.

The mission said affected individuals should be informed promptly and adequately of the legal basis for actions taken against their property. “The rule of law, transparency, and due process must be applied consistently and without distinction to all illegally constructed buildings across Kosovo,” it said.

It added that enforcement measures against unauthorised construction should follow the same legal standards and procedural safeguards for all communities. “Selective or uneven application of the law, whether real or perceived, risks undermining public confidence and negatively affect inter-community relations and trust,” it said.

Faruk Mujka, deputy Mayor of South Mitrovica municipality, wrote on Facebook on Tuesday that “11 illegally constructed villas had been removed during Tuesday’s operation”.

Mujka said the action was carried out by the Ministry of Environment, Spatial Planning and Infrastructure with assistance from the police following a request from Iber-Lepenc to return the property to the company’s management.

Ujman/Gazivoda Lake is considered strategic infrastructure for Kosovo. It supplies drinking water to several cities, supports electricity generation and provides water for irrigation.

Fitore Pacolli, acting minister of the Ministry of Environment, Spatial Planning and Infrastructure, noted at the start of demolition work in June that the operation was being conducted to return illegally occupied property in northern Kosovo to the administration of Iber-Lepenc.

“The protection of our water resources remains our highest priority. For this reason, we will continue to protect them, manage them responsibly, and develop them as a vital asset for Kosovo,” Pacolli wrote.

But the Serbian government’s office for Kosovo condemned the operation as a “violent demolition” undertaken “without any court verdict”.

“The owners of the villas found out about the demolition of their property, which they had acquired for years, from the notices that were attached to their buildings, and when they asked for court decisions today, they did not receive them,” it said.

“All this indicates that these demolitions were not carried out with the aim of implementing some kind of law, but for a political reason,” it added.

World.title: Serbia Indicts Six for Drug Trafficking Linked to North Macedonia
World.content:
Serbia’s Public Prosecutor’s Office for Organised Crime filed an indictment on Tuesday accusing six alleged members of an organised crime group of producing and trafficking drugs within Serbia and North Macedonia during 2025 until January 29, 2026.

The prosecution on Wednesday said the indictment was filed against Aleksandar Mijajlovic as the organiser, Ivan Dragnic as the co-organiser, and Nebojsa Spasojevic, Rade Spasojevic, Uros Mladenovski and Robert Zivkovic as members of the same crime group.

“The evidence collected … indicates that the organisers devised the group’s operational structure, established its hierarchy, assigned roles among its members in advance, and secured the financial resources necessary to carry out the criminal plan,” the prosecution said in a press release.

The group is suspected of transporting nearly five tonnes of marijuana from North Macedonia to Serbia and storing it in residential and commercial premises used by Nebojsa and Rade Spasojevic in the village of Konjuh, near Krusevac, central Serbia, where the drugs were repackaged and prepared for distribution to end-buyers.

Spasojevic was a local official of the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, at the time of the bust. Serbian Defence Minister Bratislav Gasic, himself from Krusevac, denied the party was involved and repeated that it was clear that there are “no protected individuals” in Serbia because they had arrested Spasojevic.

The suspects are charged with using the company Alfapharm Group, based in Skopje, as a legitimate business entity to cover the narcotics production.

The company held permits issued by the authorities in North Macedonia to cultivate and produce cannabis extracts for medical purposes.

“The company was misused to conceal the organisation of the procurement, storage, repackaging, and transportation of large quantities of the narcotic drug marijuana,” the press release said.

According to the prosecution, in November 2025, the group organised the procurement of 8,832 kilograms of dried cannabis flower from the supplier CBD Med Plant from Strumica, North Macedonia.

The drugs were stored at the premises of Alfapharm Group, weighed, repackaged and prepared for transportation. The group used documentation relating to the export of textile goods for this during international transport.

The indictment added that Robert Zivkovic is charged with managing storage of the drugs, supervising the packaging process, organising their transportation, and overseeing their unloading and storage in Serbia. Nebojsa and Rade Spasojevic are alleged to have been responsible for receiving, storing, repackaging, and arranging the further transport of the drugs.

Serbian police arrested Uros Mladenovski at the end of January in Belgrade, when he collected around a hundred kilograms of marijuana from Spasojevic’s premises and transported it to the capital.

During searches of the residential and business premises used by the Spasojevic family, police discovered various arms, such as automatic firearms, ammunition, and a “Zolja” hand-held anti-tank rocket launcher.

Dragnic, Nebojsa and Rade Spasojevic and Mladenovski are in detention.

Zivkovic is a fugitive. A detention order has been issued for him, and both domestic and international arrest warrants have been sought.

Aleksandar Mihailovic was arrested in Austria on July 1 and a Serbian request for his extradition is pending.

The prosecution added that proceedings are being conducted before the North Macedonian authorities as well, and that both countries “continue to cooperate and exchange information within the framework of international legal assistance”.

Serbia’s authorities on January 29 seized five tons of marijuana in the village of Konjuh, which the Serbian prosecution then suggested may have originated from North Macedonia. A week later, North Macedonia police seized more than 40 tons of drugs.

The record-breaking seizures in both countries fuelled questions about whether North Macedonia’s legalisation of marijuana grown for medicinal purposes in 2016 has encouraged illegal production and smuggling.

World.title: North Macedonia’s Access-to-Information Agency Accused of Hindering Appeals
World.content:
North Macedonia’s Agency for the Protection of the Right to Free Access to Public Information. Photo: BIRN.

Legal experts and transparency advocates have criticised North Macedonia’s Agency for the Protection of the Right to Free Access to Public Information after it began requiring electronic signatures on email appeals, arguing that this unlawfully restricts access to public information.

The Agency is the only institution responsible for deciding appeals when public bodies refuse or fail to provide information requested under the country’s freedom of information law.

Until recently, appeals could be submitted by email without additional formalities. However, the Agency has started rejecting emailed appeals unless they are certified with an electronic signature, which costs 2,000 to 4,000 denars (30 to 65 euros) annually.

Critics say the changes create an unnecessary financial and administrative obstacle to exercising a constitutionally guaranteed right.

“I believe they obstruct free access to public information in this country,” German Filkov, one of the authors of the Law on Free Access to Public Information and president of the Centre for Civil Communications, an anti-corruption and transparency watchdog, told BIRN.

Instead of creating new barriers, Filkov said, the Agency should focus on the growing number of state institutions that fail to respond to freedom of information requests.

The Agency has defended the new requirement by citing the 2015 Law on General Administrative Procedure, which it says obliges anyone communicating electronically with state institutions to use an electronic signature.

However, the State Administrative Inspectorate, which the Agency initially cited as the source of the guidance, told BIRN it had issued no written decision or instruction requiring such a practice.

One of the authors of the Law on General Administrative Procedure, which the Agency cites as the legal basis for its new practice, Skopje university law professor Borce Davitkovski, also questioned the Agency’s interpretation.

“They are not allowed to reject an appeal because it lacks an electronic signature,” Davitkovski told BIRN, noting that the law was designed to protect citizens rather than burden them with unnecessary bureaucracy.

Konstantin Bitrakov, an assistant professor at Skopje’s State Faculty of Law, argued that the Agency was misapplying the legislation and “setting a negative example for public institutions that hold information, whose decisions it is supposed to review on appeal”.

He said the legal provisions on electronic signatures apply to officials issuing administrative decisions, not to citizens filing appeals.

Lawyers told BIRN that citizens and organisations whose appeals have been rejected for lacking an electronic signature should challenge the Agency before the Administrative Court within 30 days.

The dispute comes amid concerns over access to public information.

A BIRN analysis found that the number of appeals filed with the Agency over administrative silence or incomplete responses had doubled last year, from over 300 filed in 2024 to over 600 in 2025.

The European Commission’s latest Rule of Law Report warned that some public institutions continue to reject information requests on arbitrary grounds or with significant delays.

In April, the new head of the Agency, Petar Gajdov, told BIRN in an interview: “As institutions, we are service-oriented towards citizens.”

World.title: Who Really Benefits from ‘Strategic Investor’ Status in Albania?
World.content:
A company granted a stretch of Albania’s Adriatic coastline lists its official address as the 12th floor of the European Trade Centre in Tirana, where, according to a BIRN investigation, “there was no company sign, and building staff said they were unaware of any company by that name”.

A public asset belonging to all citizens is now registered under the name of a company that cannot even be found at its own listed address – because its ownership has been ‘constructed’ as a chain of corporate shells, one nested inside another, with the final shell empty. In that vacuum is where the problem begins.

Attempts to frame the public debate over luxury tourist developments in Zvernec, on the Albanian coast, and nearby Sazan island as a choice between environmental protection and economic development are, at best, unhelpful. At worst, they are misleading.

World.title: EU’s Failure to Address Balkan Disputes Undermines Its Credibility
World.content:
It also underlines the consequences of the EU’s failure to put forward an overall strategy to address the many bilateral disputes in the Western Balkans.

North Macedonia’s current centre-right government led by Hristijan Mickovski, elected in 2024, has insisted that before it amends the constitution, Bulgaria should guarantee it will make no new demands that could further block negotiations down the road.

The background to this request relates to the long list of obstacles placed on the country’s aspirations to join the European Union ever since it applied for membership in 2004, and successive governments’ efforts to address them with varying degrees of success.

In her response, however, Commissioner Kos underlined that “EU enlargement is not built on guarantees given in advance. It is built on trust, commitments, dedication in fulfilling these commitments and hard work”.

A week later, she repeated the same call on the government to build trust with all the EU member states.

In doing so, she seemed to forget the number of times North Macedonia’s citizens were let down by promises made by the EU which were not kept. She should acknowledge that trust can only succeed if it exists on both sides and is based on solid foundations.

Under the so-called Prespa Agreement, signed with Greece in June 2018, the country agreed to replace its constitutional name with “Republic of North Macedonia”, to be applied erga omnes. The agreement also included recognition of the Macedonian language.

In return the EU assured the country that this agreement would open the door to EU and NATO membership, only to be confronted with a French government veto in 2019, calling for a pause on EU enlargement.

This was resolved the following year with the adoption of a revised methodology for accession negotiations, and the European Council recommendation that negotiations should start with both Albania and North Macedonia.

However, Bulgaria then decided to impose its own veto against the latter, which was transformed into an EU veto in 2022, with the adoption of the French proposal. Under this proposal, formal negotiations with both countries were launched in July 2022. But until parliament in North Macedonia adopts the constitutional amendment, its accession negotiations remain blocked.

Renewed momentum flawed by unanimity rule

World.title: ‘Nobody Mentions Us’: Silence Surrounds Wartime Rape of Kosovo’s Ethnic Minorities
World.content:
Those who fled and never returned often have no means of applying for recognition as survivors of wartime sexual violence.

That includes a fourth woman interviewed by BIRN, who was 29 years old when she was raped twice by uniformed men in the police headquarters in Gjakova/Djakovica in March and April 1999. A cleaner in the building, she fled when the war ended out of fear of being targeted for revenge as a former employee of the Serbian state.

The woman now lives in the Montenegrin capital, Podgorica, but does not possess Kosovo documents.

“Living in a refugee camp for a long time, we didn’t have food, let alone a psychologist,” she told BIRN. “Sometimes I bought sedatives when I had a few dinars.”

When the war ended, ethnic minorities were targeted for revenge by Kosovo Albanian guerrillas and civilians.

Speaking to BIRN, an Egyptian woman from a village near Peja/Pec recalled five armed men entering her house on July 27, 1999, one of them in a T-shirt featuring the symbol of the guerrilla Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA. Her husband was beaten and she was dragged into the woods. “One of them raped me, and my husband was unable to help.”

The men later went next door, where they raped the woman’s neighbour.

Three days later, the family left Kosovo. Her case was documented in a 1999 report by the Belgrade-based Humanitarian Law Centre. In the report, she says: “When they came, they asked me to find two other women and go with them. I told them I could not find any and begged them to let me go because I was a mother with small children. One of them threatened to kill my husband if I did not comply. Crying, I went there. They left me there, crying and dishonoured.”

However, Kosovo’s Law on the Status and Rights of Martyrs, Invalids, Veterans, Civilian Victims, and Victims of Sexual Violence only provides for recognition of survivors of wartime sexual violence between February 1998 and June 20, 1999, i.e. roughly a week after Serbian forces pulled out of Kosovo and the war ended.

The woman said she doesn’t “need” recognition. “But I am frustrated that nobody mentions us,” she said. “Egyptian Roma women have also been raped here.”

Agushi, the Roma rights activist, said rape survivors from minority communities barely feature in public discourse surrounding the war and wartime sexual violence; those raped after the official cessation of hostilities are doubly discriminated against.

“They are even more marginalised, and those who were victims of sexual violence after June 20, 1999, are particularly discriminated against because they are not legally recognised and remain in the shadows.”

Campaign of terror

World.title: Land Registry Cyberattack Exposes Holes in Romania’s Digital Defences
World.content:
Photo illustration: EPA/SASCHA STEINBACH

This summer was supposed to mark an important milestone for Stefania Guga. By the end of July, the 32-year-old had hoped to buy a two-room apartment in a newly built complex on the outskirts of Bucharest, fulfilling her ambition of becoming a homeowner, Guga told BIRN.

“I wanted to finalise the transaction before August 1 to avoid paying the higher VAT rate. But for more than a week now, everything has been at a standstill, and I still don’t know whether I’ll make the deadline. It’s no longer up to me – the problem lies with Romanian state institutions,” she said.

Guga’s plans have been disrupted by a cyberattack on July 14 targeting the IT infrastructure of Romania’s National Agency for Cadastre and Land Registration, ANCPI, effectively freezing property registration services and real estate transactions.

For Guga, the timing could hardly be worse. Under the government’s latest fiscal package, the VAT rate for newly built homes will rise from 9 to 21 per cent on August 1.

If she misses the deadline, it will significantly raise the overall cost of her apartment, adding thousands of euros to the price.

The ANCPI has described the cyberattack as “the most serious technical incident in the institution’s history”.

It crippled the agency’s digital systems, disrupting online land registry services, official email communications and apps used daily by notaries, lawyers, cadastral surveyors and ANCPI staff.

Authorities were left unable to register new property transactions, process pending requests, or issue essential land registry documents, bringing much of Romania’s real estate market to a standstill.

Just one day after the agency’s systems were compromised, some of the stolen data appeared for sale on a well-known hacking forum.

The leaked files included employee login credentials, internal documents and technical information about the agency’s IT infrastructure, raising concerns that the attackers had gained deep access to critical systems.

Experts say that, although the attack did not look particularly sophisticated from a technical standpoint, its consequences are serious.

“This is arguably the most severe cybersecurity incident in Romania’s relatively short history of the digitalisation of public administration,” said cybersecurity expert Andrei Avadanei.

“It affects data belonging to infrastructure classified as critical national infrastructure, including records covering every property in the country.

“It has disrupted essential public services and directly affects hundreds of thousands of citizens whose property transactions and administrative procedures are now vulnerable,” he added.

Avadanei also said the incident could likely have been prevented if the ANCPI had invested more consistently in cybersecurity and implemented stronger preventive measures.

The agency’s spending priorities appear to reinforce that criticism.

According to media reports, ANCPI has invested around 710 million lei, or about 135 million euros, in digitalisation over the past two decades. But only about 0.2 per cent of that, roughly 305,000 euros, was allocated to cybersecurity.

Experts say that figure is woefully inadequate given the sensitivity of the data the agency manages and its role in operating one of the country’s most critical public databases.

Officials have sought to reassure the public and limit the fallout from the cyberattack. In a statement, ANCPI said the incident “did not compromise the agency’s technical or legal databases” and stressed that core land registry records were neither altered nor destroyed.

The agency also said it has begun migrating its applications to the Romanian Government Cloud, a process expected to be completed on Wednesday. Once the migration is finished, specialists will carry out comprehensive integrity checks before services are gradually restored.

At the same time, the incident has exposed the fragility of Romania’s public digital infrastructure at a time when the country is facing a sustained wave of cyber threats linked to the broader security environment created by Russia’s invasion of neighbouring Ukraine.

Romanian authorities and cybersecurity experts have repeatedly warned that government institutions, critical infrastructure and public databases have become attractive targets for hostile cyber actors.

“This incident should serve as a wake-up call for the entire public administration,” interim Digitalisation Minister Irineu Darau said in a televised interview.

Darau acknowledged that the digitalisation of Romania’s public institutions has been carried out in a fragmented way, without a coherent national strategy or common security standards.

“It is time to make digital transformation and cybersecurity genuine national priorities,” he said.

“That also means offering better salaries to cybersecurity professionals working in the public sector so that state institutions can attract and retain the expertise needed to protect critical systems,” he concluded.

World.title: Dinamo Draw at the Start of Champions League Qualifying
World.content:
Dinamo Zagreb played out a 1-1 draw against Thun in Switzerland in the first leg of the Champions League second qualifying round. The hosts took the lead through a Brighton Labeau goal in the 20th minute, before Miha Zajc set the final score in the 86th minute. The tie will be decided in the return leg in Zagreb in a week.

Thun are the first of three potential opponents Dinamo must overcome to secure a place in the Champions League group stage. The second round is followed by the third round and then the play-off. Dinamo’s possible third-round opponent will be the winner of the tie between KÍ Klaksvík of the Faroe Islands and Lithuania’s Kauno Žalgiris. Should they fall to Thun, Dinamo would continue their European campaign in the Europa League third qualifying round against the loser of the tie between Hapoel Be’er Sheva and Vikingur.

After a quiet start, the Swiss side took the lead in the 20th minute. Fabio Fehr’s cross from the right caught goalkeeper Ivan Filipović out, and Brighton Labeau headed home to make it 1-0. Just a minute earlier, Filipović had misjudged a free-kick delivery but redeemed himself by saving two efforts from the home side.

Dinamo almost leveled quickly, but Dion Drena Beljo’s effort in the 22nd minute went straight into the hands of goalkeeper Niklas Steffen. The Thun keeper also did well to save a fine long-range attempt from Moris Valinčić in the 28th minute. Thun’s best chance to extend their lead came in the 30th minute, when Furkan Dursun found himself unmarked five metres out but headed wide of the post.

Dinamo created a few more openings before halftime, but efforts from Miha Zajc and Gabriel Vidović fell short, and Thun led 1-0.

Dinamo continued to press after the restart. In the 53rd minute, Beljo’s header from a corner was cleared off the line by a home defender, and in the 65th minute a Mislav Oršić effort was again blocked on its way towards goal. Thun threatened on the counter, coming closest in the 73rd minute when Valmir Matoshi’s shot went narrowly wide.

Dinamo’s persistence paid off in the 86th minute. Fran Topić, on since the 79th minute, supplied the assist from the right for Miha Zajc, and the Slovenian midfielder finished first-time from 17 meters to make it 1-1. The score remained unchanged until the final whistle, leaving the tie to be settled in Zagreb.

World.title: Will Smith Visits Rimac Campus Near Zagreb
World.content:
July the 22nd, 2026 – Hollywood star Will Smith paid a visit to Rimac Campus near Zagreb this week, where he was treated to something special indeed.

The well known actor was given a behind-the-scenes look at one of Croatia’s most celebrated technology companies, and judging by his reaction, he was thoroughly impressed! Poslovni reports that the Oscar-winning actor toured the state-of-the-art headquarters of Rimac Technology, meeting founder and CEO Mate Rimac while exploring the cutting-edge engineering and production facilities that have helped place Croatia firmly on the global automotive map.

During the visit, Smith experienced several of Rimac’s innovations firsthand, including the company’s world-renowned electric hypercars. Videos shared from the visit captured the actor reacting with visible excitement, laughing, shouting in amazement and expressing disbelief at the performance and technology on display. According to those present, Smith was particularly impressed by the speed, engineering and innovation that have become synonymous with the Rimac name.

putting croatian innovation on stage

Founded by Mate Rimac back in 2009, the company has grown from a small garage startup into one of the world’s leading developers of high-performance electric vehicle technology. Today, Rimac supplies advanced battery systems, electric powertrains and software to some of the biggest names in the automotive industry, while its Nevera hypercar has repeatedly broken global performance records. The Rimac Campus, located in Kerestinec on the outskirts of Zagreb, has become a symbol of Croatia’s growing reputation as a centre for advanced engineering and innovation.

Smith’s visit shines another international spotlight on one of Croatia’s biggest business success stories. Over the past few years, the company has welcomed politicians, investors, automotive executives and celebrities eager to see firsthand how a Croatian startup evolved into a global technology powerhouse. The visit also serves as another reminder that Croatia’s international reputation is increasingly being shaped not only by tourism, but also by world-class innovation and high-tech manufacturing.

more than just fast cars…

While Rimac’s electric hypercars often capture the headlines, the company has become equally important as a technology partner for the wider automotive industry. Its expertise in battery systems, electric drivetrains and vehicle software is helping shape the next generation of electric mobility, with technologies developed in Croatia finding their way into vehicles produced around the world. For Will Smith, the visit offered a glimpse into the future of transportation. For Croatia, it was another high-profile endorsement of a company that continues to demonstrate the country’s ability to compete at the highest possible levels of global technology.

World.title: Largest Croatian Cave System Was Discovered by Chance
World.content:
July the 22nd, 2026 – The largest Croatian cave system was discovered entirely by chance, and it revealed fascinating evidence of a 20,000 year old hunter…

The largest Croatian cave, located in beautiful Ogulin, is widely considered to be the country’s most remarkable archaeological and natural treasure. More interestingly still, it owes its entire discovery to pure chance.

The Đula-Medvedica Cave System, the largest cave complex in all of Croatia, was uncovered unexpectedly during railway construction back during the early 20th century. Putni kofer writes that what initially began as an ambitious but otherwise normal engineering project soon turned into one of the country’s most significant archaeological discoveries in history, revealing evidence of human life dating back tens of thousands of years.

the best discoveries usually happen by accident…

What eventually turned out to be the largest Croatian cave system ever discovered came to light while workers were building the railway through Ogulin, exposing a vast underground network hidden deep beneath the landscape. Subsequent exploration revealed kilometres upon kilometres of interconnected passages, underground chambers and various waterways, making it the largest known cave complex in Croatia and an important site for both speleologists and scientists.

a present-day window into prehistoric croatia

Among the cave’s most extraordinary discoveries was the bone of a prehistoric hunter estimated to be around 20,000 years old. Archaeologists also uncovered numerous traces of Ice Age human activity, confirming that the cave provided shelter to people living in the region during the last Ice Age. The finds have helped researchers better understand how prehistoric communities survived in what is now Croatia during one of Europe’s harshest climatic periods.

Beyond its archaeological importance, the deep Đula-Medvedica Cave System is renowned for its geological features. The labyrinth of passages includes underground rivers, enormous chambers, dramatic rock formations and unique ecosystems that support species specially adapted to life in complete darkness. Because of its scientific value and fragile environment, much of the cave remains protected and is accessible only to researchers and experienced cavers.

ogulin’s subterranean attraction

While many visitors know Ogulin as the hometown of Croatian fairy-tale writer Ivana Brlić-Mažuranić, this picturesque but often bypassed area is also home to one of Croatia’s most fascinating karst landscapes. The rich cave system lies beneath a region shaped by many sinking rivers and limestone formations that have been carved over millions of years, creating an extraordinary underground world hidden in depths, far beneath the town.

the discovery was a turning point for croatian archaeology

Over a century has now passed since its accidental discovery, and yet the Đula-Medvedica Cave System continues to provide valuable insights into Croatia’s natural and human history. From prehistoric hunter-gatherer human remains to utterly spectacular geological formations, this incredible cave stands as an eternal reminder that some of the country’s greatest discoveries have happened entirely by accident, lying patiently in wait, deep beneath the surface, until the right moment revealed them to the world.

World.title: Croatian Retailers Push Back Against Night-Time Alcohol Sales Ban
World.content:
July the 22nd, 2026 – Croatian retailers are strongly pushing back against the recently introduced night-time alcohol sales ban which they claim makes them feel invisible.

As Index reports, Croatian retailers are loudly voicing growing concerns over new local restrictions banning night-time alcohol sales shops between 21:00 and 06:00. They are arguing that this recently introduced measure unfairly targets their businesses only, all while leaving bars, restaurants and nightclubs totally unaffected.

The debate follows Makarska’s decision to become the first Croatian city to prohibit alcohol sales in retail stores between 21:00 and 06:00. The measure was introduced to tackle late-night noise, public disorder and anti-social behaviour during the busy summer season, with other coastal cities, including Split, actively considering similar rules.

“why is it all on us?” ask shop owners and managers

The Association of Small Retailers operating within the boundaries of Split-Dalmatia County are claiming that the new restrictions place neighbourhood shops, kiosks and convenience stores at a significant disadvantage. Its secretary, Boris Listeš, argues that small retailers weren’t even consulted before these decisions were made and that they will suffer the greatest financial impact because many rely heavily on evening sales during the tourist season. He says larger supermarkets, which generally close their doors at around 21:00 or 22:00, will barely notice the change, while cafés, restaurants and clubs will continue serving alcohol without any of these restrictions.

“these rules should apply to everyone”

Retailers insist that if authorities believe limiting alcohol availability will improve public order, the restrictions should apply equally across all businesses selling alcohol. They argue that tourists determined to drink late into the night will simply buy alcohol before the ban begins or continue consuming it in hospitality venues, meaning the new rules are unlikely to achieve their intended effect while disproportionately hurting small family-run businesses.

Rather than introducing ill-thought-out blanket bans, retailers say authorities should focus on enforcing existing public order regulations. They argue that police and municipal wardens already know the locations where disturbances regularly occur and that stronger enforcement against disruptive behaviour would be more effective than restricting legal businesses throughout an entire city. According to the association, the new measures risk penalising responsible retailers instead of addressing the individuals causing problems.

other cities are watching how the situation unfolds in makarska…

Makarska may have been the first to adopt the night-time retail alcohol ban, but it’s highly unlikely to be the last. Split is currently considering introducing similar rules, while other coastal cities are weighing whether such restrictions are necessary in their own communities. At the same time, some destinations, including Supetar and Trogir, have indicated they do not currently plan to follow Makarska’s example. As this heated debate continues, Croatia faces a broader question: how to balance the needs of residents seeking quieter summer nights with those of small businesses that depend on the tourism season for a large share of their annual income.

World.title: Domestic Flights Return to Osijek, Reconnecting Eastern Croatia With the Coast
World.content:
July the 22nd, 2026 – Domestic flights have returned to Osijek, connecting eastern Croatia with the coast once again with Trade Air.

The return of these routes strengthens domestic connectivity during the busy main summer season and provides a faster alternative for both tourists and business travellers heading to Croatia’s most popular coastal destinations.

bridging the gap between eastern croatia and the coast

As Dalmatinski portal reports, these seasonal domestic flights once again link Osijek Airport with several destinations on the Adriatic, significantly reducing travel times between Croatia’s eastern and southern regions. For many travellers, the flights offer an attractive alternative to driving for several hours or making multiple transfers by rail or bus, particularly during the height of the summer holiday season.

Although Croatia is remarkably well connected internationally during the summer months, domestic air links have traditionally been more limited. The renewed services aim to improve connections between Slavonia and the coast, making it easier for residents, tourists and business travellers to move around the country while supporting regional tourism and economic activity. Officials have long argued that stronger domestic transport links are essential for balancing tourism development and improving accessibility across Croatia’s regions.

The flights are expected to benefit not only holidaymakers but also local businesses, allowing visitors to combine different parts of Croatia within a single trip. Instead of entering the country through Zagreb, international visitors can more easily explore both Slavonia and Dalmatia, helping spread tourism beyond the traditional coastal hotspots. The renewed connections also provide residents of eastern Croatia with quicker access to the Adriatic during the peak holiday season.

strengthening croatia’s domestic air network

As Croatia continues investing in transport infrastructure, from new rail projects to airport upgrades, the return of seasonal domestic flights represents another step towards improving nationwide connectivity. For travellers looking to swap a lengthy drive for a short flight, the renewed Osijek routes offer a convenient way to travel between the country’s eastern plains and its Adriatic coastline, reinforcing links between two of Croatia’s most distinctive regions.

World.title: Croatian Clubs Discover Potential European Draws
World.content:
Croatia’s European hopefuls found out their possible third qualifying round opponents on Monday, with draws confirmed across the Europa League, Champions League, and Conference League paths.

Hajduk could face Salzburg

Should Hajduk get past Cypriot side Pafos in the second qualifying round of the Europa League, their reward will be a third-round clash with Austria’s Salzburg. Hajduk host Pafos in the first leg on Thursday in Split, with the return fixture in Cyprus the following Thursday. Should they progress, Hajduk would again have home advantage in the first leg of the third round, with the second leg to follow in Salzburg. Third qualifying round ties are scheduled for August 6 and 13.

Should Hajduk instead lose against Pafos, they would drop into the Conference League third qualifying round, where they’d face the winner of the tie between Georgia’s Dinamo Tbilisi and Lithuania’s Žalgiris, with the first leg played away from home.

Dinamo await Vikingur or Hapoel

Champions Dinamo Zagreb have also learned their potential path forward. Should they be eliminated by Switzerland’s Thun in the Champions League second qualifying round, Dinamo would drop into the Europa League third qualifying round to face either Iceland’s Vikingur or Israel’s Hapoel Beer Sheva.

Should Dinamo instead get past Thun and reach the Champions League third qualifying round itself, Mario Kovačević’s side would face the winner of the tie between Faroese side Klaksvik and Lithuania’s Kauno Žalgiris, coached by Željko Sopić. First legs in that round are set for August 4/5, with second legs on August 11.

UEFA has scrapped the previous system of forming subgroups ahead of the “champions’ path” draw this season, meaning Dinamo faced a considerably wider pool of possible opponents than in previous years.

Before turning their attention to the third qualifying round, Dinamo first face Thun in the first leg of the second qualifying round on Tuesday in Switzerland, kicking off at 8 pm, with the return leg set for Tuesday, July 28.

Rijeka and Varaždin could head to Iceland

Rijeka and Varaždin also discovered their potential third qualifying round opponents in the Conference League on Monday. Rijeka, if they eliminate Ireland’s Derry City in the second round, would face the winner of the tie between Iceland’s Stjarnan and Finland’s Ilves. Varaždin, if they see off Czech side Jablonec, would take on the winner between Latvia’s RFS and Iceland’s Vestri.

Third qualifying round fixtures in the Conference League are scheduled for August 6 and 13.

World.title: Croatia vs Spain, Greece & Italy: Which Destination Comes Out on Top?
World.content:
July the 21st, 2026 – Croatia has become one of Europe’s most sought-after summer destinations, but how does it compare to the longtime tourism giants Spain, Greece and Italy?

As Vedran Salvia reports for Index, each country offers something unique, from world-famous beaches to ancient cities and exceptional cuisine. Despite the constantly evolving competition, Croatia appears to very successfully continue carving out its own niche, attracting travellers looking for crystal-clear waters, historic towns and a more relaxed coastal experience.

the croatian coast needs very little help in attracting attention

Croatia’s greatest strength remains its spectacular Adriatic coast. Stretching for more than 1,700 kilometres and dotted with over 1,200 islands, islets and reefs, it offers endless opportunities for sailing, island hopping and discovering secluded beaches. Unlike many Mediterranean destinations where development unfortunately totally dominates the coastline, much of Croatia’s shore remains remarkably well preserved, with national parks, hidden coves and picturesque, ancient fishing villages sitting alongside popular tourist hotspots like Dubrovnik, Split and Makarska.

how does that compare with spain?

Tourism heavyweight Spain continues to attract visitors with its vast array of long, sandy beaches, lively nightlife and major cities such as Barcelona, Valencia and Málaga. It also offers year-round sunshine in many regions. Croatia, however, appeals to travellers seeking a more intimate experience. While destinations like Dubrovnik can become crowded during peak season, much of the coastline remains quieter than Spain’s busiest resorts, particularly away from the best-known locations.

greece – the home of influencer islands

Nearby Greece is globally renowned for iconic, entirely different islands such as Santorini, Mykonos and Crete, along with its ancient history and rich Mediterranean cuisine. Croatia, located just up north, offers a different style of island holiday. Rather than focusing on a handful of internationally famous islands which have become totally swamped by influencers over more recent years (see Mykonos, for example), visitors can choose from hundreds of inhabited and uninhabited islands. Each of them has its very own character, from the lavender fields of Hvar’s interior and the vineyards of Korčula to the untouched nature of Mljet and Lastovo.

the home of the romans is hard to contend with, yet croatia manages to do so

Neighbouring Italy remains one of the world’s most visited countries thanks to remarkable cities such as Rome, Venice and Florence, alongside the Amalfi Coast and Sicily. The country that gave the world the Romans would be difficult to compete with for anyone, and yet Croatia, in its own way, still manages. Naturally, Croatia cannot match Italy’s sheer number of globally recognised cultural landmarks or its geographical size, but it often provides a similar Adriatic atmosphere at a more accessible price point. This is particularly true for sailing holidays, waterfront accommodation and seafood dining outside the very height of the summer season.

croatian prices – a gap that is narrowing (and quickly)

One of Croatia’s traditional advantages has always been affordability, although that gap has greatly narrowed in recent years. Since the country’s accession to the Eurozone, prices for accommodation, restaurants and tourism services have spiked noticeably, especially in popular coastal destinations. During the peak summer months, visitors may find Croatia approaching the prices of parts of Italy or Greece, particularly down in Dubrovnik, as well as in central Dalmatian destinations such as Hvar and Split. Despite that being the case, many lesser-known destinations continue to offer excellent value, particularly along the Kvarner coast, northern Dalmatia and of course away from the sea entirely in inland Croatia.

croatia is so much more than “just beaches”

Croatia’s appeal extends well beyond the coastline and 1,000+ islands. Visitors can explore the marvellous Plitvice Lakes National Park, hike through the imposing mountains of Velebit, discover a great many Roman monuments in Zadar, Pula and Split, sample world-class wines up in Istria and down Pelješac, or experience vibrant festivals and cultural events throughout the entire summer. Combined with its strong reputation as one of Europe’s safest destinations by far, these experiences continue to attract travellers looking for far more than a traditional beach holiday.

the verdict – croatia is the small country that could (and very much has)

Spain offers energy and variety, Italy delivers world-famous culture, and Greece remains synonymous with idyllic island escapes. Croatia, meanwhile, combines elements of all three: spectacular islands, historic towns, exceptional natural beauty and a coastline that remains one of the cleanest and most diverse in Europe. For travellers seeking a Mediterranean holiday that balances relaxation, adventure and history, Croatia continues to prove that it deserves its place alongside the region’s biggest tourism giants.

World.title: Europe’s Smallest Bible Is Hidden in Croatia, And It Fits in the Palm of Your Hand
World.content:
July the 21st, 2026 – You don’t have to be religious to appreciate the wonder of religious architecture and items, and one of the most fascinating (and tiny) items can be found in Croatia. Europe’s smallest Bible is actually hidden in a relatively overlooked part of Croatia.

Croatia is home to countless historical treasures, but few are as surprising as the smallest Bible in all of Europe, a tiny masterpiece that can fit comfortably in the palm of your hand. Putni kofer writes that this truly remarkable miniature Bible is kept in the town of Ludbreg, widely known as “the centre of the world” in northern Croatia, where it has become one of the area’s most unusual cultural attractions.

ludbreg – full of surprises

Despite its incredibly small dimensions, the Bible contains both the Old and New Testaments, printed in microscopic text and bound with exceptional craftsmanship. Its pages are so small that visitors are often astonished that an entire Bible could be produced in such a compact format, making it as much a feat of printing as it is an object of religious significance.

The miniature Bible forms part of Ludbreg’s exceptionally rich cultural and religious heritage. The town is already well known as one of Croatia’s most important pilgrimage destinations thanks to the Sanctuary of the Precious Blood of Christ, which attracts thousands of visitors each year, but this tiny book offers another fascinating reason to visit.

Visitors to Ludbreg are often surprised to discover that such a unique artefact is housed in a small Croatian town rather than in one of Europe’s larger museums.

more than a mere religious object

While the Bible’s size makes it an instant conversation piece, it also reflects the extraordinary skill of the printers and bookbinders who created it. Miniature books have long fascinated collectors around the world, but examples containing the complete biblical text are exceptionally rare, making Ludbreg’s specimen one of the continent’s most unusual literary treasures.

As touched on above, Ludbred is known as the “Centre of the World” thanks to a local legend. This small, humble northern Croatian continues to surprise visitors with attractions that extend far beyond its famous pilgrimage traditions. From its historic streets and castle to one of Europe’s tiniest Bibles, the town proves that some of Croatia’s most remarkable stories are found in places many international visitors have yet to discover.

World.title: Gallery: Scottish punk act The Exploited rock Tallinn's Paavli Kultuurivabrik
World.content:
The band had been supposed to perform in the capital in early February, but the gig was postponed due to the singer's health problems.

With the arrival of summer it went ahead at the same venue, this time outdoors, after the change of date was announced in April. The band had played in Tallinn before, most recently in 2019.

Founded in Edinburgh in 1980 and led by singer and frontman Wattie Buchan, The Exploited is considered one of the central names of the UK82 movement, an aggressive, fast-paced sub-genre of punk rock that emerged in the U.K. in the early 1980s. The band was founded by former soldier Buchan, whose signature mohawk, raspy vocals and uncompromising energy have become iconic elements of punk culture. The Exploited emerged at a time when the U.K. was being shaken by economic crisis, high unemployment and growing social discontent, and their songs reference some of these events.

The Exploited's lyrics tackle war, political power, class struggle, police brutality and social inequality with unflinching anger and directness. Their music also influenced the later development of hardcore as well as thrash and crossover metal, with members of bands including Slayer, Sepultura, Napalm Death and Municipal Waste citing The Exploited as an inspiration.

The albums "Punk's Not Dead" (1981), "Troops of Tomorrow" (1982), and "Let's Start a War..." (1983) helped shape and accelerate the second wave of British street punk in the early '80s. "Punk's Not Dead" became a manifesto for an entire generation, while the follow-up releases helped define the sound of British street punk, characterized by blistering tempos, raw guitar work and scathing social commentary. They released several more studio albums, though the most recent, "Fuck the System," came out back in 2003. Despite this, the band has continued to perform actively and has never disappeared from the live circuit.

In addition to Buchan, the band comprises Gary Sullivan, also known as Gman, Irish Rob (Robert Halkett), and Steve Campbell.

Support acts were Germany's Antinorm and local performers Skoone and Huiabella Fantastica.

World.title: 9 drownings recorded this summer, mostly men over 50
World.content:
Nine people have drowned this summer and most of the victims have been men over the age of 50, under the influence of alcohol. No women have drowned this summer.

In Estonia, men account for nearly 90 percent of drowning victims. Head of Prevention Services at the Rescue Board's Prevention Department Kristina Eesmets said men tend to be more reckless and overestimate their abilities.

Last year, more than 60 percent of those who drowned were intoxicated, with some having a blood alcohol level exceeding 2.5 per mille. "It is very difficult for a person to survive in the water with that level of intoxication," she added.

This summer, there have been instances where adults swam too boldly past the buoys and needed to be rescued. The Rescue Board has been called out three times this year to search for people who went missing while using a stand-up paddle board.

The agency has also recorded three cases of a child going missing at the beach. All the kids were found, and none were in danger of drowning.

There have been 11 cases in which the Rescue Board has saved people from drowning. Most drownings occur in inland waters such as lakes, rivers, and bodies of water close to home, like ditches. This summer, one person has drowned in the sea.

Eesmets said that if an intoxicated person wants to go swimming, they should be stopped. If it is not possible to stop the drunk person, then the emergency services should be called.

This year, spring was significantly more tragic than summer, as several fishermen drowned after venturing onto the ice during volatile weather in March. The Rescue Board's data shows that there were seven drowning deaths in March.

World.title: Ministry to begin offering €10,000 grants to young creators
World.content:
The Ministry of Culture plans to introduce a new state cultural scholarship of €10,000 starting in August 2026. The support is intended for five creative professionals up to age 35 with higher education, to help them develop their careers and build international contacts.

According to the explanatory memorandum of the draft regulation by the minister of culture, the aim of the support is to assist young professionals.

"After leaving the higher‑education system, young creative professionals find it difficult to build an international career and acquire specific professional knowledge and skills. The scholarship supports activities that allow emerging creators to pursue self‑development, build networks and prove themselves professionally, both in Estonia and internationally," the authors of the draft wrote.

The €10,000 support for each scholarship recipient covers participation in international programs, including fees as well as living and travel costs. The total budget for the scholarship competition this year is €50,000.

The explanatory memorandum notes that the new scholarship will not increase costs for the state budget.

"The scholarship amount is planned at €10,000. The previous scholarship budget was €46,000. The restructured scholarship base is the same. In 2026, the ministry's budget base will be increased by €4,000," the memorandum states.

In the future, the possibilities for the scholarship budget will be assessed annually during the budget‑planning process.

Support can be applied for by Estonian citizens and long‑term residents up to age 35.

"The scholarship applicant must have at least a bachelor's degree or equivalent qualification, preferably higher education in a creative field," the memorandum states.

According to the memorandum, a creative professional may also have education in another field, as the ministry takes into account the specifics of cultural and artistic disciplines. The Ministry of Culture will accept applications electronically. Applicants must attach a portfolio, CV, letters of recommendation and confirmation from the program provider.

An assessment of the applicant is given by a five‑member committee appointed by the minister of culture. In making its decision, the committee considers the applicant's previous preparation, the impact of self‑development on professional fulfillment, and the potential broader impact on Estonia's cultural sphere. In the case of equally strong applications, the ministry prefers choices that ensure representation of different creative fields among the scholarship recipients.

The scholarship recipient must submit a report within 30 calendar days after the end of the program. The Ministry of Culture will demand repayment if the applicant provided incorrect information or discontinued the program. The regulation enters into force on 1 August 2026.

Last year, the Ministry of Culture ended its cultural scholarship program funded from its budget, which supported studies at foreign universities as well as important cultural projects and creative commissions. At that time, the ministry awarded 20 scholarships worth €2,300 each. The ministry justified ending the program due to low interest from applicants.

World.title: Estonia's women fencers mostly make it through to world championships main draw
World.content:
Estonian fencers Irina Embrich and Veronika Zuikova are through to the women's individual épée main draw at the ongoing world championships in Hong Kong.

Teammate Julia Beljajeva just lost out, however.

Embrich, Zuikova and Beljajeva are joined at the tournament by top fencer Katrina Lehis. As world number one, Lehis does not have to go through qualifying, while the other team members do.

In that qualification, Embrich won all six of her matches in her group, securing direct qualification for the main draw, which begins with the round of 64.

Zuikova had the most difficult route in the group stage. In her first match, she defeated Egypt's Aya Hussein 15:13, and in her second match secured a 10:9 victory over former European champion Aizanat Murtazajeva (Russia). Overall, she posted three wins and three losses, but still went through.

Veronika Zuikova. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

Beljajeva is out, despite having a four-win streak after losing her initial bout against Venezuela's Lizzie Asis. After beating Filipino fencer Hanniel Abella 15:4, she lost narrowly, 15:14, to Romania's Natalia Constantini, and so is out. She will be able to compete in the women's team event next Tuesday, July 28.

Lehis, Embrich and Zuikova, meanwhile, will fence in the individual main draw this coming Saturday.

The Estonian men's team, comprising Sten Priinits, Kasper Tafenau, Oliver Laasik and Markus Salm, all have to go through qualifying for the individual event.

Lehis, Embrich and Beljajeva were part of Estonia's gold medal-winning team at the 2020 Tokyo Olympics (held in 2021).

World.title: Horse rescued after getting head stuck between trees on Pärnu beach
World.content:
First responders had a relatively unusual callout in Pärnu this week, after a horse got its head lodged between two trees, Maaleht reported .

The Rescue Board (Päästeamet) was notified a little after 6:30 p.m. Monday that a horse had become stuck by the head and neck between two trees on Raeküla Beach, on the town's southern outskirts.

The animal was apparently unable to free itself, and when rescuers arrived at the scene and, after assessing the situation, they tarted the process to release it.

Other horses looked on with apparent interest as their companion's head was freed.

The rescue attempt ended successfully around 7 p.m., and the animal was unharmed and able to move about freely.

Trying to forcefully free a horse or other large animal is hazardous and could lead to injury to all parties. If you notice an animal, domesticated or wild, which is injured or in other difficulty, call the national help line on 1247 – operators speak English and will provide instructions on what to do, and forward the issue to the relevant authority if needed.

World.title: Pärnu leaders' clash puts coalition at risk
World.content:
Pärnu City Council chairman Andrei Korobeinik (Center Party) accuses mayor Kristel Voltenberg of interrupting a discussion on coalition functioning and of breaking agreements. Voltenberg says the current coalition has exhausted itself.

"​The mayor's unexpected departure from today's coalition council meeting interrupted our discussion about the functioning of the coalition," Korobeinik wrote to his coalition partners after Tuesday's coalition council meeting.

According to Korobeinik, the coalition partner has not adhered to agreements.

"In my political experience so far, I have not previously been in a situation where agreements made with one coalition partner have consistently not held. With other partners we have occasionally had disagreements, and in such a diverse coalition this is completely natural. The difference has been that we have resolved these issues through open, respectful and transparent discussion," he said.

A meeting full of tensions

Korobeinik noted that the position of mayor carries greater responsibility, and if agreements do not hold and discussions on difficult topics end because someone leaves the meeting, the coalition cannot function effectively.

At the same time, Korobeinik emphasized that he considers the coalition agreement good.

"I believe that we can continue this cooperation in one form or another. If you decide in favor of a new coalition, I ask you to proceed from what is best for our city," he added.

Kristel Voltenberg, leader of the electoral alliance Südamega Pärnu, said that she intends to continue as mayor of Pärnu. At the same time, she accused Korobeinik of aggressive behavior and said the coalition has exhausted itself.

"Yesterday's coalition council meeting ended at the moment when it became exceptionally aggressive from the meeting chair, Andrei Korobeinik, and the room became figuratively so tight that there was no space left for any constructive cooperation," Voltenberg said.

"Both I and our electoral alliance Südamega Pärnu have been very cooperative and flexible partners. In politics, making compromises is necessary, especially when shared responsibility is carried by political forces with different worldviews," she added.

She noted that there is a clear difference between compromise and pressure, and she cannot be forced to make decisions based on feelings or pressure without substantive arguments.

Mayor refused to run on Center list

Voltenberg said that things between her and Korobeinik turned sour when the mayor refused to run in the upcoming Riigikogu elections on the Center Party list.

"I came to City Hall in the morning and continue my work as long as it is my time. I have promised to do this with heart and reason, and I will not deviate from that principle," the mayor said.

When asked whether the current coalition has collapsed, she replied: "I would put it this way — the current coalition has exhausted itself in this format."

Pärnu City Council chair Andrei Korobeinik says he is not aware of the governing coalition having collapsed, despite rising tensions between coalition partners.

He confirmed that the dispute began after mayor Kristel Voltenberg declined to run for the Riigikogu on the Center Party list, a move Korobeinik says broke a three‑party agreement tied to the planned handover of the mayor's post to EKRE.

While Voltenberg has said the current coalition has "exhausted itself," Korobeinik maintains that the Center Party has not left the coalition and that talks on forming a new one can begin only once the existing agreement is officially over.

Informal consultations are ongoing

Other coalition partners acknowledge a crisis but say continued cooperation is still possible.

EKRE's Pärnumaa chairman Valmar Veste says the Pärnu governing coalition has not collapsed, though he acknowledges the latest meeting was highly emotional.

Veste said the mayor left the room when key issues still needed discussion, creating a crisis but not a full breakdown. He added that coalition partners remain in contact and that continuing together is still possible, as politics requires compromise.

Siim Suursild, a representative of Isamaa in the opposition, said that sounding out possible other combinations is underway, and Isamaa has received proposals to form a coalition both from the current coalition and from the opposition.

"It is difficult to call these negotiations. Consultations are taking place, but negotiations will begin only when the current coalition has clearly collapsed," Suursild said.

A member of the Parempoolsed belonging to the coalition, Kari Maripuu, noted that the controversy that has erupted is connected to the upcoming Riigikogu elections.

"The Riigikogu elections have begun here in the middle of summer, and that is actually the central point carrying this whole issue. The interpersonal disputes and frictions that have already been stated in the media are all, in one way or another, preparation for the spring," he said.

Maripuu also listed possible new governing coalitions.

"The first combination that has been discussed is EKRE, the Center Party and Isamaa. The second possible combination is the Reform Party, Isamaa and, for example, Südamega Pärnu. The third possible combination also concerns us: the Reform Party, Isamaa, Pärnu Ühendab and the Parempoolsed. These are three realistic combinations," he said.

On 24 October last year, five political forces signed Pärnu's coalition agreement.

According to the agreement between EKRE, the Center Party, Parempoolsed, and the electoral alliances Südamega Pärnu and Pärnu Ühendab, Pärnu's mayor for the first two years is Kristel Voltenberg, leader of Südamega Pärnu, who will be replaced in 2026 by an EKRE representative. Voltenberg will then continue as council chair.

This article has been updated on July 22 with additional comments by Pärnu City Council members.

World.title: Expert: Ukraine's defense changes unlikely to have a 'direct' impact on battlefield
World.content:
Changes to Ukraine's top defense officials are unlikely to have a "very direct impact" on the situation on the battlefield, said security expert Rainer Saks, former secretary general of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2015-2020) and Foreign Intellegence Service (2011-2015).

Last week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy removed popular Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov (35) from his position, which triggered street protests across the country.

Rumours suggesting that Fedorov had lost his job due to a conflict between him and army commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrskyi (60) were later confirmed.

However, on Tuesday, Zelenskyy dismissed Syrskyi (60), replacing him with Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi (43).

ERR: How do the decisions made by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy appear to you? He has dismissed both Defense Minister [Mykhailo] Fedorov and Commander-in-Chief [Oleksandr] Syrskyi. What should we conclude from all of this?

Saks: At the moment, looking at it from the outside, without having been present at the discussions President Zelenskyy has been holding over the past six days, it seems that the government reshuffle was primarily motivated by a desire to resolve the conflict that had arisen between the commander-in-chief of the armed forces and defense minister Fedorov.

It appears that the president initially chose to replace the minister while keeping the commander-in-chief in office. That was the arrangement he tried to implement, but it has now become clear that, for political reasons, it was not feasible. The president's intention triggered very serious protests and a concealed opposition that may not be visible publicly.

The president now realized that he also had to dismiss the commander-in-chief. Although at the very beginning, when he decided not to appoint Minister Fedorov to the new government, he did say once that both of them should actually be replaced. The president either did not realize this or, for some very serious reason, did not wish to do so.

He has now nevertheless reached the point where the commander-in-chief also had to be replaced.

I think this is a process in which the president genuinely set out to resolve the situation because he realized that it was no longer possible to keep Ukraine's difficult situation under control in its existing form if the minister and the commander-in-chief were unable to resolve their disagreements themselves. He may have made a somewhat hasty and political decision that ultimately did not withstand criticism from Ukrainian society.

Was the problem more a difference between generations or a difference in technological approach? Fedorov wanted to introduce more new technologies. What caused this disagreement?

I think the disagreements were more about details than about any broad strategic vision. To claim that Fedorov was in favor of innovation while Syrskyi was against it would be entirely inappropriate.

When General Syrskyi became commander-in-chief of the Ukrainian armed forces in the summer of 2023, he said from the very beginning that to succeed on the battlefield, Ukraine had to surpass Russia technologically. That is the only way to actually defeat the Russian army. It is not possible to create a mass army to counter the Russian army like the one Russia uses or has used up to now.

I would point out that technological innovation is also taking place in the Russian army to some extent. The use of many traditional categories of weapons has almost been abandoned or reduced to a minimum. Instead, entirely new weapon systems are being used, predominantly unmanned systems.

The Ukrainian army cannot wage war in some old-fashioned way, as Syrskyi has been accused of doing, and in my opinion General Syrskyi has not really tried to do so either. I think the issue is perhaps more about style, methods and certain minor issues that gradually accumulated.

Of course, this is not just about disagreements between General Syrskyi and the minister. There were probably also disagreements within the Ministry of Defense itself. Minister Fedorov faced opposition for various reasons. It is noticeable that the procurement processes he initiated departed more from established routine.

Fedorov certainly had many ambitious and innovative ideas that neither the armed forces nor the Ministry of Defense were always able to keep up with. Undoubtedly, this does, in a sense, reflect a generational conflict: some wanted to continue doing things the old way and were not particularly willing to reform themselves, while others came to lead the Ministry of Defense and wanted to change things very quickly. That is how conflicts like these can arise.

I do not think the issue is so much one of strategic vision as the fact that Minister Fedorov wanted to direct almost all available resources toward the use of new technologies and accelerate that process even further.

Perhaps General Syrskyi believed that it was simply not possible to achieve proper results with the army in that way.

Who knows? There may be many more details behind it. Some of these kinds of problems certainly arose even before Fedorov was appointed defense minister.

I think personal character traits or psychological factors may also have amplified all of this. It seems that both Minister Fedorov and General Syrskyi are rather stubborn people. In this case, that may have worked in favor of the conflict.

When we talk about the state of the war and the situation on the battlefield, the Ukrainians actually have very good momentum at the moment. But now that both the commander-in-chief of the armed forces and the defense minister have been replaced, what could this mean for the situation on the battlefield?

It should not have a very direct impact on the situation on the battlefield. Command processes are much more complex and are not so dependent on the day-to-day decisions of two individuals, but primarily on strategic decisions.

If this process had dragged on, it would undoubtedly have had a negative impact on the combat capability of the Ukrainian forces. People would inevitably have become involved in other activities, and commanders in particular would have been drawn into the process in one way or another.

It appears that the choice of the new commander-in-chief should appeal to and suit Ukrainians, at least emotionally. There is no reason to doubt that he is a capable general. In that respect, I would be quite calm, and I do not think the Ukrainian army will suffer any major setbacks simply because of the change in leadership.

It must be said that, in the shorter term, the commander-in-chief is certainly a more important figure than the defense minister. But if the wrong person becomes defense minister, problems stemming from that person's wrong decisions will begin to emerge after some time. That is the potential negative impact if that happens, but if the person appointed is capable of handling the job very well, there should be no problems.

What do you think? Will Zelenskyy give in to public anger and bring Fedorov back after all? I read that he has already been offered new positions, but he has refused them because he believes he could best implement his vision as head of the Ministry of Defense.

Fedorov has sent that signal. He has not said it quite so openly himself, but the former minister should understand that the president of Ukraine cannot appoint him to the position again. Doing so would turn the entire process into a farce and make the president appear completely incompetent as a leader.

I nevertheless think there must have been more substantial reasons why President Zelenskyy initially considered it more sensible to replace Minister Fedorov, who is a very important person to him, while keeping General Syrskyi in office, who is also a very important person to him. Otherwise, the president might have tried to resolve the situation differently.

I think that, from Minister Fedorov's point of view, it is very difficult to imagine that he would now obediently go off like a sheep to become a presidential adviser or take on some other symbolic role. He seems to be a much bigger and stronger personality than has been apparent so far. He is certainly still young and not as experienced in political life.

Nor does President Zelenskyy have any need to push him aside. Looking to the future, he will certainly still need Fedorov. How he will now be able to motivate Fedorov remains a big question.

It is unlikely that Fedorov will start building a separate opposition to the president or anything of that sort. Under wartime conditions, that is not an issue at the moment, but after the war it could prove to be a decision that affects not so much President Zelenskyy personally as his party's chances of succeeding in future elections.

Can you tell us anything about the new commander-in-chief, Mykhailo Drapatyi? He achieved the status of a national hero back in 2014, but after that he also suffered some setbacks. He even resigned himself after one incident.

It is very difficult to wage a perfect war. I would not want to start criticizing him here, but he seems to be a very proactive and decisive, relatively young officer.

He certainly became a general only because of the war with Russia, and his courage in making decisions and his effectiveness as a field commander, as well as a commander of larger formations, became apparent very quickly.

He seems to be very popular because in 2014 it was the actions of his 72nd Brigade that gave Ukrainians hope that, alongside the volunteer units, the Ukrainian army was also capable of carrying out more serious military operations.

One of the criticisms directed at General Syrskyi as commander-in-chief was that he became too deeply involved in the details of specific operations on different fronts. We also saw that General Syrskyi visited frontline areas very frequently and travelled to different sectors.

This illustrates the dilemma: on the one hand, if you do not do that, people start accusing you of not taking an interest in what is happening on the ground. But if you do go there, talk to people and give them guidance, you are accused of interfering.

Strategic leadership is inherently very difficult. I think that over the next six months to a year we will see whether the new commander-in-chief, General Drapatyi, also has that ability or whether it will somehow remain less visible. It is extraordinarily difficult to predict, but at least the army will probably welcome him warmly. He has all the prerequisites to accomplish something together by bringing other commanders into the effort.

What is quite interesting is that when General Syrskyi took office, he had hardly communicated with the public beforehand. General Drapatyi seems to be the same type of person – he apparently does not like speaking publicly at length and in detail about his plans and activities, but now he will be forced to start doing so, just as General Syrskyi increasingly had to speak publicly to explain the army's plans and objectives.

Perhaps the biggest challenge will be how he carries out that role as commander-in-chief and whether he can involve someone else alongside him in public communications.

Recruitment into the armed forces remains the Ukrainian military's weakest point and its biggest challenge. The formation of new units is another issue – Ukraine has struggled more with that than with technological innovation or other aspects.
