Tech.title: States Want ICE Agents to Show Their Faces. The Trump Administration Is Blocking Them
Tech.content:
The Trump administration has sued at least five states and the city of Philadelphia over laws that supporters say would hold law enforcement—including Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers—accountable for misconduct on the job. The specifics of the laws vary, but the Trump administration takes particular issue with the fact that the laws would prohibit ICE officers from wearing masks during immigration raids, and require them to wear some sort of individual identifier.

Having to show their faces, lawyers for the Trump administration argue, would put ICE officers in danger.

In complaints filed against New York, Virginia, Connecticut, New Jersey, and Philadelphia, attorneys for the federal government claim that people take photos of ICE officers to “run them through facial recognition applications that search social media and doxing sites,” specifically calling out an art project called ICESpy. (California was subject to a similar lawsuit months before the other states, but the DOJ did not mention ICESpy in that complaint.)

There's just one problem, according to ICESpy’s creator, artist Kyle McDonald: the art project's face-recognition software cannot recognize most, if any, ICE agents currently in the field.

ICESpy is based on photos, job titles, and names of people who self-identified as ICE nearly a decade ago on LinkedIn. WIRED viewed a version of the list, which had just over 700 entries, and found that the most common title was “assistant chief counsel,” and many of the people appeared to have executive, administrative, or legal roles. Only 39 people on it had “deportation officer” in their title, and an additional 27 had related titles such as “enforcement and removal assistant” or “immigration enforcement agent.”

Many deportation officers joined the agency well after the data was collected. In January, ICE announced that it had more than doubled its number of agents and officers in just a few months, from 10,000 to 22,000. None of those additional people would be in the database, unless they had another job with ICE in 2018 (and posted about it online).

“They make this claim that people are using this site and others to search for family members. They offer no evidence of this in the filing,” McDonald tells WIRED. “The idea that someone could use a site like ICESpy and find an active ICE deportation officer in 2026 is absurd.”

ICE did not respond to a request for comment.

Data issues aside, ICESpy is not popular. WIRED reviewed activity logs for ICESpy between June 30 and July 6, which showed there were only 84 page views that week—a remarkably small number, even for a niche art project website. Only two face-match attempts were made, and the results of both were so bad that McDonald says they could not possibly be a match of anyone in his dataset of 2018 LinkedIn users.

“Like, I'm sure people were playing with it at some point?? But it is not an active threat to ANYBODY Imao,” McDonald says in a text message.

Attorneys for the federal government also blame another site, ICE List, for aiding people interested in "doxing" ICE agents. ICE List describes itself as an accountability initiative, and keeps track of people involved with ICE and other agencies involved in deportation efforts, along with vehicles used on the job and incidents that occur during enforcement actions.

Individual agent pages on ICE List typically include the person’s name and general information about what their job title is, the field office they are associated with, and any incidents they might have been involved in along with links to public sources that corroborate the claims on the page. When WIRED analyzed the site in January, we found that it too relied mostly on data that self-described ICE employees had posted on LinkedIn. It also doesn't have any sort of public-facing way for visitors to try to computationally analyze photos, though some agent pages include headshots.

Tech.title: A Teen Reporter Searched for His Community in the Epstein Files. Adults Freaked Out
Tech.content:
Ben Mueller’s assignment for his journalism class was to tell a news story—any news story—in the form of an extended Instagram slideshow. So when the high school senior got home on the afternoon of February 10, 2026, he grabbed a snack, went upstairs to his room, and settled in to work.

After allowing himself a few minutes of procrastination—scouting prospective college campuses on Google Earth—Mueller navigated over to the Department of Justice’s Epstein Library portal and clicked through the page asking whether he was 18 or older (he was, just barely). Then he began poking around for ideas in the 3 million pages of Epstein files that had been added 11 days earlier.

Mueller really liked working in his bedroom, with its beanbag chair and view of people strolling and biking along one of Marin County, California’s sun-dappled waterways. Having lived his whole life in one of the wealthiest parts of America, Mueller couldn’t help thinking his area probably had some ties to Jeffrey Epstein. “I think it’s very difficult to get an immense amount of money without—this is my opinion—without doing something a little shady,” Mueller says. So he sat on his bedroom floor and spent the next five hours combing the federal database for links to the towns and cities of Marin.

He found thousands. Most of them were trivial (Epstein liked to shop online at Restoration Hardware, headquartered in nearby Corte Madera). But a few things stood out: a 2014 art gala in Sausalito that Epstein helped promote; a meeting with Woody Allen in Tiburon; and—above all—a 2013 email exchange between Epstein and a woman from a modeling agency called Mill Valley Connection. “Regarding Hannah, my Austrian model,” the woman wrote in one particularly chilling message, “we can come and see you this evening if you are interested, and in that case let me know how I can get my fees.”

Two days later, on February 12, Mueller posted his story to the Instagram feed of the Redwood Bark, his school’s student-run publication. It was a carousel-style slideshow pitched at readers across the county. “Which Marin towns were mentioned in the Epstein files?” the first panel reads. “Scroll to see how many times your town was mentioned.” Rather than quote from the most alarming document he’d found, Mueller kept his descriptions fairly general and brief: “Mill Valley was mentioned in the context of providing models to Epstein from a woman named Gisele Attias Bonnouvrier.”

Kids These Days The youngs are facing problems that didn't even exist half a generation ago. They’re handling it better than you think.

More than 4,000 people liked the story. The comments filled up with praise: “This is the kind of journalism we need.” “Higher quality reporting than local outlets.” “High schoolers doing better reporting than national news.” “Didn’t think I’d be following a random CA HS newspaper in 2026 for their breaking reporting but here we are.”

As Mueller watched the numbers climb, he felt excited but also a little perplexed. “I didn’t really think I was doing groundbreaking journalism,” he says. “I was just like, this is another piece of homework that I have to do today, and I’ve just got to get it done—but also be thorough, because people are going to see it on the internet.”

About a week and a half later, Mueller was home sick with a light fever and cough when the phone rang. It was his journalism teacher, Erin Schneider, with bad news. “This person mentioned in your post is now threatening to sue the district,” she said.

On Monday, February 23, Bonnouvrier, the modeling agent, had sent an email to the principal of Redwood High School, calling Mueller’s post defamatory, demanding its immediate removal, and promising legal action if the school did not comply within 48 hours. And now the district superintendent was demanding that the Bark either redact Bonnouvrier’s name or delete the slide entirely.

Tech.title: Flipper Busy Bar Review: An Expensive Focus Tool
Tech.content:
The Busy Bar is a focus tool that blares a bright red BUSY sign. Stick it on your desk, mount it on your monitor, or put it outside your office—the device works as both a productivity timer and an indication that you are not to be interrupted. It costs $250.

It's made by Flipper Devices, the company known for the Flipper Zero—a handheld hacking tool that uses a Tamagotchi-esque Dolphin to monitor and manipulate certain radio-frequency identification (RFID) frequencies. It freaked some governments out enough that they temporarily banned the product. But the Busy Bar is a much quieter device, meant to sit on your desk or hang on your monitor to let people know you’re in the zone and not to be disturbed. It was announced in 2025, and sales kicked off in June. Flipper recently released the open source firmware on GitHub.

The device is small, roughly the size of a sunglasses case. The default screen reads BUSY, but you can swap between themes that change the message on the screen, like “KEEP OUT,” “OUT TO LUNCH,” or “LOW SOCIAL BATTERY.” The bar also works as a digital clock, and for now that’s the only other app on it.

Tech.title: Is the All-New Range Rover GT Stepping on Jaguar’s Tail?
Tech.content:
In what looks to be a radical departure from its existing lineup, Range Rover has confirmed an entirely new fifth vehicle: the Range Rover GT, an all-electric grand tourer built on the company's Electrified Modular Architecture (EMA), the same platform that will underpin other midsized cars for the brand.

Range Rover has only shared camouflaged prototype pictures for now, as the GT is supposedly still undergoing final testing, ahead of a full launch expected later this year. That means details on this completely new model are scant to say the least: no price, no range, and no power figures have been disclosed. As for a release date, Range Rover confirmed the GT hits the road in 2027.

What is evident from the camo images is the GT's sleek silhouette and coupé proportions, more typically associated with Range Rover's sister brand, Jaguar, than with the marque known for its commitment to SUVs. Both companies sit below the parent company, JLR (formerly spelled out as Jaguar Land Rover).

The clean Range Rover GT interior shows a small driver’s display and larger central screen, but the company has shunned the auto industry's return to physical switchgear. Courtesy of JLR

In a statement, Martin Limpert, global managing director at Range Rover, says the Range Rover GT is intended to “redefine the grand-touring segment” with its “GT poise, proportions and long-distance refinement,” adding that the EV will offer “capabilities no conventional GT can match.”

The inclusion of the word “conventional” is doing some heavy lifting. Range Rover will likely take pains in the coming months explaining how this new all-electric grand tourer isn't a direct competitor to Jaguar's new all-electric grand tourer, the hugely anticipated and polarizing Type 01, intended to signify a complete reset for Jaguar, also arriving in 2027.

“We have spent the last few years working obsessively on the fundamentals of the GT formula, reinterpreted in a sophisticated, uniquely Range Rover way,” says Limpert, adding that this GT, like its SUV stablemates, will apparently still be able to off-road. “The result is the most car-like Range Rover ever created. Its blend of effortless EV performance, first-class long-haul refinement, and all-terrain capability is pure Range Rover, while its interior previews our vision of a modern grand tourer.”

Tech.title: Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 Is for Everyone Who Can’t Stop Scrolling
Tech.content:
Samsung has finally made a book-style foldable that’s geared less toward productivity and more toward entertainment. It seems the company has realized that some of us just want a better way to scroll and binge-watch.

The $1,900 Galaxy Z Fold 8 is Samsung’s new baseline book-style foldable, sitting between the $1,200 clamshell-style Z Flip 8 and the top-of-the-line $2,100 Z Fold 8 Ultra, which carries on the design of last year’s Z Fold 7. The phones debuted at the company’s Galaxy Unpacked event on Wednesday, and they’re available for preorder now before hitting shelves on Aug. 7.

With a 4:3 aspect ratio and a passport-sized design, the Z Fold 8 feels equally optimized for watching horizontal videos, multitasking in landscape mode and browsing vertically oriented apps in portrait mode. That versatility and compactness make the Z Fold 8 one of the most enjoyable phones I’ve used so far this year — though I still have some lingering questions I look forward to addressing in my full review.

The boldly reimagined Z Fold 8 arrives at a crucial time, as Apple reportedly gears up to launch its first foldable iPhone in the fall. Rumors suggest that device could also have a squarish 4:3 aspect ratio (similar to some iPad models), so this may well be Samsung’s attempt to stay ahead of the curve. And while Apple’s expected entry will mean fresh competition, Samsung has the advantage of several foldable generations — and years of consumer feedback — under its belt.

“This is Samsung going on the offensive,” Francisco Jeronimo, IDC’s vice president of client devices, said. “By bringing a wider, passport-style foldable to market ahead of Apple, Samsung gets to define the new format on its own terms rather than reacting to it later.”

He added, “With Apple’s announcement less than two months away, this is the first Unpacked where Samsung has to defend the category it created, and that’s why it cannot play it safe.”

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 takes up less space when closed than many other phones. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

What makes the Z Fold 8’s design different

I first got my hands on the Z Fold 8 during a visit to Samsung’s Korea headquarters last month, and I was eager to spend more time with it at this week’s Galaxy Unpacked event in London. The phone feels compact and palm-sized while folded. It’s a welcome break from the monotony of today’s smartphones, including Samsung’s other foldables, which haven’t changed much from last year’s models.

The Z Fold 8 fits snugly in my hand, giving the feel of a small pocket notebook you’d use to quickly jot down notes. It’s simply a fun phone to use because of its size and design. It’s not much thicker than the super-thin Z Fold 8 Ultra, measuring 4.5mm when open and 9.7mm when closed. It’s also the lightest Z Fold device, clocking in at 201 grams.

Samsung EVP Kihwan Kim told me the Z Fold 8 is “very well suited for people who really enjoy media and social networks.” He added that the company “collected a lot of feedback from different types of users” to better understand the needs of people who prioritize media consumption. I can see myself using the Z Fold 8 in landscape mode when watching a movie or browsing across multiple apps, and then rotating it vertically when I’m on Instagram or reading an ebook.

In portrait mode, the Z Fold 8 is great for scrolling through vertical social videos. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Customer feedback also led Samsung to make its new book-style foldables easier to open. That involved reducing tension on the hinge, which causes the phone to spring open. You won’t be able to unfold the Z Fold 8 partway, unlike the Z Fold 7, but it takes noticeably less force to pry it open.

One key spec hasn’t changed: The Z Fold 8 maintains an IP48 rating, meaning it can be submerged in up to 1.5 meters of water for 30 minutes and is protected against solid objects larger than 1mm, but not dust or sand. That aligns with most foldable phones, though last year’s Google Pixel 10 Pro Fold boasts an IP68 rating, which places its resistance to liquids and particles on par with premium non-folding phones.

Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Display upgrades on the Galaxy Z Fold 8

The Z Fold 8 has a 5.5-inch cover screen and a 7.6-inch inside display. Both screens have an anti-reflective coating, which Samsung says can reduce glare up to 50%. Paired with a 3,000-nit peak brightness, it should be easier to use apps and watch shows, even in the bright outdoors. I noticed the reduced reflections even while filming the phones indoors ahead of Unpacked.

The Z Fold 8 uses a new display technology called Flex Titanium. It combines a titanium-alloy film with a titanium plate to create a thinner, more durable display structure that should better withstand drops and other impacts. I watched Samsung put those displays through their paces at its headquarters, offering some reassurance that the screen is designed to withstand everyday use and hundreds of thousands of folds.

Flex Titanium also reduces the display’s crease, a longtime sticking point with foldable phone critics. While I found the crease in last year’s Z Fold 7 to be negligible, the Z Fold 8’s is even harder to notice when using the phone. This could be yet another way Samsung is hoping to beat Apple to the punch, as rumors suggest the foldable iPhone could have a creaseless screen — which could also be made by Samsung Display.

The Z Fold 8’s 4:3 aspect ratio follows in the footsteps of other wider foldable phones like the Microsoft Surface Duo, the first Google Pixel Fold and the Huawei Pura X Max. Notably, the Galaxy Z TriFold also has a 4:3 aspect ratio, albeit with a more sprawling 10-inch main display. The Z Fold 8 reduces that into a more compact design that’s a better fit for people who don’t want to carry around a miniature laptop.

Still, it’ll be an adjustment for those of us who are used to bar-style phones. The Z Fold 7 was one of my favorite devices I reviewed last year because using the cover screen feels remarkably like holding a slab phone. I’m curious to see whether the Z Fold 8’s squareish cover screen will make me more inclined to unfold the phone and use the main display — something I didn’t do very often with the more conventional-feeling Z Fold 7.

Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Battery life gets a boost on the Galaxy Z Fold 8

Samsung has equipped its foldable phones with a higher-capacity silicon-carbon battery. While the Z Fold 7 had a 4,400-mAh battery, which made it through the day but didn’t last much longer, the Z Fold 8 bumps that capacity up to 4,800 mAh. That should hopefully reduce the urge to anxiously check battery levels.

The Z Fold 8 also supports 45-watt wired charging, which Samsung says can get you from 0% to 63% battery in 30 minutes. That’s a notable upgrade from the 25-watt charging on the Z Fold 7, which was one of the phone’s weak points. The Z Fold 8 also supports 20-watt wireless charging, up from 15-watt charging last year. I look forward to testing these faster speeds, which are especially welcome given the high price tag.

Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Cameras on the Galaxy Z Fold 8

One compromise you’ll make when opting for the Z Fold 8 over the Z Fold 8 Ultra is the more scaled-back camera system. The Z Fold 8 has just two rear cameras, a 50-megapixel wide-angle and a 50-megapixel ultrawide. There’s also a 10-megapixel selfie camera on the cover screen and another 10-megapixel camera on the inside screen.

That should be enough for most people, but the lack of a telephoto lens may leave some wanting more. I’m no professional photographer, but I do take a lot of photos, so I’m curious to see whether I’ll miss having a dedicated zoom lens. Hopefully, though, sensor cropping on 2x and 4x shots will feel like enough.

Photo Assist lets you enter a text prompt for how you want to change an image. I asked for sunnier skies. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

AI and processor on the Galaxy Z Fold 8

The Z Fold 8 has a handful of AI updates for the camera, including My FanCam. In videos you’ve shot with several people moving, like a ballet recital or a soccer match, you can choose one person for AI to track. You can also select the aspect ratio, so you can crop a horizontal video for posting on social platforms. It’s a fun feature, though video quality will be compromised as My FanCam zooms in on a subject.

As debuted in this year’s Galaxy S26 series, Photo Assist now lets you enter a text prompt for AI to alter an image to your liking. I tested this on a photo with cloudy skies, which I asked Galaxy AI to make sunny instead. I was impressed with how it even altered the shadows on the building below to better reflect this faux reality, though the brick detail became grainier. Unlike Generative Edit capabilities that let you erase someone in the background of a photo, this feature comes off as a bit more misleading, so I’m not sure I’ll ever really opt for it.

The Z Fold 8 is powered by a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip for Galaxy. That should make tapping into AI features, endlessly scrolling and multitasking a breeze.

Andrew Lanxon/CNET

A new foldable design at a critical time

Beyond its whimsical look, the Z Fold 8 underscores Samsung’s efforts to stay ahead in a category it’s dominated for years. But competition is heating up. Earlier this year, Motorola debuted its first book-style foldable, the Razr Fold.

Apple’s expected entry could give the foldable phones market an overall boost. In fact, global foldable phone shipments are expected to grow 21% year-over-year in 2026, according to Counterpoint Research. Samsung is projected to maintain the top spot with 32% share, compared to Apple’s anticipated 25% share. But the Korean phone-maker will have to keep innovating to maintain its lead, and the Z Fold 8 feels like a deliberate effort to stand out in an increasingly crowded space.

“Competition is good, actually,” Kim told me. “For the last seven generations, we’ve already experienced a lot of things [and received] a lot of feedback from users and the market, and we’ve evolved for those needs. … We’re pretty confident about what we’ve done.”

Now that I’ve spent some time getting a feel for the Z Fold 8, I’m eager to take it out into the real world to see how it fits into my media habits — and whether it pushes the foldable category forward.

Tech.title: Samsung Reveals More About Its Upcoming Google Glasses, Including New Designs
Tech.content:
Back at Google’s I/O developer conference in May, I tried Samsung and Google’s smart glasses, which are expected this fall. At Samsung’s latest phone and watch-focused Unpacked event, a few more details on those glasses have emerged. New frame designs, some promised battery life and specs, and also, how Samsung and Google aim to address privacy concerns with glasses that Meta’s currently facing.

Samsung and Google’s first wave of smart glasses are display-free, but have a camera, microphones and speakers, much like many of Meta’s glasses. Display-enabled versions are also on the way, like Meta’s Ray-Ban Displays, but afterwards. They run Qualcomm chipsets inside, much like Meta’s glasses also do.

The big difference for these glasses is how they support Gemini AI and deep connections to Android phones, along with working with Google Wear OS watches. Samsung’s watches will control the glasses, something I got to try a bit of during a glasses demo in May.

The glasses, as we already knew, are designed with Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. But Samsung showed off two new frame designs at Unpacked, to go with the two already revealed at Google I/O. The four frames revealed so far look good, but from a distance won’t seem much different from Meta’s existing glasses designs. Won-Joon Choi, Samsung’s COO of mobile experiences, confirmed that more designs are yet to be revealed when he spoke to reporters in London before Samsung Unpacked.

The new Warby Parker frame design (Photo by Tara Brown/CNET).

Choi revealed more details about the upcoming glasses in an on-record chat. He said that durability tests for the glasses show better strength than standard eyewear, “multiple times stronger than regular glasses.” Samsung has already filed more than 200 patents filed for its smart glasses tech.

The Warby Parker and Gentle Monster glasses use Qualcomm Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 chipsets, the processor that’s also in Meta’s glasses. The battery life sounds better, though: according to Choi, they can run for 9 hours on a charge (one hour better than Meta’s latest models), and even do that while handling video recording and Gemini Live AI modes, although we’ll see how battery life actually handles in a future review. The glasses case can charge the glasses an additional seven times.

The charging case for the Gentle Monster glasses. (Photo by Tara Brown/CNET)

The privacy problem

The glasses will run both Google Gemini and Samsung Bixby AI, offering at least a bit of a choice compared to glasses like Meta’s. But privacy concerns sound like they’re still at play. Google and Samsung’s glasses will show a recording light when taking photos or videos, but they need to be on your face to work. If the LED is blocked, the camera won’t record either.

But Choi acknowledges that privacy concerns on camera-enabled AI glasses is a shared industry problem.

But this is also, according to Choi, “just the beginning” for where Samsung wants to go with its interconnected wearables. These glasses still use Bluetooth and Wi-Fi to connect. Choi says that “is not enough” for where camera-enabled eyewear needs to be, and that Qualcomm and Samsung are working on future ideas.

The two newly revealed frame designs designs have a pretty familiar-for-smart glasses look (Credit: Samsung)

Better connections for wearables, especially for future higher-bandwidth devices like display glasses or full AR glasses, feels like a must. And even more so when you might have a watch, earbuds and glasses all connected at once. And Choi acknowledged that AI services, too, still need to evolve.

But so do privacy considerations. Samsung’s acknowledgment of the industry problem around glasses privacy doesn’t solve the problem. Choi feels that “if you stop the innovation, you don’t go anywhere,” and expresses confidence that Samsung (and Google) will find a way to “optimize the right solution” going forward. I’m curious to see how Samsung and Google’s AI privacy settings will feel compared to Meta’s. And also, how much better the phone and AI hook-ins will feel in everyday use.

For more, it looks like we’ll need to wait till the fall.

Tech.title: Samsung’s Galaxy Z Flip 8 Gets the Cover Screen Right — for a Price
Tech.content:
Samsung’s Galaxy Z Flip 8, announced Wednesday during the company’s Unpacked event, launches with the price hike we expected, along with a few welcome tweaks to its design and software that could make the phone easier to use.

I got to demo the $1,200 Z Flip 8, and even though that’s a $100 spike from the starting price of last year’s Z Flip 7 for the same 256GB of storage, the phone is noticeably lighter and thinner than prior iterations. Samsung says that at launch, the 180-gram Flip 8 will be the lightest flip-style foldable phone on the market. When unfolded, the phone is 6.1mm thick, which is noticeably thinner than the Z Flip 7 (6.8mm) and Motorola Razr Ultra (7.2mm).

Samsung’s Galaxy Z Flip 8 now lets you add apps with a simple function in the app drawer on the cover screen. Joseph Maldonado/CNET

But I was more impressed by a number of software tweaks coming to the Z Flip 8 that make it easier to use while closed. For starters, you can now add apps to the cover screen by scrolling up on the app drawer and tapping “Add apps” to access any app installed on your phone. Previously, you had to dig through various settings menus to do the same thing. This is also much closer to how the latest Motorola Razr phones let you use any app you want on their cover screens.

The Z Flip 8’s cover screen is also getting the “Recent apps” shortcut button for the first time — which is wild, since quickly switching tasks is such a basic function on the rest of Android. When I test flip-style phones, I’m most likely on the cover screen using Maps for transit directions while playing music and texting friends — that simple button means I can now swap between these directly without having to kick back to the lock screen. That’s also a feature already available on the Razr.

You can now easily switch apps on the cover screen. Joseph Maldonado/CNET

The Z Flip 8 carries over several features that debuted on Samsung’s Galaxy S26 phone line — for instance, the foldable’s video camera includes Super Steady with horizontal lock to smooth out movement while filming. And I had a lot of fun playing with a new camera feature called My Fan Cam, which uses Galaxy AI to identify subjects in a video and create a crop that only follows that person throughout the recording, as if the camera is exclusively focused on them.

Samsung’s My FamCam lets you make videos focusing on individuals within a clip. The center example is the original, while the other two focus on me and my colleague Tara Brown. Mike Sorrentino/CNET

The Flip 8 is powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy — which is the same custom version of the processor used for the Galaxy S26 phones as well as the foldable’s pricier siblings, the Z Fold 8 and Z Fold 8 Ultra, which were also announced at Unpacked.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 has a 6.9-inch display when unfolded. Joseph Maldonado/CNET

Other specs carry over from last year’s Z Flip 7, including the 6.9-inch internal display and the 4.1-inch cover screen. It’s the same for the cameras, which are a 50-megapixel wide-angle, 12-megapixel ultrawide and 10-megapixel selfie camera. The phone’s 4,300-mAh battery, 25-watt max wired charging speed and 15-watt max wireless charging are also the same. We’ll have to see when testing the phone whether the newer processor is efficient enough to improve the overall battery life.

The Galaxy Z Flip 8 in pink, cream and graphite colors. A mint color is also available as an online exclusive. Joseph Maldonado/CNET

The Galaxy Flip 8 comes in four colors: pink, graphite and cream, as well as mint as an online-exclusive offering. The phone goes on preorder today and will go on sale Aug. 7.

Tech.title: Inside Samsung HQ: An Early Look at the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Hints at the Future of Foldables
Tech.content:
If not for the massive “Samsung” display hanging in the vast, minimalist lobby, it would have been hard to tell I was standing inside the headquarters of one of the world’s largest mobile brands.

Safety signs throughout the shimmering steel-and-glass building warned against using phones while walking or riding escalators. I had to reconcile the lack of glowing screens in people’s hands with the reality that I was at the heart of Samsung’s mobile research and development operations in Suwon, South Korea, roughly 20 miles from Seoul. Here, on a sweltering mid-June day, I’d be one of the first people outside the company to see its upcoming foldable phone lineup.

Standing outside Samsung’s research and development building at its global headquarters. Samsung



In a sleek wood-paneled room called the Mobile Studio, I got my hands on three unreleased devices, one of which stole the show. The Z Fold 8, which rumors leading up to its reveal dubbed the Fold 8 “Wide,” has a 4:3 aspect ratio and a palm-sized design. The emphasis on a wider rather than taller layout makes it feel fun and fresh, like a pocket-sized notebook a movie character might pull from their coat to jot down a clue.

The room at Samsung’s headquarters in Korea where we were the first people to learn about the Galaxy Z 8 series. Samsung

Meanwhile, the book-style Z Fold 8 Ultra is the modestly upgraded follow-up to the Z Fold 7 (with a noticeably less prominent crease). The clamshell Flip 8 similarly packs more subtle upgrades to last year’s phone.

But throughout the hour I spent holding and photographing the devices, I couldn’t stop thinking about the Z Fold 8’s bold, squarish redesign. It’s a first-ever move for Samsung, but one that may hint at the future of foldable phones.

You can turn the Z Fold 8 to optimize for the media you’re consuming. Turning it vertically is ideal for watching short-form video. Samsung

A fresh take on the Galaxy Z Fold

Before seeing the Z Fold 8, I wasn’t sure I’d be interested in a device with a 4:3 aspect ratio, since it’s so different from a regular phone. After all, the Z Fold 7 was my favorite foldable I reviewed last year, thanks to its slim profile and a cover display that felt remarkably like a standard slab phone. That configuration helped it land a CNET Editors’ Choice Award.

But after getting my hands on the newly reimagined Z Fold 8, which is around the size of a passport when closed, I understood the appeal. It’s a refreshing, versatile format that appears ideal for browsing through content and watching videos while still being pocketable. The compact size also makes it flat-out adorable; I had to resist the temptation to walk out with it.

I liked using the Z Fold 8’s cover screen to scroll through vertical social videos. Samsung

In portrait mode, the 7.6-inch inside display is optimized for streaming movies, watching YouTube videos and playing video games. Turning it to portrait mode is best suited for scrolling through vertical social videos, browsing the web or reading an e-book. I look forward to using the phone in my everyday life and seeing how often I opt for the inside display over the 5.45-inch cover screen.

“There is not one type of foldable user,” Minseok Kang, Samsung’s head of smartphone product planning, told me. “We found some great opportunities regarding consuming media, including social media and videos.”

The Z Fold 8’s main screen is suited for watching videos and simultaneously reading comments. Samsung

Supplementing rather than replacing a more standard foldable shape, like the Z Fold 8 Ultra, the Z Fold 8 gives people more options. Those willing to spend the most to get the best cameras and battery life won’t hesitate to shell out for the Ultra. If you’re looking for a more versatile configuration and want to try something new, the Fold 8 may be more alluring.

“The new Fold gives you the best of both worlds, both from a productivity perspective, but more so from a content consumption perspective,” said Carolina Milanesi, president and principal analyst at Creative Strategies. “[Releasing the Z Fold 8] now as an extra product versus changing the Fold is absolutely the right thing to do, because there is a market for both.”

Reshaping the foldables market

The Z Fold 8’s 4:3 aspect ratio isn’t entirely new. Several earlier foldables had similarly squarish displays, including the Microsoft Surface Duo, original Oppo Find N and the first Google Pixel Fold, which had a larger 6:5 aspect ratio. Those devices were widely praised for their compact, palm-sized design. More recently, book-style foldables with proportions closer to traditional slab phones have become the dominant design, though there are exceptions like the wide-format Huawei Pura X Max.

That trend may be shifting. Samsung’s latest foldables arrive as speculation builds that Apple could finally unveil its long-rumored foldable iPhone this fall. Leaks suggest it, too, could adopt a 4:3 aspect ratio — potentially signaling renewed interest in squarer foldable phones.

Samsung has previously dabbled in 4:3-ratio territory with the Galaxy Z TriFold. The sprawling 10-inch screen makes it feel more like a tablet than a phone when open, but the broad display is great for multitasking and watching videos. The wide-body Z Fold 8, though smaller, could offer a similarly practical interface for media consumption that’s more comfortable to hold and easier to pocket.

The Galaxy Z TriFrold, which came out in the US in January, also has a 4:3 aspect ratio. Patrick Holland/CNET

“The TriFold is an important milestone for our upcoming innovative devices,” Kang told me. “We introduced that 4:3 display in the TriFold. We learned how much people love to use that kind of ratio in that device, [and] that can be evolved to this new Fold 8.”

The fresh naming convention for the Z Fold 8 Ultra also indicates the way the foldables sector is evolving. Tacking “Ultra” onto the title — while slightly confusing — helps align it with Samsung’s top-of-the-line Galaxy S26 Ultra, with its high-end cameras, larger screen and long battery life. And even if the upgrades over the Z Fold 7 are relatively minor, those who want the best foldable Samsung phone are still likely to opt for it, Milanesi says.

Notably, the rumored foldable iPhone could also be called the iPhone Ultra, helping to position it as a high-end device among Apple’s smartphone lineup. Samsung may be attempting to align its own pricey foldable with that of its competitor — and beat it to the punch.

One big way Samsung has improved the Z Fold 8 Ultra is by reducing the crease, as seen in this comparison with last year’s Z Fold 7. Samsung

Chinese phone-makers have found considerable success in the foldables market globally. But in the US, where Samsung, Motorola and Google are the primary players, Apple’s entry could give us more options while raising the entire category’s profile.

Samsung is likely wary of the competitive threat, Milanesi said, while also recognizing the upside.

“They know that Apple is going to nail the marketing,” she said. “They know that they’re going to put a lot of money behind it and give the category a reason to exist.”

Back at Samsung’s headquarters, I realized I’d gotten an early peek at what could be a pivotal moment for foldables — not just for Samsung, but for the wider category. If Apple enters the race as expected, Samsung’s latest bet could soon face its biggest test yet. Now, it’s time to see how the rest of the world responds.

Tech.title: I Tested the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 for a Week and It’s a Rugged Scene-Stealer
Tech.content:
Samsung’s new rugged smartwatch hasn’t changed much on the outside, but the biggest upgrades on the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 are all hiding inside.

It has a larger battery, more powerful processor and new adventure features to take you from the office to the trails without extra gear. At $700 ($50 more than the original Galaxy Watch Ultra), it’s the most expensive watch in Samsung’s lineup, but it’s also the most durable — and arguably the most interesting.

I’ve spent the past week testing the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, and while the verdict is still out on its long-term features, like health tracking and battery life, it’s clear that it can pull double-duty as both an adventure-ready companion and a luxury smartwatch.

Whether its $700 price tag is justified depends on what you’re looking for. If you want Samsung’s most rugged watch with the biggest battery, brightest display and the most outdoor features, it could be worth the premium. But if the package matters less than the core smartwatch features, you may be better off getting the standard Galaxy Watch 9 (or even older models) for nearly half the price.

The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 keeps the squircle frame, but increases the size and brightness of the screen.

Galaxy Watch Ultra 2: First impressions

The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 looks identical to the original. It has the same premium titanium case, sapphire crystal display, signature squircle design and three programmable physical buttons. But look closer and you’ll notice a few subtle upgrades.

The display is slightly larger (1.52” compared to 1.5” on the original), even though the overall watch is smaller and lighter. Samsung also redesigned the bands, making them thinner and more breathable so the watch sits flatter against your wrist, which the company says improves sensor contact. The new clasp mechanism makes them easier to swap than traditional watch bands, though it also locks you into Samsung’s proprietary system.

A side-by-side look at the two new Galaxy Watches: Galaxy Watch 9 and Ultra 2. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The fact that I slept a few nights without ripping it off halfway through the night says a lot about a watch this size. I still wouldn’t choose to sleep with it long term, but it’s noticeably more comfortable than I expected.

Samsung watches already have the best displays in the business, and the Ultra 2 kicks it up a notch with an even brighter, 5,000-nit display (versus 3,000 nits on the original) that looks flawless even in harsh mid-morning summer sun.

Galaxy Watch Ultra 2’s new trail running and diving features

The Ultra 2 edges closer to sports watch territory with a dedicated trail-running mode that surfaces real-time climb and elevation data, has offline trail map access and hydration reminders. I live near a regional park with hundreds of trail options, and I’ve been frustrated by traditional smartwatches that don’t account for uneven terrain or give me enough credit for tackling extreme elevation changes.

I took the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 on a trail run to test the new feature.

After a 5-mile trail run through the Northern California hills, I was impressed by two things: turn-by-turn audio navigation and real-time elevation tracking. I don’t like wearing headphones when I trail run because I prefer to stay aware of my surroundings, so hearing directions through the watch speaker is the perfect solution. It’s worth noting that getting a route onto the watch for those directions was tedious. Samsung says you’ll eventually be able to search for nearby trails directly from Google Maps, but that feature wasn’t ready during my testing, so I had to load a trail route from a .gpx file on my phone.

With real-time elevation tracking, the watch automatically broke my route into individual climbs and showed my progress. Having a live progress bar as I approach a hill gives me a tangible goal, making it easier to push through steeper sections.

The trail-running feature on the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 shows real-time elevation.

I was less enthused about the hydration reminders. I’d traded my water bottle for my tripod that day, so the three reminders I received during my hour-long trail run mostly fell on deaf ears. Considering the heat, I probably should have listened. But because the reminders are based on AI estimates of hydration loss rather than a dedicated sensor that measures sweat loss directly, I found myself trusting them less.

The Ultra 2 also debuts a recreational diving feature developed in partnership with Italian diving company Mares. Because it doesn’t track gas or oxygen consumption, it’s not meant to replace a dedicated dive computer. Instead, it seems aimed at casual recreational divers who want basic dive information on a device they’re already wearing. The app won’t be available at launch, so I’ll reserve judgment until I can test it myself later this year.

The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 has big changes under the hood, including a new processor and bigger battery.

Galaxy Watch Ultra 2’s raise-to-talk Gemini

My favorite feature, however, has nothing to do with rugged adventure sports. It’s Gemini. I’ve already raved about how useful Google’s AI assistant is on your wrist in smartwatches such as the Google Pixel 4, and the new raise-to-talk feature makes it even better.

No button presses or wake words required, just raise your wrist and start talking. This added layer of convenience made me much more likely to use it and helped me get things done completely hands-free. At the risk of sounding like a trad wife, I use it a lot in the kitchen. I had meat sitting in the fridge that was about to go bad, so I asked for a simple slow-cooker carnitas recipe, and it delivered. I didn’t even have to smudge the screen with meat juice to get the step-by-step instructions read aloud. It’s also been handy for settling debates with my endlessly curious 9-year-old before he loses patience and I have to dig my phone out of my pocket.

Better battery life in theory, in practice its still TBD

The Ultra 2 packs an 800-mAh battery, up from the 590-mAh on the original, paired with Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon Wear Elite processor, which should be more power efficient. On-device AI optimizes battery life as it learns your habits, too. Samsung rates it for up to 60 hours with the watch’s always-on display enabled.

The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 is rated for 10ATM and can be used for recreational diving.

It’s still too soon to know if that 60-hour claim is realistic because my initial results haven’t been great. That 5-mile trail run chewed through nearly 30% of the battery, and I have yet to reach the watch’s promised 60-hour mark. I have gotten closer to 48 hours before needing to recharge, though.

Either way, don’t expect sports watch-level endurance. A Garmin Fenix 8 Pro, for example, can last more than a week on a charge. The Ultra 2 powers a brighter display, Wear OS and always-ready Gemini, all of which demand far more energy than what a dedicated sports watch usually takes on.

Extra health and recovery tools

Both watches also get a new suite of health features, which feed into the redesigned Samsung Health app on your phone.

Vitals tracking can flag possible signs of illness by monitoring metrics such as heart rate variability, resting heart rate, respiratory rate, blood oxygen and skin temperature. There’s also a new Heart Health Score, Daily Cardio Load to help guide recovery, and a Fitness Index assessment that uses AI to build you a personalized training plan.

Many of these features require at least seven nights of sleep before they unlock (which I haven’t yet logged), so I’m holding off on judging for now.

I appreciate that Samsung isn’t putting these health insights behind a subscription the way companies including Whoop and Oura do. Some guided workouts and iFit content still require separate subscriptions, but the core health features are included with the watch.

Samsung also hasn’t confirmed whether these software features will come to older Galaxy Watches. So, for now, they’re another point in favor of upgrading.

The three new Galaxy Watches: Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, Galaxy Watch 9 (44mm) and Galaxy Watch 9 (40mm). Joe Maldonado/CNET

Should you upgrade to the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2?

After a week of testing, the Ultra 2 feels like more of an upgrade than its familiar design would suggest. If you’re coming from an older Galaxy Watch and want the latest hardware with the peace of mind that it’ll hold up to the elements, this is the one I’d be looking at.

But I still have plenty left to test. Many of the health features haven’t unlocked yet, and I need to spend more time with the battery before delivering a final verdict. Battery life, in particular, will make or break my recommendation — both over the Galaxy Watch 9 and for anyone considering upgrading from the original Ultra.

Tech.title: How to Get Rid of Old Tech Without Paying Anything or Throwing It in the Trash
Tech.content:
Wiping your data before dropping off an old device takes about five minutes and is the one step worth doing before anything else. Johner Royalty Free/Getty Images

The decision to finally do something about all your old electronics is usually the hardest part. Once it’s made, the process turns out to be shorter and cheaper than almost anyone expects. Major retailers run free drop-off programs that accept old computers, laptops and printers regardless of brand or condition. Plus, most manufacturers offer take-back programs that cover their own products, sometimes including free mail-in shipping. The only thing that generally needs attention before handing anything over is the data on it, and wiping a hard drive only takes about five minutes on most devices. Here’s how to handle all of it in a single afternoon.

Major retailers such as Best Buy and Staples have become drop-off hubs for digital junk. You can walk into a store with a dead PC or a clunky old scanner and hand it over for free, regardless of where you bought it. Some of these places will even give you a discount on new gear or a trade-in credit just for helping them reclaim the heavy metals and plastics that don’t belong in a landfill. It’s the easiest way to recover your storage space without feeling like a jerk for tossing electronics in the trash.

The only real “work” on your end is making sure you aren’t handing over your entire life history along with the hardware. Before you dump a device, you need to do a legitimate data wipe — not just drag files to the trash can. A 10-minute factory reset or a dedicated drive-scrubbing tool ensures your old tax returns and saved passwords don’t become someone else’s property. Stop acting like you’re going to “fix” that laptop from 2015 and let a professional recycler break it down for parts instead.

What to do before you recycle your old computer

Wherever you take or mail in your items to be recycled, you’ll want to protect your data by removing it as best you can. One way to do this is to perform a factory reset on your computer. Our guide walks you through the process.

Where to recycle your old printers and computers

Some retail stores will accept computers and printers for recycling, but it’s not always a free service. Policies vary by company.

Apple

You can recycle your old Apple computers, monitors and peripherals, such as printers, for free at an Apple store, but there’s a costly catch. According to the Apple Free Recycling program, you must purchase a qualifying Apple computer or monitor to receive this service. Need another option? A third-party company called Gazelle buys old MacBooks to recycle them. After accepting Gazelle’s offer, you print a prepaid label or request a prepaid box and ship the machine to them.



Best Buy

Best Buy generally accepts up to three household items per household per day to be recycled for free, including desktop computers and printers, as well as other items ranging from e-readers to vacuum cleaners. While three is the limit for most items, there’s a higher limit for laptops — Best Buy will take five of those per household per day. Note that rules for dropping off monitors vary by state, and it’s not always free to do so. Best Buy also offers a mail-in recycling service for select items, but that’s also not free. A small box that holds up to 6 pounds costs $23, while a large box (up to 15 pounds) costs $30. One CNET editor recently lugged in an old, nonworking tube TV-VCR combo for e-cycling, and was happy to pay $30 to be rid of it.

Office Depot

Office Depot and OfficeMax merged in 2013. The retailers offer a tech trade-in program both in-store and online, where you may be able to get a store gift card in exchange for your old computers and printers. If the device has no trade-in value, the company will recycle it for free. Office Depot also sells e-waste recycling boxes that you can fill with electronics to be recycled and then drop off at the stores, but they aren’t free. The small boxes cost $8.39 and hold up to 20 pounds, the medium ones cost $18.29 and hold up to 40 pounds, and the large boxes cost $28 and hold up to 60 pounds.

Staples

You can bring your old desktop computers, laptops, printers and more to the Staples checkout counter to be recycled for free, even if they weren’t purchased there. According to a Staples rep, the retailer also has a free at-home battery recycling box, which has led customers to recycle thousands of batteries per week, up from an earlier average of 50 per week. Here’s a list of everything that can be recycled at Staples.

Where to find electronics recycling centers

If you don’t live near a major retailer or would rather take your computers and printers to a recycling center, you can locate places near you by using search tools provided by Earth911 and the Consumer Technology Association.

Earth911

Use the recycling center search function on Earth911 to find recycling centers near your ZIP code that accept laptops, desktops and printers. Note that the results may also turn up places that accept mobile phones and not computers or printers, so you may have to do a little filtering.

Greener Gadgets

Consult the Consumer Technology Association’s Greener Gadgets Recycle Locator to find local recycling centers in your area that will take old items. The search function also allows you to filter the results to separately hunt for places that take computers versus printers.

Tech.title: How to Watch Samsung Galaxy Unpacked: Weird Foldables, AI Glasses and More Today
Tech.content:
Samsung’s last Galaxy Unpacked event was in February in San Francisco. Samsung/Screenshot by CNET

Samsung’s summer Galaxy Unpacked event is happening today, July 22, in London. CNET will be on the ground and ready to see all the new devices the company is gearing up to unveil. Samsung usually showcases new foldable phones at its mid-year event, like the Galaxy Z Fold 7 and Z Flip 7, but this year things might take, let’s say, a different shape. Last week, the company began running Instagram posts teasing a new rectangular form and “new form factors,” the company said in a statement announcing the event.

If you’re ready for what’s next, keep reading for how to tune into Samsung Unpacked today. The event kicks off at 9 a.m. ET / 6 a.m. PT, or 2 p.m. BST for our CNET reporters and others attending the event in London.

Unpacked comes just months before Apple’s annual fall event, giving Samsung time to flex its foldable phone prowess ahead of the rumored launch of the foldable iPhone in September. Though Apple’s been rumored to have been working on an iPhone Fold for years, I’ll believe it when I see it. It’ll be interesting to watch what Samsung does with its latest generation of foldables in the meantime.

Samsung’s next Galaxy Unpacked event is in London on July 22. Samsung

We’ll be on the ground in London to see everything that Samsung has to offer, but for those of you impatient to wait, the rumor mill has been churning with predictions about which new devices might be revealed, like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Wide and Z Fold Ultra. We could even see Galaxy smart glasses. Let’s dive into what the rumors suggest we’ll see.

How to watch Galaxy Unpacked

Samsung’s event will be livestreamed on Samsung’s website and Samsung’s YouTube channel, beginning at 2 p.m. BST local time on July 22, which is 9 a.m. ET or 6 a.m. PT. That’s pretty early for US viewers (remember, the event is in London), so set your alarm clocks if you want to be the first to see what Samsung unveils. You can watch the company’s livestream below:

Galaxy ‘wide’ foldable

The Galaxy Z TriFold isn’t the only odd-shaped foldable Samsung has been apparently working on. Patrick Holland/CNET

Samsung is currently in its seventh generation of Galaxy Fold devices, and we expect that both the Z Fold 7 and Z Flip 7 will be refreshed with new processors, a few other tweaks and the number eight on their packaging. But it seems that the company’s designers might be getting bored, as they’ve experimented with the folding form factor enough to bring new designs to market.

We’ve already had the wild Galaxy Z TriFold with its tablet-sized display released back in January, and now rumors suggest a wide version of the Fold that packs a 7.6-inch inner display with a 4:3 aspect ratio. That’d make it wider and narrower than the current squarish, almost 1:1 aspect ratio of the Z Fold 7’s internal screen, which would theoretically make the new foldable’s inner display better for watching movies, with less wasted space for black bars at the top and bottom.

There’s expected to be a more “regular” version of the Z Fold 8, which is said to follow the proportions of the Galaxy Z Fold 7. However, rumors suggest it will be rebranded with the “Ultra” moniker to differentiate it from its wider-format (and potentially less powerful) sibling.

Galaxy XR Glasses

Samsung and Google’s glasses have already been announced, but we’re still waiting on more details. Scott Stein/CNET

Google talked for some time about its mixed reality glasses at its I/O event earlier in the summer, including showing off Samsung’s upcoming glasses made in partnership with Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. But details about the glasses themselves were a bit thin, with the extent of Samsung’s role held back — likely for the summer Unpacked event.

So while we know the glasses exist — and CNET’s Scott Stein has already tried some prototypes on — we’re excited to hear more details. The glasses will feature cameras and microphones (how else will you interact with Google’s Gemini AI?), but we don’t yet know how much they’ll cost or exactly when they’ll go on sale.

There’s likely to be more talk about features and usability at Unpacked, and I’m hoping it’ll have a fancy try-on section where I can pop some on my face and see whether my wife can still stand the sight of me.

Galaxy Watch 9 and Watch Ultra 2

The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 might be unveiled at Samsung’s event. James Martin/CNET

Rumors fueled by firmware updates and certification filings suggest Samsung will showcase two new smartwatches at this year’s Unpacked event. The Watch Ultra 2 — the company’s more rugged, outdoor-focused model — is rumored to get a huge battery boost up to 800 mAh. That’d be the biggest of any Wear OS watch and should help it keep on tracking your wilderness hikes long after your legs have given up from exhaustion.

The Galaxy Watch 9 is also rumored to get a bit of a battery boost, along with both models featuring new processors and potentially refreshed designs.

Galaxy Ring 2 — but probably not

Samsung has confirmed its working on a new Galaxy Ring, but it might be too early to see it this summer. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

According to Forbes, Samsung has confirmed that it is working on the Galaxy Ring 2, the follow-up to its 2024 finger-based health tracker. The company’s next ring is expected to get a boost in battery life, feature more advanced tracking and likely come with a refreshed design.

But it’s worth noting that while the ring might be in active development, it likely won’t get launched at July’s Unpacked event. While I wouldn’t be surprised to see a teaser of some kind, it’s likely that Samsung would unveil its next Galaxy Ring either at CES at the beginning of 2027 or at Mobile World Congress shortly after.
